sentence.sent_text: Mii geget sa mii dash omaa noongom o’o nindinendam apiitendaagwak chi-mazina’iganiing miinawaa akina izhitwaawininaan Anishinaabewin.
Geget sa azhigwa dash dibishkoo mino-mashkikiwan akina gegoo ingashkitoomin omaa noongom keyaabi odaapinigaadeg geget sa o’o manido-miinigowin mii sa geget omaa.
Mii wenji-apiitendaagwak o’o.

paragraph.text_eng: So here now, I will talk a little bit more about the Anishinaabe way of life in a respectful way here. We remember the same as what they did long ago, those knowledgeable and adept ones. I too, I wish for this still. In the future our young people will do just as they did long ago, and me too. I am happy, as I too am able to remember what they did at that time.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash omaa noongom omaa bebang!
azhigwa dazhindaan imaa o’o Anishinaabewin weweni sa go omaa.
Mikwenimang eh wiinawaa gekendaasojig miinawaa wiinawaa waawiingeziwag mewinzha gaa-ichigewaad.
Geniin bagosendamaan weweni sa go keyaabi.
Niigaan keyaa oshki-Anishinaabeg omaa waa-izhi-doodamowaad dibishkoo wiinawaa gaa-izhi-doodamowaad mewinzha mii miinawaa dash omaa geniin omaa.
Minwendamaan azhigwa dash geniin keyaabi gashkitooyaan da-mikwendamaan gaa-izhichigewaad iw wapii.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what I am going to say now. Indeed today, I know only a little bit here, and also this; some Anishinaabe people, they always used this word carefully, he said, “naniizaanad,” and also this word, “onjinewin.” This is what some of the knowledgeable people said; it is just like judgement. If the Anishinaabe people go around somewhere, its just like the spirits are making a decision. This is what the young people must go out and do; it has to be correct. If he does not do it correctly at this time is where this, “onjinewin” will happen. Today, I am begging that this is why the tobacco Anishinaabe carries is so important; he should use his tobacco firstly.

sentence.sent_text: Mii o’o waa-ikidoyaan azhigwa dash omaa noongom.

Geget sa omaa noongom geniin omaa bebangi, bebangi ningikendaan mii miinawaa dash o’o aanind Anishinaabeg o’o ikidowin ogii-ayoon azhigwa dash weweni sa go apane gii-ikido, “naniizaanad,” miinawaa dash oo ikidowin, “onjinewin.” Mii o’o gaa-ikidowaad aanind gekendaasojig mii geget sa dibishkoo inaakonigewin.
Mii sa geget dash omaa azhigwa ingoji wii-izhaad imaa Anishinaabeg nandawenjiged mii geget sa dibishkoo manidoo gaa-inaakonigewaad.
Mii o-waa-izhichigewaad oshki-aya’aag geget sa weweni sa go.
Giishpin gaawiin izhichigesii o’o geget sa i’iwapii onjinewin ezhiwebak.
Mii geget sa omaa noongom ninaandootaamaage geget sa weweni sa go mii wenji a’a apiitendaagozi o Anishinaabe asemaan geget sa aakawe wii-aabaji’aan.

paragraph.text_eng: So indeed, if somebody is to harvest a deer he will do just as the ancestors did. Andevery now and then these young people will distribute to the elders this venison, and rice, and also fish, if this young person is able to. Everything that they had given to the elders, everything that has been received, this is what the knowledgeable ones said. And so, I too sometimes will give my fellow Anishinaabe and elders these things— venison, wild rice, and Anishinaabe sugar; these various things I try to give to our fellow Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Mii geget sa azhigwa dash giishpin awiiya wii-nisaan waawaashkeshiwan geget sa i’iwapii weweni sa go waa-izhi-doodang dibishkoo imaa gete-aya’aag doodamowaad mii miinawaa dash naaningodinong miinawaa dash wiinawaa weshki-aya’aag wii-maada’ookii mii miinawaa dash wii-miinaa gichi-Anishinaabeg o’o waawaaskeshi-wiiyaas miinawaa Anishinaabe-manoomin miinawaa gaye gigoonyan mii geget sa giishpin gashkitood a’aw oshki-aya’aag geget sa gewiin azhigwa gete-aya’aag geget sa i’iwapii.
Gakina gegoo gaa-miinandwaa weshki-aya’aa wiinawaa gichi-aya’aag geget sa i’iwapii miinawaa dash odaapinigaadeg o’o mii sa geget o’o gaa-ikidowaad wiinawaa gekendaasojig.

Mii dash geniin naaningodinong mii wii-miinaan niiji-Anishinaabeg miinawaa gichi-aya’aag gegoo waawaashkeshi-wiiyaas Anishinaabe-manoomin miinawaa Anishinaabe-ziinzibaakwad anooj gegoo wii-kwajitooyaan geniin da-miinaa wiiji-Anishinaabeg.

paragraph.text_eng: And also here nowadays I sometimes ask the old ones here at Lac du Flambeau, “What they did long ago, and how is it that you all are able to have a long life?” So indeed, this is what I am asking the elders here at Lac du Flambeau. And I too get my little bit of knowledge; this is how I have come to know things. And so the elders here in Lac du Flambeau are very knowledgeable, and still today are highly regarded. Certainly here nowadays, I too always do just like my father and mother did in how they lived their lives; always visiting the elders so that they could know the Anishinaabe way of life. This is a little of what I am saying here.

sentence.sent_text: O’o dash omaa noongom gagwejimagwaa pichi-aya’aag omaa Waaswaaganiing naaningodinong, “Aaniish gaa-izhichigewaad mewinzha aniish wenji gashkitooyeg da-ginwenzh bimaadiziyeg?” Mii geget sa o’o gagwejimagwaa gichi-aya’aag omaa Waaswaaganiing.
Mii dash omaa noongom omaa mii wenji bangii omaa geniin gikendamaan mii oo de-bi-gikendamaan.
Mii dash omaa gichi-aya’aag omaa Waaswaaganiing niibowa ogikendaanaawaan mii miinawaa dash weweni sa go omaa keyaabi ishpendaagoziwag gichi-Anishinaabeg.

Mii geget sa omaa noongom geniin weweni sa go pane mii wenji pane geniin dibishkoo nibaabaayiban miinawaa nimaamaayiban gegoo dibishkoo gaa-izhichigewaad azhigwa dash gaa-izhi-bimaadiziwaad pane gii-mawadisaan gichi-aya’aag nawaj da-gikendaanaawaan o’o Anishinaabewin.
Mii dash noongom omaa eta go bangii omaa gaagiigidoyaan imaa.

paragraph.text_eng: My late father’s name was Moi-ye-kamig, and my late mother’s name was Inaate’ebiig. So indeed that is how they lived while they were here, and indeed this is the reason why I am trying do just as they lived. Truly, once in a while they went out during the summer. They fished with a rod and reel, and we were always laughing as they caught various fish there. Definitely here today I still remember what we did at that time, and here now we are merely speaking only a little of it today.

sentence.sent_text: Moi-ye-kamigiban izhinikaazo indedeyiban, miinawaa dash Inaate’ebiig izhinikaazoban nimaamaayiban.

Geget sa weweni sa go gaa-izhi-bimaadiziwaad azhigwa omaa ayaawag mii geget sa mii wenji omaa geniin wii-gwajitooyaan imaa da-doodamaan dibishkoo wiinawaa gaa-izhichigewaad azhigwa gaa-izhi-bimaadiziwaad.

Mii sa geget naaningodinong gewiinwaa ge-gii-izhaawaad imaa mii ke imaa niibiing azhigwa dash gii-wewebinaabiiwag geget sa apane ingii-paapidimin azhigwa dash anooj giigoonyag wiinawaa gaa-debininaawaan azhigwa gii-giigoonikeyaang imaa.
Mii geget sa geget sa go omaa noongom geyaabi mikwenimaa gaa-izhichigeyaang i’iwapii mii dash omaa noongom ajina eta go gaagiigidoyang omaa noongom geget sa omaa noongom geniin.

paragraph.text_eng: Thank you, I say as you all listen to me here today. I also wish, all of the young people will receive long Anishinaabe life, strength, and good health.

sentence.sent_text: Miigwech, indikid azhigwa bizindawiyeg geget sa dash omaa noongom.
Geniin bagasendamaan gakina oshki-aya’aag niikaan keyaa gewiinawaa gaye waa-izhi-odaapinowaad giinwezh Anishinaabe bemaadiziwin mashkawiziwin mino-ayaawin.

paragraph.text_eng: And also these young people will once in a while go to where the elders are, and at that time they will visit with the elders, so they will know more of the Anishinaabe way of life. And that is all I am correctly trying to say. Once again, I thank all of you, and I am wishing that you were able to know my words, and also what it is that I have said here today. Thank you, thank you again, that is it, that is it, that is it.

sentence.sent_text: Mii miinawaa dash gewiinawaa gaye weweni sa go naaningodinong wii-izhaawaad imaa mii keyaa eyaawaad gichi-Anishinaabeg geget sa i’iwapii dash owii-izhi-mawadisaan gichi-Anishinaabeg nawaj gikendaan o’o Anishinaabe bimaadiziwin.
Mii eta kina gwayaak-ikidoyaan.

Mii azhigwa mii dash geniin miigwech gidagoon miinawaa dash omaa noongom nandoodamaagen gii-gashkitooyeg da gikendaanaawaa indikidowinan miinawaa dash gaa-ikidoyaan azhigwa gaagiigidoyaan imaa noongom.
Miigwech, miigwech miinawaa mii iw, mii iw, mii sa iw.

paragraph.text_eng: Okay then, okay then. So lam going to be talking about someone, the Tan-bird. That one who is tiny or small bird, he was tan. When he was born, he was not taken care of, he was not cared for. He was orphaned; he was discarded. He was an orphan because he did not listen. He did not listen.

sentence.sent_text: Nahaw, nahaw.
Na’aa sa nii-debaajimaa, Zaa’aa-bineshiis.
E-gachiiyet bineshiis, zaawzi.
Pii, endaadzid agaa’yi agii-naagadwe-enjigaasii, agaa’yi agii-naagadwe-enjigaasii.
Agii-iwebinaa, agii-iwebinigaaza.
We-binigaa maaba agii-awe zaam agaa’yi apii-bizinzii.
Agaa’yi agii-bizinzii.

paragraph.text_eng: Okay then, then he had to reside or be alone, all alone. It is hard when one is alone. In spite of this, he tagged along with his fellow bird flock. But in spite of that, he found it difficult to fend for himself. He found it hard. Instead then, instead then he stole food. He stole from his fellow birds, the birds’ food. He stole everything, this Tan-bird. He also stole their beds, those nests. And on top of that he was very quick. He did not listen. He would listen to no one.

sentence.sent_text: Nahaw, mii sa aabidek agaa-zhin-chikeyozit, chike.
Zaganot dash chikeyozing Aanawe gwa nopinakii wiiji-bineshiin baa-nopinanad.

paragraph.text_eng: So then at one time, it came to be, that he was to speak to his Maker, the Kind-spirit. “Okay then, how are you little bird? How are you Tan-little-bird?” said this Kind-spirit.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa ngooding, aabidek azhinaagwak awii-ge-ginonad Mindoman, Gizhe-manido.
“Nahaw, aaniish naa ge-gii-bineshiish?
Aaniish naa ge-gii-Ozaawaa-bineshiis?” kida, sa ge’eh maaba Gizhe-manido.

paragraph.text_eng: “Ooh, it is not too good,” so answered the Tan-bird. “I am always scrounging for food; I am always hungry, and also alone. I am always by myself; I am always alone.”

sentence.sent_text: “Ooh, agaa-gwa kitchi-nezhizino,” azhin-da-kwen tam ge’eh maaba Ozaawaa-bineshiis.

Chike pane bi-miyaa, chike pane bi-miyaa.

paragraph.text_eng: “Ooh, ooh,” the Spirit stated. “Ooh, oh, well then, for sure you are going to have to find a way to start getting along with your fellow birds,” responded then this Kind-spirit. “This is what must be done, this coming of age, this growing up,” so that is how the Kind-spirit responded to him. So then he departed, that Kind-spirit then returned to where he came from. I do not know where he came from, but he returned to that place.

sentence.sent_text: “Ooh, ooh,” kida sa ge’eh maaba Manido.
“Ooh, oh aanhshnaa, aabidek sa gwa ka-daa-zhichige ge’eh agii-na’yii waa-zhi-mina-gwa-mad kwii-ji-maadis kwii-ji-bineshii’ik,” kida gay’yi-maaba Gizhe-manido.
“Mii-aabidek waa-ezhichigekeng.

paragraph.text_eng: He just barely left, that Kind-spirit, and Tan-little-bird then resumed to his old ways. Full of mischief, a prankster, a nuisance. He deliberately does things to provoke others. He was bad, but not without purpose.

paragraph.text_eng: Over there where the birds always lived, at the nests over there, over there at the nests, so over there is where he went to harass, He would throw those small birds out. He would throw them out of the nests. When these who are responsible for these little birds returned, they gathered up their off-spring. They put them back in their nests, their homes, and while at the same time, also drive him out. “Tan-bird, get out of here, go away! Do not come back!” So again this Tan-little-bird would be chased away.

paragraph.text_eng: So then the Kind-spirit returned. Okay, so the Kind-spirit had arrived. He then relayed a teaching. Then this is what the Kind-spirit says, “Okay then, what color you shall come to be I shall give to you now, what you shall always look like, what shall be a pleasant colored plumage. That is it, what I am going to give at this time now,” said this Kind-spirit. He announces to the bird species, the feathered ones, then this, “And so it will be known where you belong, from which species you are born, from where your roots are, where you belong. That is how you will be able to self-identify,” said this Kind-spirit, “And so at dawn, in the morning at dawn is when I shall return.”

paragraph.text_eng: This one little bird who is tan was absent. He was out there causing mischief; he was not there. He is a nuisance, teasing. He really liked to play with water; he really liked playing with water. He sprinkled it about over there. He would hit his fellow birds with water. Probably everyone he did that to, the birds, the creatures, the insects, probably everything he could get to or see he found a way to tease. He even teased the snakes, even the snakes he would tease, or he would really hurt them. He would cause them pain, which is how mischievous this Tan-little-bird was.

He is very red up front, brightly colored, he is so pretty colored.

paragraph.text_eng: And then a yellow-colored one, yes, the one that is really truly yellow-colored arrived. And at the end of his wings, over there at the end of his wing tip, it was colored black. They are black-tipped, those wings. Oh does he ever look nice too, is he ever an impressive color. Everyone is happy, everyone is so proud. They are all impressed.

So that is why we now call it the White-bird, then that is also what you shall be named, White-bird. That is it, he is white all over. Oh he is also very beautiful. They all are beautiful.

paragraph.text_eng: He is so impressive to look at, this bird, he looks so beautiful. So then it came to be that he finally completed this task, this Kind-spirit. He had done his task for all the birds.

paragraph.text_eng: “You are all beautiful; all of you are brightly colored. You shall live a good life that is how you shall feel. As the color that you are is the way you shall be.” So then every departed. These birds they are so very happy. And then even He returned to wherever He came from.

paragraph.text_eng: “Well then there is nothing that I can do,” said the Kind-spirit, “Not on purpose. paragraph.text_eng: “Okay,” replied this little bird, “okay.” But he does not fully believe the Kind-spirit. “I think he is deceiving me,” thinks this the little bird. Oh, but he abides this time.

paragraph.text_eng: The Spirit arrived again. “Okay then, this is what shall be of good the life to you. This will be your talent. You shall sound very good. You shall sound very good. aapiji kaam taanigam.

paragraph.text_eng: “Ooh” this little bird ponders. So he began singing, he began to bring forth song. Oh, and he is so pleasing to the ear, so very much so. It is so pleasing the way he makes his song, and everyone listens. Anyone that can hear him listens; they try to mimic his sounds. They arrive singularly and in groups, his fellow birds. His fellow birds listen. They listened to this song. They listened to this song, how this one bird can sound so good.

sentence.sent_text: “Ooh,” naanaa agaa-odwengaan maaba bineshiis.

paragraph.text_eng: In the morning one time he plays one tune. When the sun is mid sky, up high, when that sun hangs in the middle of the sky, he would begin singing again, but he would sing a different song. In the west when it becomes dark, when it becomes dark they can still hear him. Those sounds that he makes are so pleasing to hear. Morning, half day, when it becomes night, that is it.

sentence.sent_text: Kizhep baa-gaak gooding goop gooding winamaaza.

Kizhep, aapto giizhagak, nenaakshik, mii wi.

paragraph.text_eng: He is so very happy to open his eyes in the morning, this little bird, and everyone that hears is of good heart. Everyone’s thoughts are pleasing when they hear the little earth-colored bird sing. Midday is the same, and evening is the same, a variety of sounds this little bird would make.

sentence.sent_text: Miigwech endam doskaabdoobat kizhep maaba bineshiis, miinawa kina awaya e-nondang aapiji gwo nowanagooze.
Nanendam, noondwat.
Nendan nagamoonet maaba akii-aazi bineshiis.
Naakwek mii go naasap, inaakshik mii gwa nasaap, nonj agii-namaazimaaba bineshiis.

paragraph.text_eng: He no longer makes mischief. He uses his gifts; he sings. He no longer plays mischief, no longer is a trouble maker; he no longer teases or antagonizes. Although he is of the same color, earth-colored, he is no longer associated with that trouble-making color. He respects, he respects that gift he was given for his life. He sings, he now sings. He is very happy.

sentence.sent_text: Gaa’ii geyaabe agii-zhendowgzisii.
Aadaa’aan adankaazan maanda ezhi miin egwe’ewzit negamwa, gaa’ii gii-owzhing didowgzasii.
Gaa’ii geyaabe pogadasii, mii shii gwa bezhik gwa enaadzid kiiowza.
Agaa-shwiigwe enaadzid, e-zhiyaasiiyaabe.
Minaadendan, we e-zhik shke’ezid ge’e gaa-zhinmiinin bimaadziiwin.
Nagabanamo, maaba naagam.
Kitchi-nendam-pii.

paragraph.text_eng: He is no longer hungry. He no longer has to steal. He is able to provide for himself. In the evening before he retires, he gives thanks for the things he was able to complete or do this day. So that is it, up to this time, up to this time you probably hear this bird. He sings morning, midday, in the evening, and any time after he finishes eating when he is very pleased.

sentence.sent_text: Wiisanit gay’i yabipkadesii.
Gay’i gaachiam gaa-bigamootsii.
Shki-damaadzii wiwii minitsad.
Nenakshik, wanizagaakii eni, e-nizigaakiin pii miigwech endamnik azhiksheazid nongwa depiichego.
Mii dash wi, biineshagwe nongwa, biinashagwe nongwa ganoodoo aadik maaba bineshii.
Niigamoo kizhep nakwek ninakshek, miinawaa gwa minjigo pii goosh ko woiisinid kitchi-nenadam.

paragraph.text_eng: That is what the Spirit, the Kind-spirit, gave to this bird, the ability to sing, the gift of sound. The sound, the sound that is his own sound, that is his own, this little bird. Today you all hear this sound. During the summer sometimes at night I hear that, over here. In the morning, very early morning I can hear him from afar, this little earth-colored bird. I go outside; I go stand outside to listen to him. I hear him; I hear him; I smile; then I smile. I smile when I hear him.

sentence.sent_text: Mii wi Manido, Gizhe-manido agaa-zhimiinat endash shki bineshiien nigamwen, nwewin.
Nwewin, nowe’e jidigoon we’e maaba bineshiis wi.
Nongwa naa’ewe nigamwin nwewin.
E-pii-ji-niibing e-naanagwodnong niibaadamik nondane, maampii.
Kizhep, kitchi-kizhep noon deptoon noodooon maaba bineshiis e-kiiaadzid.
Nzaagajiin tam gwa kojing donaanibwo e-bisidowak.
Noondowa noondowa, zhoomiin gwen dash, zhomiin gwen.
Mii gwe ezhi zhoomiin gwen yaa nondak maaba pii.

paragraph.text_eng: So this one that was so mischievous at one time, so this is what I think about, this story, about this little earth-colored bird. How he also was cast out; nobody wanted to be around him. When he came to see what he was capable of, and had the skill in applying his skill, he helps, assists his fellow living creatures. He now lives the right way, and also like myself. When I hear this little bird, I hear these songs; I feel so very good. I have good thoughts; I smile. So this is how this little bird’s life changed. He is no longer mischievous; he is gifted instead. Instead he is eager to help out his fellow beings. He is going to change lives at least one time during the day. That is it. That is what happened one time. So we have come to the end this telling. That is what happened one time. Okay.

sentence.sent_text: Maaba sa agaa-zhiingendozing gooding, mii zhoomin kwedima, tabaajowen maanda nii’ii aansokaan, maaba e-zhowzid bineshiis.
Ge’eh-ing gooding, agaa-mizhiaanwenmin aazhinigaazit.
Pii yaang dang e-zhikshezit nakaazit wi e-zhik shke’ezin.
Naadawon wiijib maadziin, nongmazid maaba, miinawaa dash, dash koodniin.
Nonda gwa maaba bineshiis, nondaanin endaa nigamwenan, aapiji shkom minizhayaa.
Nmino-nendam, nzhoomiingwen.
Mii dash maaba agaa-zhiase bimaadziwin maaba gooding agaa-zhigedows.
Gay’i geyaabe zhiigendowsasii, miinagwe ooze meshkoot.
Meshkwoot gandamaademowin wiijim maadsiid.
Wii onj to nan bimaadziwin, wi kina ge’eh goong, gooding epiiche giizhigo.
Mii wi, agaa-zhwe ebang gooding.
Mii sa ekosing wandan dimajamowin.
Mi we agaa-zhwe ebang gooding.
Nahaw.

chapter.eng_title: The Elder Woman Who Raised Me

paragraph.text_eng: Also that old lady that raised me was indeed an elder. She wasn’t able to go out and about; all she did was rice all the time. And she also did blanket making, sewing; she was a skilled seamstress, that old lady sewed everything by hand.

sentence.sent_text: Aw gaye minidmooyehn gaa-nitaawigi’id geget mii gichi-aya’aawi aw.
Gaawiin ogii-kashkitoosiin ingoji da-baa-izhaad, mii eta go gii-manoominiked apane.
Mii dash wiin gaa-izhichiged apane gii-waaboyaanike gii-kashkigwaaso gii-nitaa-gashkigwaaso a’aw mindimooyenh iniw gaa-izhi-michi-gashkigwaadang gegoo.

paragraph.text_eng: She made a lot of blankets and moccasins, things that the Anishinaabe uses; that old lady was always was making things.

sentence.sent_text: Niibowa ogii-ozhitoonan waabooyaanan miinawaa ge iniw bashkwegino-makizinan aw Anishinaabe ayaabajitood, niibowa ogii-ozhitoonan apane mindimooyenh.

paragraph.text_eng: And I used to watch her tan hides, when she worked on deer hides. First she would soak them; I’m not sure how long she would soak them, and she would make a hide-scraper and also everything that she would use. I’m not sure how to call that knife she used.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa ge ingii-kanawaabamaa ko gii-aseked, waawaashkeshi-wayaanan gii-tazhiikawaad.
Akawe gii-agonjimaad namanj minik gaa-agonjimaagwen miinawaa gii-ozhitood iw jiishaakwa’igan akina gegoo waa-aabajitood iw gaye.
Amanj gaa-izhinikaadamogwen iw mookomaan gaa-aabajitood.

paragraph.text_eng: Up until she had finished a deer hide, after smoking it, when she was done with the hide, that is when she would start to make all sorts of things. She made bags and buckskin moccasins. That old lady made everything, and she made blankets.

sentence.sent_text: Biinish igo gaye gii-kiizhi’aad iniw waawaashkeshi-wayaanan gaa-ishkwaa-giikanaamozowaad, gii-kiizhi’aad iniw waawaashkeshi-wayaanan, mii iw apii gii maajitaad gii-ozhitood anooj igo.
Ogii-ozhitoon gegoo gijibayi’ii mashkimodan ge ogii-ozhitoonan miinawaa bashkwegino-makizinan.
Akina gegoo ogii-ozhitoon, miinawaa gii-waaboyaaniked aw mindimooyehn.

paragraph.text_eng: After all, they were always having dances. Today there are still dances all the time. She made blankets and her offerings she would use in the dance hall, she made them. That old lady didn’t sit around for nothing. You see, that old lady was also a great cook.

sentence.sent_text: Aaniish naa, apane gii-niimi’idiwag.
Geyaabi go noongom niimi’idi wag apane.
Waabooyaanan gii-ozhitood miinawaa waa-aabajitood waa-pagijigejin imaa niimi’idiwigamigong gii-ozhitood ge.
Gaawiin anishaa gii-nanaamadabisiin aw mindimooyenh.
Nashke, ge gii-nitaa-jiibaakwe aw mindimooyenh.

paragraph.text_eng: And that old lady also used to make a lot of medicine. She made different medicine all summer long. She asked me to help her with that kind she used to use; she showed me how it looks and where I went to pick whatever it was that she wanted to use. There used to be a lot hanging from the rafters, all around our house, bags of medicine hanging all over that that old lady had. That is another one of her things she did.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa ge a’aw mindimooyenh niibowa ko ogii-ozhitoon iw mashkiki.
Bakaan mashkiki ogii-ozhitoon gabe-niibin.
Gii-kagwejimid da-naadamawag o’ow dinowa waa-aabajitood iko gii-waabanda’id ezhinaagwadinig gaa-izhaayaan idi gii-o bakwajibidooyaan wegodogwen waa-aabajitoogwen.
Niibowa ko gii-agoodewan imaa ishpiming imaa endaayaang giiwitaa-aya’ii gaa-izhi-inagoodeg mashkimoodan mashkiki minik gaa-ayaang aw mindimooyenh.
Mii ge-wiin ge bezhig gaa-inanokiid.

paragraph.text_eng: And there was that old man when he used to go out into the woods somewhere, “Come on my son, come along with me!” When I would go along with that old man in the woods, he would point it out for me, “This is a good one here.” And when he saw another one over there, “This is a good one here.”

sentence.sent_text: Nashke aw akiiwenzii ko ingoji megwayaak gii-paa-izhaad, “Ambe ningwis ingwis baa-wiijiiwishin!” Gaa-baa-wiijiiwag akiwenzii megwayaak gaa-baa-izhinoo’amawid iw, “Mii iw wenizhishing o’ow.” Miinawaa ge ow bakaan iwidi ani-waabandang, “Mii iw wenizhishing o’ow.”

paragraph.text_eng: I didn’t pay attention to him; I just played around. Sometime after becoming a man, that old man passed away. So then I moved to where he lived, that old lady was still alive.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin ingii-paamitawaasiin eta go baa-dazhitaayaan.
Ingoding sa gaa-ininiwiyaan gii-ishkwaa-ayaa aw akiwenzii.
Gaa-izhi-izhigoziyaan idi gaa-taad geyaabi aw mindimooyenh gii-pimaadizi.

paragraph.text_eng: One time some Anishinaabe people stopped by to ask her, “Please, do you have that?” whatever it was that they asked that old lady for. “Yeah hold on,” she said. Then one Anishinaabe that stopped by told me, “Go pick that for me!” I don’t know how she referred to it.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding gii-pi-noogitawag imaa Shinaabeg bi-gagwejimaawaad, “Indaga gidayaan ina iw?” Awegodogwen iidog gaa-nandodamawaagwen mindimooyenh.
“Haw bekaa,” ikido mindimooyenh.
Gaa-izhi-wiindamawid bezhig Anishinaahe gaa-pi noogitaad imaa “O-bakwajibidamawishin bina i’iw,” namanj gaa-izhi wiindamogwen.

paragraph.text_eng: “I don’t know what kind it is,” I told him.

sentence.sent_text: “Haa namanj sha niin ingikendanziin wegonen dinowa iw,” ingii-inaa.

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh!” After they had driven off, that is when that old lady chewed me out. “That is why that old man took you into the woods, to teach you all of those things, all of those medicines.”

sentence.sent_text: “Ooh!” Gaa-ni-maajiibizowaad mii apii aw mindimooyenh gii-mimigwamid.
“Mii gaa-paa-onji-izhiwinik aw kiiwenzii idi megwaayaak baa-gikinoo’amook akina gegoo iniw mashkikiinsan mashkikiwan.”

paragraph.text_eng: See when someone came over, I didn’t know it [what medicine], she scolded me good.

sentence.sent_text: Shke dash imaa awiiya bi-noogitaad mii gaawiin ge ingikendanziin.
Ingii-naniibikimig sa go.

paragraph.text_eng: It turns out that is why that old man went with me over there, to teach me. I was busy playing around.

sentence.sent_text: Mii ingwana gaa-paa-onji-wiijiiwid aw akiwenzii oodi da-baa-gikinoo’amawid.
Ingii-ondamiz niin wii-paa-dazhitaayaan.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what that old lady did; she made a lot of medicines. I know some of them,a little bit, but not much. Okay.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iw gaa-izhichged aw mindimooyenh ogii-ozhitoon niibowa mashkikiinsan.
Aanind igo bangii ingikendaanan, but gaawiin dash igo aapiji.
Ahaw.

paragraph.text_eng: Greetings, my name is Barbara Nolan. Before I was married, my name was Head-front-wing. I am from South Bay, that’s what it was called. Over there on Spirit Island, over there at the Bay of the Beavers, far from the Bay of the Beavers. That place where the Anishinaabe were was called South Bay.

sentence.sent_text: Abozho, Barbara Nolan ndizhnikaaz.
Nagaanagone kwa jiibwa niibweyaan, giizhinkaaz Nagaanagone.
Iing ngii-binjibaa Dooganing, gii-zhinkademagat maanda.
Minido minising odi, Wiikwemkong oodi, waasa piish Wiikwemkong.
Dooganing gii-shinkaade odi Nishnaabek gii-yaa’aat.

paragraph.text_eng: We were raised over there. I was raised by my grandfather and grandmother. My grandfather’s name was John Simon and my grandmother’s name was Nancy. I remember them, and they very much lived a traditional lifestyle. Traditional Nishnaabe, real Nishnaabe, they always spoke the Nishnaabe language, also we spoke the Nishnaabe language. No one spoke English, nobody. Later when I was five years old, me, that’s when we were taken to the big school, where we were going to be taught. That is where we were whipped for speaking Nishnaabe language. We were there for four years, and then we went back to South Bay.

sentence.sent_text: Geniinwi odi ngii-binji-kwognigwomi.
Yaa dash gii-bi-koganigoog nmishomis miinwaa nnookomis.
Shaanziimo gii-zhinkaaza nmishomis, miinwaa Nancy gii-zhinkaaza nnookamis.
Nmaamninenmaag dash ko gondag, aapiji go gii-Nishnaabeyaadziwag.
Nishnaabek, we’eni go Nishnaabek, pane ngii-Nishnaabemook, geniinwi kina ngii-Nishnaabemi.
Gaa’ii gwaya gii-Zhaagnaashiimsii, gaa go gwaya.
Baamaapii e-naanaboonagisiiyaanh, o naanaboon e-ninaanaboonagisiiyaanh, niin, mii gii-maadjiinagowaang gchi-kinomaagegamgong waa-nji-kinomaagoziiyaang.
Mii odi, ngii-pshizhegwomi Nishnaabemiiyaang.
Niiwo-bboon eta odi ngii-yaami, mii dash gii-pskaabiiyang miinwaa odi Dooganing.

paragraph.text_eng: Iremember my grandfather; he was a very good worker. There was always food for us to eat at home. He got it right there, where we lived. For example deer, we ate deer. We also ate fish. Fish, we ate all kinds of fish. Also partridge, I dont know how it sounds, something like this. We also ate those partridge. Rabbits, we also ate rabbits. There are no moose there, no moose there on Spirit Island, not a one. Not until over on the mainland, that’s where the moose are. We did not eat squirrel. Yes, we used to eat seagull eggs. Do you know that white bird? White bird, seagull, over there on the water, he is a noisy one. We used to eat seagull eggs.

sentence.sent_text: Nmaamninenmaa dash nimishomis aapija maaba gii-ntaa-nokii.
Miijim pane gii-temagat endaa’aang waa-miijyaanh.
Mii dash go zhwe’e gaa-ndinang, gaa-dnakiiyang zhe, gaa-ndinang waa-miijyaang.
Dibishkoo gwa naanh, waa’aashkesh.
Waa’aashkesh ngii-mwaanaa.
Yaa’aa ge ngii-mwaanaa giigoonh.
Giigoonhik no’onj zhizhnaagziiyook giigoonhik gaa-mwongit.
Miinwaa bine, bine manjiidig enwe egwenh wa enikiiyaa.
Bine.
ngii-mwaanaanik go gewiinwaa ge’ek binek.
Waabooz-oog, waboozoonh-iik ngii-mwaanaanik.
Gaa wii odi moos yaasii, gaa wiiya moos odi Minidoo Minising, gaa go gwaya.
Baamaapii oshtoodi kitchiking.
Mii odi moozoog yaa’aad.
Kaawiin chidimo, ngii-mwaasiinaa.
Enh, oo ni’iin ge ngii-miijnaanin kwa gaayashk waawnoon.
Kii-gkenmaa na owa waabshki-bineshii?
Waabshki-bineshii, gayaashk, nbiing odi.
aapija go mbiigzi owa.
Gaayaashk waawnoon ngii-miijnaanin kwa.

paragraph.text_eng: And so, I remember this time of spring. Spring is when my grandfather used to leave, well then later, when the snow melted. Well into spring when there is no more snow; there’s no more snow. That’s when they left rowing by boat. They left by rowing, him and Jerome, that was my brother’s name. He went with my grandfather. They would leave. They would go to the other side over there, that bay; there is a bay here in South Bay. There at the mouth of the bay, that’s what it’s called, that’s what it does. So that’s where the bay flows out. So that is where there are big cliffs. Theres a big cliff there, and there’s water there.

sentence.sent_text: Ni’ii dash nmaamninendaan maanda pii minokamik.
Minokamik mii kwa nmishomis gii-maajaat.
Aashinaa baamaapii, gwa naa goon bmi-nigizat.
We’eni go minokamik, ga’ii geyaabi goonkaasno.
Gaa’ii geyaabi goonkaasno.
Mii ko gii-maachiikozhowet jiimaaning.
Gii-maajiikozhowe, wiin minwaa Jerome gii-zhinkaaza n’wiikaane.
Gii-bbaa-wiijiiwaan ne’en nmishomsan.
Maajaa-oog dash.
Mii odi zhaa’aat aazhwiiying odi, maanda go naa wiikwedoong, wiikwe’aa zhonda Dooganing.
Odi dash aabideg zaagadowaang azhinkade odi zaa-azaagada.
Mii odi nazaagiiyejong.
Mii dash odi kchi-giishkaapkaag.
Giishgaapkaa odi.
Mii dash go maa biish tek.

paragraph.text_eng: And so there is an abundance of rock cuts, these large stones. That’s where those seagulls are, the seagulls, those white birds who frequent the shore. That’s where those eggs are. Nests, theres many nests there. That’s where they used to go, my grandfather and Jerome. They’d go over there. They would use buckets, a bucket. He’d place the bucket down carefully. Those eggs were very large in size. Not small, they were not small, not like a chicken. The chicken, their’s are this size. This seagull’s eggs are much bigger. Maybe they are this much bigger. And so they were gathered, and they were placed right here in the bucket. Lots, maybe two, maybe four, four of those buckets. They’d put them there, go back to the boat and place them there. Then they’d return and so then they would return over there.

sentence.sent_text: Maanda chi-msiniin giishkaapkaa dash.
Mii odi gwanda gayaashkoog, gayaaskgoog ge’e yaapshkizjig beneshiiyag jiigabiik e-tazhiigagejig.
Mii odi waawnoon temagag.
Saswinan, niibina saswinan odi tek.
Mii-dash kwo odi gonda gii-zhaa’aad, naa’aa nmishomis minwaa Jerome.
Bbaa-zhaa’aad oodi.
Ni’iin dash gii-nakaaznaa’aan kikoon.
kik.
Kikoon mii nengaatch kii-tood, maangminagaanoon age ne’en waawnoon.
Gaa’ii gaachiinh, ga’ii gaachiznoon, ga’ii naasaap baakaakwenh.
Ow baakaakwenh, maanda ngokwaadigenan.
Maanda gayaashk waanoon mchaanoon waashme.
Gnomaa ge gwa maanda nogmingaadigenoon ne’en Mii-dash ne’en gii-moozhaginmowaad maampii kikoong gii-toonaa’aan ne’en.
Niibina, maa ge niish, maa ge niiwiin, niiwin ge’ek kikoog.
Mii zhe’ne’en towaad.
neyaab dash odi jiimaaning ne’en da-toonaa’aan.
Mii-yaa pskaabiiyaad, bskaabiiyoog, mii-dash ko odi.

paragraph.text_eng: These eggs were not fried. Okay, like in a frying pan. Or maybe, they didn’t cook those eggs like that. They’d boil them. They’d set up a fire for this outside over there They’d set up, they’d make a fire, and so right here this one stick would be placed there. So that’s where the pail would hang. They’d put water and those eggs inside there. So this fire, the fire, and so the boiling would start. That’s how they’d cook the eggs in the spring. Maybe one more month, they would do that. We used to eat those; today I don’t eat them. So this is how I remembered them.

sentence.sent_text: Gaa’ii nondan waawnoon gii-zaasgokwaajikaadesnoon.
Nahaw, dibishko go naa zaasagwookwaan.
Maa ge ga daa nii’ii, gaa’ii nikeyaa gii-zhi minozasiinaa’aan ne’en waawnoon.
Gii-oonzaanaa’aa ne’en.
Maanda gii-naapkistonaa’aa shkode kojing odi.
Gii-naapkischige-oog, gii-boodwe-oog.
maampii dash bezhig maaba mtik gii-naakshimagaaza.
Mii-dash odi gii-goojing ow akik.
Mbiish gii-toonaa’aa zhe biinji’ing miinwaa dash ne’en waawnoon.
Mii zh’kina gii-namigo.
Maanda-dash shkode, shkode, mii maanda gii-maajii-owindek.
Mii wi gaa-zhi-mnasmowaad ne’en waawnoon mnokamik.
Geyaabi go gonamaa ngo-giizis, mii ji-zhichigeyaad wi.
Ngii-miijnaanin dash ko ne’en, nongwa niin gaa’ii miijsiinan.
Nii’ii dash ngii-maamninenmaak gonda.

paragraph.text_eng: This person, my grandfather, before he’d leave, before he’d go get the eggs, he would smoke the pipe. First my grandfather would always load the pipe early in the morning. Early morning, before the sun peeks, before dawn that’s when my grand-father did his pipe. He smoked that pipe in a good way. He always smoked the pipe. He’d make fire outside. So, this is what he used to do, my grandfather, my late grandfather.

sentence.sent_text: Maaba go naa nmishoomis, jiibwaa ni-maajaat, jiibwaa zhaad odi waawnoon naadid.
Ntam, pwaaganan agii-zagaswaanaan.
Pane gwa gii-biindaakwe nmishomis gchi-kizheb.
Gchi-kizheb, maanda go odi giizis jiibwaa bi-zaagiingwenad, jiibwaa biidaabang, mii wi pii gaa-biindaagwed nmishomis.
We’eni ne’en pwaaganan zagswaanaan.
Pane maaba pwaaganan gii-zagaswaanaan.
Pane gojing oodi gii-toon shkode.
na, mii dash ko gaa-zhichaged maaba nmishomis.
Nmishomsiba.

paragraph.text_eng: Also, he held tobacco in high regard, tobacco. He always had tobacco in his pocket, he also always took with him his pipe wherever he went. He took his bundle iwth him the bundle where he put his medicine. His own medicine that he made, Nishnaabe medicine. Pipe, tobacco, cedar, there was everything there, sweetgrass, everything that was medicinal, that which is medicine he took it with him, and he had sage with him halso. He always budled this up to take it with him. He always carried that tobacco. He held that tobacco in high regard. That’s what I first remembered when I was asked to speka here. Oh, when they used to get those seagull eggs, right about this time, no not about this time, maybe in another month. That’s what they always did.

sentence.sent_text: Nii ii ge’e semaan aapiji gii-kchipiitenmaan, semaan.
Pane semaa mii-biindaagnowaan, pane ge gii-bbaamwinaan ne’en doo-pwaaganaman.
Gii-maajiidoon shkibchigaanhs, shkibchigaanhs mshkiki tood, Nishnaabe mshkiki wiin go naa.
Pwaaganan, semaa, giishkaandag, kina go zhe, wiingash, kina we go zhe meshkiiyong, emishkiikiiyong gii-maajiidoon wi, miinwaa mshkodwoshk ge go zhiwe gii-toon.
Mii dash maanda pane gaa-wiikwejiipadood.
E-maajiidood ge’ii wi.
Pane go gii-bmwinaan ne’en semaan.
Aapii gii gchipiitenmaan nmishomsiba ne’en sa semaan.
Mii wi n’tam gaa-mjimenmaanh meanda ggwejmigowaanh wii-giidowaanh zhonda.
O gaayaashko-waanoon ko gii-naadowaad maanda pii o’o gaa’ii wii go maanda pii, gnomaa ge geyaabi ni-ngo-giisagak.
Mii gaa-ntaa-zhichgewaad wi.

paragraph.text_eng: And also when it got warmer, before summmer at this season change between spring then summer, right about here, they used to go deep into the woods. They would go into the woods over there and go get that birch bark. There were a lot of birch trees that stood there. It is such that he would do the same thing, he would take that tobacco along. Well he’d do pipe ceremony early morning before he’d start. He always smoked pipe, and then he’d put that tobacco out there, offering. We never knew wey grandfather did that: well, we were kids; grandfather took his tobacco; we never knew about things like that when we were children.

paragraph.text_eng: So when they used to get that birch bark over there, they never took all the birch bark. Maybe a ladder would be leaned on this one tree over there. They would cut that tree. They’d cut the tree then they’d peel the bark. They’d peel that bark, and then they’d throw that down on the ground. When this would fall there, it would still look like this, It’d fall over there.

paragraph.text_eng: Often it would be wet just like water, as if there was water on it. That which was there still looked like that, it looked like this as it was laying on the ground over there. He’d tie it; they would tie them.

paragraph.text_eng: These trees that stood there, they did not take bark from every one of the trees, “No, this one. Yes, this one, no. That cutting, if you clear all your hair off. Not these trees, that was not done to them, those trees there. Only one here, this one no, this one here, this person no, this one here, right here no. That’s what they used to do. If they peeled too many of them, all of them, my goodness, all the trees that are here, would probably die. These trees would be cold, as they would have no coats. Also you are taking away something. You are taking away his coat. If you take only this one, not that one, every once in a while that’s what they used to do to these trees.

paragraph.text_eng: They made use of everything that grows, just like in the early summer, or, yes, in the beginning of summer. We used to pick strawberries. The strawberries were not big, those strawberries, they were very small. Over there, the wild strawberries, they were over there in the wild. That’s where those strawberries grew. They were very small. So that’s what was done. It depended on the tobacco. We would be given it, well, oh well, we were girls. We were given tobacco, and so wed put down tobacco. And so, not until then, could you go pick strawberries, or go pick blueberries, or go pick raspberries, whatever was there, not until then, until you put down tobacco. First, you must offer down tobacco. One time my grandfather said, “If you take something from the earth, if you take something, you must put something there in return with something.” That’s what we did. First we’d offer, “Thank you Kind Spirit,” so that we could have something from the earth.

paragraph.text_eng: So it was the same for hunting. If grandfather went hunting, that is what he had to do. He did pipe ceremony, using his tobacco; he always took his tobacco with him out looking, while looking for those deer. That is what he had to do; he had to put down his tobacco. He would ask this way: he would hope that the deer would give his life so that he could live, this deer to give up his life. That’s what he always used to say. That is what is meant by requesting; he would ask; he”d request of that deer to give up his life for him. So that is how they requested.

paragraph.text_eng: That's where that came from, to say requesting. That is what I remember this here my grandfather. He really lived the traditional life; he was of a traditional lifestyle. Always silently, by himself. He didn’t tell everyone, just alone, he did it by himself.

paragraph.text_eng: He was good at fishing too, my grandfather, he would go about fishing very well. In the fall, and right in the spring, sometimes almost all winter, he would set nets, this net. So then he’d go home. In the morning again, when it was morning, he’d load the pipe, pray, always with tobacco. He’d take that tobacco. And so then over there, where hed go get the net, he’d put down the tobacco, there in the water. He would offer that tobacco praying, and then he’d leave.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what I remember from when when my grandfather used to go about fishing. He knew a lot. He knew when he should go fishing, He knee whee he should set out nets, when the fish would get caught. In the spring and in the fall, that’s when these big fish would be caught, also all winter, when the water was cold. In the summer the water would be too warm. These fish would not taste good because the water is too warm,” he said. Not until the fall, all winter until early spring, but not during the summer. Only certain ones, maybe the smaller fish like the bass, bass, the bass that has a big mouth, and the small bass, or perch, these kinds of fish could be caught in the summer. Not these larger fish, supposedly, the water is too warm. They would not come near anyway. Over there, these larger fish go farther away in the summertime. The water’s too warm; they would not like it because of the water being too warm. We used to do this also, my grandfather used to always do this. That is all the meat we used to eat: deer meat, fish, rabbit, partridge. This is the kind of meat we ate.

So that is where we used to plant, planted those potatoes, or carrots. Not too many, just enough. Turnips, some of the things we’d plant. We had to take care of the garden. We had to weed.

paragraph.text_eng: Also sometimes too, we had to do the potato bugs. We used to take a little pail. Wed take that little pail, and he’d put coal oil in there, it’s called coal oil, just a little. He used to use a coal-oil lantern so we’d have light by lamp. That’s what he used to put in that little pail. He’d put in coal-oil, just a little, a little. We had to take that little pail and go over to the garden, in the garden over where the potatoes grew. Those little bugs, we had to go over and remove them, place them in these little pails, in the little bug pails. Because these little bugs, when there’s many there, they’d eat everything, and so the plants would spoil. So we had to go look for all the bugs here, in the potato garden. We used to plant many potatoes, We used to store things away in the fall. We used to harvest all that we planted, That is where we got all that we needed to eat. We hardly used to go to the store. That store was far away.

sentence.sent_text: Miinwaa naadgondoong oo aabideg ge gii’e pinii-mnidooshensag.
Yaa’aash ko ngii-maajiinaanaa kikoons.
Kikoons gii-maajiinaanaa, ni’ii dash ko zh’e gii-toon maanda gikii-bmide, giikii-bmide zhinkaade wi, bangii.
Nii’ii ko gii-nakaazan giikii-bmide waaskonenjigan wii-waaskonek waaskonenjigan.
Mii dash ko zh’e gaa-tood wi kikoonsing.
Giikii-bmide gii-toon, bangii go naa, bangii.
Niinwi dash, aabideg o kikoons nii-maajiinaanaanh mii-dash odi gtigaaning zhaa’aang, gtigaaning, mii dash odi gondag piniig enji-zaakiiwaad.
Minidooshensag, aabideg nii-oo-maanaanig, maampii dash kikoonsing nii-saanaanig.
Minidoshens kikoonsing.
Zaam goondag minidooshensag baatiinwaad zh’e kina go gegoo miijnaa’aa, mii sa banaadag wi gaa-zaakig.
Aabideg dash nwii-bbaa-ndowaabnaanaanig kina minidooshensag maampii, pinii-gtigaaning.
Niibina wii go pinig ngii-gtiganaanig kina minidooshensag maampii, dagwaagik.
Kina ngii-bbaa-daapnaanaanh kina gegoo gaa-gtigaadmaang.
Mii go zh’e kina gaa-dinmaang waa-miijyaang.
Gchi we’iikaa daawegamgoong ngii-zhaami.
Waasa ge wi daawegamig gii-te.

paragraph.text_eng: also remember this; although they were prayerful, my grandfather and grandmother always went to the church. There used to be a church standing there; they’d go there, come back. We used to smell something. That was smudging, he’d use medicine; my grandfather could fix anything; he always did that. We’d smell that when wed come in from playing outside, coming in then. It smelled good, that sage when it was burned. If someone was sick, if someone was real sick, or perhaps should someone die, my grandfather would go there and give medicine to them. Return-to-health medicine is what it was called. He used to make that return-to-health medicine, I don’t know what he used to use, but he used to use that return-to-health medicine.

sentence.sent_text: Ni’ii dash nmakwendan, aanwi go aanwi, gii-ntaa-namaa’og, nmishomis miinwaa nnookamis pane gii-oo-namawag namegamgoong, namegamik odi bdaksing.
Gii-zhaawag oodi, gii-pskaabiiwaad.
Niinwi dash wii gwa, nbiijmaandaanaa gegoo.
Mii wi pkwenensgeng mishkiki dankaazan.
Wegdigwendig go daa-naawtoon nmishomsiba, pane gii-zhichige wi.
Nbiijmaandaanaa dash wi bi-biindge aang gojing giishpin bbaadamnoyaang, bi-biindeg’aang dash.
Esnaa mnomwaagwad, ni’ii mshkodewashk skagaadeg ko.
Giishpin gwaya aakozid, giishpin gwaya gchi-aakozid, nowaa ge go gwaya ndaa nibwa, mii maaba nmishomis zhaad, mshkiki, da-oo-mna’aan ne’en.
Aabiziichigan zhinkaade.
Gaa-zhitood kwa Aabiziichigan.
Gaa’ii ngii-gkendziin gaa-nakaazat, Aabziichigan dash ko gii-nakaazan.

paragraph.text_eng: Also for the women to be strong after having a child, after having a child, it was called Esigamdeg. It was black, and it was sticky that Esagimdeg, as it was called. Boy that tasted bad. It was good though, very good that Esigamdeg. That was supposedly for someone to gain their strength back if their blood is weak, this here Esigamdeg, if one teaspoon, one teaspoon. It was very good that Esigamdeg; me, I would throw that up. That is one thing that I remember that used to be made. They used to make that.

sentence.sent_text: Miinwaa ko kwe wii-mshkoziid binojiisan shkwaa yaawaad, shkwaa yaawaad binojiisan, nii’ii Esigamdeg gii-zhinkaade ko.
Gii-mkadewaamgad, gii-bzigwaa ge’e Esigamdek gaa-zhinkaadeg.
Taak, taak ezhi-maanaaj-pogwak wi.
Gii-nishin shwii gwa taak gaa zhi-nishing Esigamdek.
Mii giiwenh owi owaya wii-mshkoziid giishpin i miskwiim niinmadnig, wi miskwiim, maanda Esigamdek, giishpin ngod-emkwaanens, ngod-emkwaanens.
Niin wii geniinh ndaa-shagwaadaan wi, aapji dash gii-nishin wi Esgamdek.
Mii wi bezhik mekwendmaanh gaa-zhichigaadek kwa.
Wiinwaa gii-zhitoonaa’aa wi.

paragraph.text_eng: They also had great regard for bear grease. Ooh, bear grease was good. The bear was never shot. They would never kill that bear. Sometimes if he heard that someone has killed a bear, they would go there. They cleaned all the fur and gut that bear, so that they would take the grease. They would melt that grease and would mix something in it. I do know that they would mix in, spruce; they’d also use something from the pine tree. That’s why you can smell pine sometimes in that medicine.

sentence.sent_text: Miinwaa gii-kchipiitendaanaawaa mko-bmide.
Ooh, gii-nishin mko-bmide.
Gaa’ii wiikaa gii-baashkzigaasii mkwa.
Gaa’ii wiikaa gii-nsaasiiyaan ne’en, mkwan.
Naadgondoog shwii gwa giishpin noondang waya gii-nsaad mkwan, mii oodi gii-zhaa’aad.
Gii-pkwanaa’aan ne’en mkwan, kina go biwyay pkwanaa’aad ne’en wi dash bmide mii wi gaa-daapnamwaad.
Mii yi’ii gii-ngizaanaa’aa wi bmide miinwaa nonj go naa gegoo zhe gii-dgonaanaa’aa.
Ngii-kendaan wii gwa zhagoobiinsan zh’e gii-dgonaa’aan, naa’aa ge zhingwaa-mtig, zhingwaak, ge’ii zh’e gegoo wii-dningaade gaachigat.
Mii enji-biijmaagog zh’e zhingwaak naadgondoong gbiijmaandaan gibiich maandaan zh’e mshkikiing.

paragraph.text_eng: They’d make liquid drink from it, it was sticky. It is good that medicine, if someone is sore, or if someone cuts himself, he would use that. Then you would not see anything from the mishap. It was very good, that bear grease. Also, if someone has a sore throat, or has a bad cough, or if they’re sore here in the lung, if something is happening there, they’d spread it on along the back. Someone would recover quickly.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-naabookaadaanaa’aa, gii-bzigwaa go wi.
Nishin wi mishkiki, giishpin gwaya gaagaagiidzid, maa ge giishpin gwaya giishkwondizad, mii wi nakazad.
Ga’ii gegoo zh’e gdaa-waamdaziin, waya wiisgishing.
Aapji gii-nishin wi mko-bmide.
Ni’ii ge gwa giishpin gaagiijgwandaagang gwaya, maa ge gchi-sasdang, maa ge zhonda gaapaagiidzid, maanda biipiishden gegoo gnomaa daa-zhiyaamgadni, daa-shoonaan manpii ge’ii boknaang daa-shoongaade.
Gwetaani-we’iib mi mnoyaad waya.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s how my grandfather lived. He had respect for everything, everything, everything that grew. He never wasted anything. He never killed a deer for no purpose. Everything was plentiful. Sometimes, he’d catch many fish. He would put that fish in a wooden box. He’d put them away. Then he’d leave travelling, he’d put the wooden boxes in the back. He’d leave then, by horse. He’d give the fish away. Here’s the fish, already gutted, all these fish spread out. He’d take them over there where an old woman lived, distribute a few, and he would continue on. Everyone was given a little of something, whatever it was, fish, seagull eggs, deer meat, or rabbit meat, whatever. If we had a lot, we’d give some away. He was very sharing of everything that we had. Not him, he did not keep it all. He gave it away; he gave fish; he gave dear meat, everything. It was not only for him. He Kept just enough for us, just enough to sustain us. Well ave 90m e ned e three of us children then, and over there were a few people whom he gave some to.

sentence.sent_text: Mii maanda gaa-naadzid nmishoomsiba.
Kina go gegoo gii-gchitwaawendaan, kina go gegoo, kina go geoo e-zaagiik.
Gaa go wiika gegoo gii-binaachigaadesnoo.
Gaa’ii wiikaa nishaa gii-oo-nsaasiin waa’aashkweshwan.
Pane niibina gegoo gii-temigad.
Niibina giigooniin naadgondoong gii-debnaan.
Nii’iing chkoo gii-saan ne’en giigooniin msagaako-mkakoong, gii-zgagnaan.
Mii dash zh’e gii-maajiidaabaangwad, skweyaang gii-toonan ne’en msagaako-mkakoon.
Gii-maajii-daabaangwad, bezhigoogzhiin.
Gii-maamaamiigwenan dash nondan giigooniin.
Maampii giigooniin, zhaazhi go gii-pkazhaaye, kina zhonda giigooniig swe’aabkishnoog.
Gii-maajiidimaaged ooshta oodi mdimoyen endaad aanind gii-miingaaza, maajii-daabiid miinwaa odi.
Bebebangii kina waya gii-minagaaza gegoo.
Wegdogwendig go-giigooniin, gayashko-waawnoon, waa’aashkesh wiiyaas, maa ge waaboos wiiyaas, wegwendig gwa.
Giishpin niibna yaamaang niinwi, gii-miigwenaa ko.
Aapiji go gii-ntaa-maadookii kina gegoo e yaamaang.
Gaa’ii wiin kina, gaa’ii wiin kina gii-gnawendziin.
Gii-miigwen, gii-miigwen giigooniin, gii-miigwen waa’aashkesh wiiyaas, kina go gegoo.
Gaa’ii wiin.
We’eni eta gwa minik waa-debseaang, mii wi minik gaa-gnawendang.
Mnik eta niinwi waa-debseyaang.
Aanshnaa ngii-nswimi, binoojiinyag miinwaa oodi aanind gii-yaawag ge’iinwaa aanind gii-miingaazoog.

paragraph.text_eng: He was always a good worker, my grandfather, very much so. I know that. Also he always held that tobacco in high regard. Us today, we should carry that tobacco. Where ever we may go, that tobacco should be carried in a bag. You would need that tobacco at some time, you should always carry it. That’s what I know. Also if someone carries a pipe, morning, every morning at dawn, not at ten o’clock, not later, it has to be in the early morning. That’s when it’s ceremony pipe time. Before the sun peeks out, that is when that spiritual life is strongest. That is what I know. That is all, I will finish here.

sentence.sent_text: Pane gii ntaa-nokii maaba nmishoomsiba, aapji go.
Ngii-gkendaan wi.
Miinwas semaan gii-gchi-piitenmaan, pane-gwa.
Gegiinwi dash nongwa, aabideg semaa gdaa-bmwinaanaa.
Dibi iidig go ngoji zhaayiing, shkimdaang daa-biinzo ow semaa.
Maanj go iidig go pii gidaa-mnwenzin semaa, pane dash gdaa-bmwinaa.
Mii gaa-zhi-gkendma.
Miinwaa pane awaya giishpin pwaaganan bmwinaad naa.
Kizheb ge, enso kizheb, pii go biidaabang, gaa’ii baamaapii mdaaso-dbagane’eg, gaa’ii baamaapii aabideg go gchi kizheb, mii wi pii biindaakweng.
Jiibwaa bi-zaabid go ow giizis, mii genh wi pii maawnji-mshkooziimgak maanda minidowaadziwin.
Mii go naa ezhi-gkendmaa.
Mi wi mnik.
Nga ke boontaa.

paragraph.text_eng: I have been given tobacco by Niiyo Giizhik and over there I can’t ever remember all of her name; Anangookwe I always say to her. When you guys gave me tobacco carefully I accept your tobacco. I will tell a little bit about what I was taught when I was small. What I knew when my body was small, when my knowledge was small. When my thoughts were really small.

sentence.sent_text: Anish naa, anish naa asemaa ningii-pi-miinigo Niiyo-giizhig minaawa iwedi gaawiin kina niminikwenimaasiin izhinikaazo Anangookwe dash apane indina.
Gii-pi-miizhii igo asemaa weweni go odaapiniged mooninim agood indasemaawaa.
Weweni dash imaa dadibaadadomaan bangii, bangii gaye niin keyaa gaa-pi-gikinoo’amaagooyaan gii-pi-agaashiinyeyaan sa go, gii-pi-agaasaag iw niiyaw gii-pi-agaasaag ningikendamoowin.
Gichi-agaasaag iw indinendamowin.

paragraph.text_eng: When I was about seven years old, I remember a little bit well it was like when I knew I was alive. And I was over there with my grandmother and my grandfather. Those are the ones I lived with. My older brother joined us soon after, Mashkoowab is his name; we lived together with them. My grandfather was called Ze Zaa, and also he was called Ojiig-Anang. And we called him dedenaan; well after all he was our father; he took care of us; he raised us, that old man. And the one he married my ; grandmother. likwez was that old lady’s name. Over there they lived we arrived there and we called her “Gwem.” Dedenaan and Gwem, we lived with them, when we stayed there when we arrived.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash awedi ingoji go gii-niizhwaaso-biboonagiziyaan mii iw apii bangii go ni-minjimendamaan igo gegoo gii tibishkoo gii-gikendamaan bimaadiziiyaan.
Mii dash widi ayaayaan owidi nookomisag nookomis miinawaa nimishomisiban mii ingiw gaa-wiiji-ayaawagwaa.
Naawaa-sh igo maa wayiiba gii-tagoshin nisaye aw Mashkoowab ezhinikaazod mii maa gii-ayaayaang gii-wiiji-ayaawangwaa.
Nimishomisiban gaa-izhinikaazod Zezaa miinawaa Ojiig-anang gii-inaa.
Dedenaan niinawind ningii-inaanaan mii aw indedenaan aaniish naa ingii-kanawenimigonaan minawaa igo ningii-nitaawigi’igonaan aw akiwenzi.
Miinawaa-sh igo iniw gaa-wiidigemaad mii aw nookomisiban.
Iikwez gii-izhinikaazo a’aw mindimooye.
Mii iwidi gii-taawaad mii widi gii-tagoshinaang naawaa-sh igo niinawind ningii izhinikaanaanaan “Gwem” Mii aw “Dedenaan” miinawaa “Gwem” gaa-wiiji-ayaawangwaa odi gii-ayaayaang gii-tagoshinaang.

paragraph.text_eng: When we first arrived over there, what’s called Minisinaakwaang now, that little Indian community, it is called East Lake in English. And when we first arrived there we did not know the Ojibwe language. We only spoke English when we arrived over there. I arrived there first, maybe two months over there, I was there, before my brother came.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-oshki-dagoshinaang owidi Minisinaakwaan izhinikaadeg noongom Anishinaabe oodenawens odi keyaa zhaagashiimong izhinikaade “East Lake.” Mii dash owidi gii-oshki-dagoshinaang gaawiin ingii-kikendaziimin ojibwemowin.
Mii eta go gii-shaaganaashiimoyaang odi gii-tagoshinaang niinatam ingii-tagoshin maagizhaa niizho giizis odi niin ningii-ayaa jibwaa-dagoshing nisaye.

paragraph.text_eng: And I just now know a little something. And outside we always played, me and my brother Mashkoowab; unknown somewhere over there out in the woods, we always played. We did all kinds of things there in the brush over there where there were many trees over there. When Gram started shouting and hollering, we heard her when she was hollering for us. And our name in the Anishinaabe language that’s what she used when she called us that old lady. When she was calling us her grandchildren. “Mashkoowab! Niibaagaabaaw!” She really hollered out to us. And somewhere wandering around in the bush, we heard her.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash iw bijiinag gikendamaan imaa bangii go gegoo.
Agwajing dash apane ningii-tazhitaamin niin gaye nisaye Mashkoowab dibi go odi megwayaak megwekob mii odi pane gii-tazhitaayaang.
Anooj igo gegoo ningii-izhichigemin owidi megwekob gii-baa-dazhitaayaang odi mitigokaag owidi.
Baamaa dash ingoding noondawaanaan… ninoondawaanaan Gwem bi-biibaagi’angid.
Mii dash indizhinikaazowinaan Anishinaabemong mii iw mii iw ayaabajitood gii-kanoozhiyaang aw mindimooye.
Ingiw sa go gii-kanooniyaang oozhisheyan.
“Mashkoowab!
Niibaagaabaaw!” chi-biibaagi’angid.
Dibi dash widi babaa-ayaayaang widi megwekob noondawaanang.

paragraph.text_eng: That is when we took off towards her, we came running arrived there, where that old lady was there outside. And that’s where she built a fire there outside. And then that old lady told us take that tobacco; she said take this tobacco; well we took that tobacco. She said right there put that tobacco in the fire so our tobacco was put in the fire; me and my brother threw our tobacco in the fire. And this is what that old lady also says, “Your names, and you should say, here is my tobacco.” That’s what I said, what I did, “Here is my tobacco, Niibaagaabaw, and that’s what I said. And then that old lady began to speak. Carefully she sent them to those thunderbirds (her words). We did not know anything.

sentence.sent_text: Mii pi-maajaayaang, pi-bagamibatooyaang, dagoshinaang imaa endazhi-ayaad imaa agwajing aw mindimooyenh.
Mii dash imaa poodawed, poodawed imaa agwajing.
Mii dash imaa mii dash imaa gaye niinawind wiindamaa gii-wiindamaaged aw mindimooye wa’aw asemaa mamik ikido aniish naa mamaang aw asemaa.
Mii dash ekidod mii imaa ishkoding ashi aw asemaa mii dash imaa ishkoding ezhi asang iniw nindasemaanaan niin gaye nisaye ishkoding apaginang ea asemaa.
Mii dash ikidod aw mindimooyenh.
“Gidizhinikaazowm gaye gidaa-i cid asemaa wa’aw.” Mii dash izhichigeyaang “Asemaa wa aw Niibaagaabaaw” gaye niin gii-ikidoyaan.
Mii dash iw gii-maajii-gaagiigidod aw mindimooyenh.
Weweni gii-apagazondamawaad iniw binesiwan.
Gaawiin go gegoo niinawind ingii-gikendaziimin.

paragraph.text_eng: Now after that old lady was done talking now we took off running. In a little while now we hear them, me and Mashkoowab, me and my older brother; we hear them those thunderbirds now that they have arrived. After a bit of time after we are out and about now suddenly, we know there very soon they will arrive, the hot breath of those thunderbirds. And it will start raining so we run inside.

sentence.sent_text: Naa giizhiitaa gaa-ishkwaa-gaagiigidod aw mindimooyenh naa maajtibatooyang niinawind.
Noomaya dash mii zhigwa noondawangwaa niin gaye Mashkoowab niin gaye nisaye noondawangwaa ingiw anamikii zhigwa ani-dagoshinowaad.
Miinawaa go maa noomag igo babaa-ayaayaang mii azhigwaa gikendamang azhigwaa imaa wayiiba wii-tagoshinowaad, gizhinaamowaad ingiw binesiwag.
Mii dash wayiiba go mii wii-maajibiisaamagak biindigebatooyaang.

paragraph.text_eng: Thats it. That’s all I will tell about today, Thanks for listening.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iw.
Mii o minik waa tabaajibatoonago noongom.
Miigwech bizindawiyeg.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what I know about the bear. It is him that takes good care of you; when something happens to you he will help you. And maybe when you go hunting, see when you put tobacco here on the ground, you ask the Spirit for things to go good for you there in the woods. And also it is the bear that is my clan. Say there’s one woman you know, maybe you are in love with her, and she is of the bear clan too. This is the way I was told, you cannot marry that woman. It’s just like you are marrying your sister, See, she too is of the bear clan. That’s the way I was told. You can’t marry her. That’s all I know. That’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Ya’aw makwa keyaa ezhi-gikendamaan.
Mii ya’aw genawenimik sa go weweni, da-izhi-izhiwebiziyan da-wiidookawik iw sa gegoo.
Maagizhaa ge-giiwoseyan, ke aw asemaa omaa akiing asad gagwejimad a’aw manidoo sa go weweni da-izhi-izhiwebiziyan imaa megwekob.
Ke gaye ya’aw makwa indoodem.
Ke ge a’aw bezhig gikenimad ikwe maagizhaa noodenimad, mii go gaye wiin naasaab makwan odoodeman.
Mii ow keyaa gaa-izhi-wiindamaagooyaan, gaawiin gidaa-wiidigemaasiin a’aw ikwe.
Indago aw gishiime a’aw waa-wiidigemad.
Ke, odoodeman gaye wiin makwan.
Miish gaa-izhi-wiindamaagooyaan akeyaa.
Gaawiin gidaa-wiidigemaasiin aw.
Mii eta go minik ezhi-gikendamaan.
Mii iw.

paragraph.text_eng: Greetings my name is Nancy Jones. I live here in Red Gut. The muskrat is my clan.

sentence.sent_text: Ahaw boozhoo, niin Ogimaagwanebiik, Ogimaakwewobiik indigoo.
Nigigoonsiminikaaning omaa indaa.
Wazhashk indoodem.

paragraph.text_eng: Iam going to talk about animals. This topic that I am talking about, think kindly of me as I am not trying to step over anyone’s teachings. have what I was taught when I was growing up.

sentence.sent_text: Aya’ii maawiin owe inga-dazhimaag ogowe-ag awesiiyag gaa-inindwaa.
Owe gaa-wii-tazhindamaan gegoo, bebekaa initawishiyog gaawinoon awe gegoo inga-gagwe-gagaanomaasii.
Owe eta go gegiin gaa-pi-izhi-gikinoo’amaagowaan gii-pi-ombigiyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: My grandmother and grandfather raised me. It’s them who taught me this. Maybe your teachings are different from what you heard from the way I was given these teachings.

sentence.sent_text: Nookomosiban ingii-nitawigi’ig nimishoomisiban ge.
Mii dash ko owe gegoo gaa mii igiwe gegoo gaa-waawiindamawiwaad.
Maagizhaa ge bakaan giinawaa gegoo gii-gigii-izhi-noondaamwaadog owe geniin omaa gaa-naajimotaagowaan.

paragraph.text_eng: They use to talk about this one they call Nenabush. That is who made the world; this is what they told me. He made the world before the arrival of the Anishinaabe. He made everything first is the way I was told. He made things such as trees and animals, and he made all the species of all the animals.

sentence.sent_text: Owe aya’aan ogii-tazhimaawaan.
Nenabozhoo ogii-izhinikaanaawaan Nenabozhoo akiwenzii.
Mii iidog awe gaa-ozhitood awe akiing ingii-izhi-noondawaag ako.
Gii-ozhitood awe aki mii iidog awe gaa-ayaad, jibwaa dago, jibwaa ayaawaad, jibwaa ayaawaad maawiin, jibwaa dagoshinowaad Anishinaabeg.
Gakina gegoo iidog akawe ogii-ozhitoon ingii-izhi-noondam ako.
Nashke ge mitigoo’ ogii-ozhi’aa’ miinawaa awe awesiiya’ bebezhig gii-ani-ayaad gii-gaa-giizhi’aad endaswaabiminaagozid awesiinh.

paragraph.text_eng: All of these animals have names, all the fish too along with all the flyers. That is what she talked about, these animals.

sentence.sent_text: Anishinaa akina wiinzowag ogowe awesiiyag gaa-endaswaabiminaagoziwaad owe ge giigoowag owe ge gaa-bimisewaad ishpiming, Mii dash ako ogowe aya’aag ogii-tazhimaa’ awesiiya’.

paragraph.text_eng: So Nenabush was the one that created the animals. So he invited all that he made to come here. So this is how people gathered to smoke their pipes. As they sat in a circle, he spoke to each one individually.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog owe gaa-giizhi’aad a’a Nenabosh awesiiya’.
Mii iidog gakina gaa-izhi-ayaad gaa-izhi-andomaat omaa.
Mii iidog imaa gii-sagaswe’iding gii-ikodong.
Mii dash omaa iizan gaa-giiwitaabinit bebezhig ogii-izhi-gaganoonaa’.

paragraph.text_eng: “The reason why I ask you to come here is, I am going to ask you all this. People will soon arrive; the Anishinaabe will soon arrive here. I am going to ask you ahead of time, how are you going to help the Anishinaabe when they get here. You are called animals, and you all each have a different name. This is how the Anishinaabe will survive, by you the animals. This is how they will get their food to survive.”

sentence.sent_text: “Aya’ii omaa wenji-andominagog, giwii-gagwejimininim owe.
Awiiyag omaa bijiinag da-tagoshinoog Anishinaabeg omaa bijiinag da-tagoshinoog.
Akawe idash giizhaa giwii-kagwejiminim aaniin giinawaa waa-izhi-wiiji eg Anishinaabe omaa pi-dagoshing.
Awesiiyag gidigoom bebezhig endaswaabiminaagoziyeg bebikaan gidizhinikaazom.
Owe dash mii omaa ge-ondaadizid awe Anishinaabe owe giinawaa awesiiyag egooyeg, Mii omaa gii-ondinang owe wiisiniwin ge-ondaachi’idizod.”

paragraph.text_eng: So the moose was the first to start talking.

sentence.sent_text: Waa’, miizan zhigwa ayaad gaa-giigidod aw mooz.

paragraph.text_eng: “This is what I would like to give the Anishinaabe, they will eat my meat. If you ook at (study)the things that I eat. This is medicine that I go about eating all over. I eat grass, twigs and roots from the water. I eat all these things wherever I go; that is how I eat.

sentence.sent_text: “Ahaw niin sa awe aya’ii inga-izhi-miinaa Anishinaabe niwiiyaas owe niwiiyaas oga-miijin.
Nashke owe gii-naanaagaji iyeg owe gaa-inanjigeyaan.
Mashkiki owe gaa-baa-miijiyaan miziwe.
Mishkosiisan ge nimiijinan, mitigoonsan gaye jiibikensan gaye nibiikaang.
Miziwe mii iniwen gaa-mijjiyaan, mii inanjigeyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: So Anishinaabe eats my meat. This how they will cure themselves. This is how he will lead a good healthy life.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke dash owe Anishinaabe miijid owe niwiiyaasim.
Mii go omaa ji-nanaadawe’idizod.
Mii owe ge-onji-mino-ayaa ge-onji-minogininig obimaadiziwin.

paragraph.text_eng: If they show respect to my meat. If they show respect of my gift. When they offer tobacco, that is what I like when they show me respect with tobacco.

sentence.sent_text: Weweni, weweni izhitood iwe niwiiyaas.
Weweni ge izhichiged owe, gii-inenimag owe ji-debinid.
Nashke owe gii-biindaakoojiged awiiya mii sa awe geniin ezhi-minwendamaan, ezhi-minowendamaan weweni gegoo izhi-igowaan.

paragraph.text_eng: The trimmings (from the meat)and also the bones. My wish is that they put these in the woods. Not to throw them over there in the garbage is my wish. When the bones are returned in the woods, another one of me will arise from there.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa onowe zhiithgozhagonan okanan maawiin igo.
Begish weweni omaa noopiming awiiya gii-atood.
Gaawinoon Ingoji iwidi ziigwebiniganing ji-izhi-bagijiwebinang indinendanzii.
Mii go miinawaa gaa-izhi-gaabawiyaan gii-atood omaa ini weweni okanan omaa noopiming.

paragraph.text_eng: These four-legged little runners and also the large birds and little birds. They too will eat from this. When you put things back in the woods. And when one picks the meat from the bones, that is what I appreciate. They too will eat these animals that are all called and the birds. That is how I will help the Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ogowe gaa-babaamiba’idiwaat awiiyag awesiiyensag gemaa gaye binesiwag, bineshiiyensag.
Mii omaa gewiinawaa ge-ondanjigewaad owe.
Weweni gegoo gii-ateg omaa ate omaa noopiming.
Nashke ge awe gii-jiichiigwanjiged awiiya, mii go iye izhi-minwendamaan.
Gewiinawaa indanjigewaad igo awe awensiiwesag gaa-inindwaa ogowe ge binesiwag.
Mii sa niin owe ge-izhi-wiiji’ag awe Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: And also my jacket, my skin, this is what they will use to lace up their snowshoe, the hide.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ge owe nimbiiskawaagan nimbashkwegin, mii owe ge-aabajitood wii-ashkimaanaad odaagima’ owe dashwiin nimbashkwegin.

paragraph.text_eng: I will not be far away when I know that the one that is looking for me has done the proper protocols. I will be here waiting, because I care, and I will care, for the Anishinaabe that is going to arrive. That is what I will do.”

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiinoon ge waasa inga-ayaasii giishpin gikendamaan ingoji wii-pi-andawaabamid weweni gaa-izhichiged.
Mii go imaa ge-dazhi-baabii’ag, Aaniishinaa inzhawenimaa, inga-zhawenimaa awe Anishinaabe waa-tagoshing.
Mii iye niin ge-izhichigeyaan.”

paragraph.text_eng: Then there was another one that deer too.

sentence.sent_text: Waa’ mii sa miinawaa bezhig waawaashkeshiinh gaye wiin.

paragraph.text_eng: “That is the same for me, I too think the same thing. They will cure themselves from (eating)my meat that Anishinaabe. I too appreciate when I am showed the proper respect.

sentence.sent_text: “Waa mii go ge-niin iye, mii go ge-niin bezhigon enendamaan.
Oga-noojimoshkaagon owe niwiiyaasim aw Anishinaabe.
Mii go ge-niin owe ambegish weweni gegoo izhi’igowaan ako indinendam.

paragraph.text_eng: So this tail that I carry, the Anishinaabe will know how to make something out of it. Sometimes we will see Anishinaabe dancing. He will be wearing the head roach made from the hair of my tail. My tail, my tails, the hair from my tail. This is what I will give to the Anishinaabe, my gift to the Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke-ge owe, owe ninzow gaa-bimiwidooyaan, gegoo go imaa oga-onji-ozhitoon aw Anishinaabe.
Nashke ingoding giga-waabamaanaan maagizhaa da-babaa-niimi aw Anishinaabe.
Mii dash owe ge-miskwaanjiganid owe ninzow.
Ninzow ige, ninzowan, aya’ii ezhi-obii-ayaawang, obii-ayaawang inzow.
Mii owe ge-niin ge-izhi-miinag aw Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: And then my bones, they will use them for something. For example the marrow from my bones, eventually they will recognize my gifts.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ge onowe nikanan, gegoo go oga-inaabajitoonan.
Nashke ge owe ezhi-obaasayi’ganiyaan, booch igo ingoding ogani-gikendaanaawaa owe aaniin.

paragraph.text_eng: I too have the same gifts like the others, medicine that I carry, as you see me standing around. I too shall help the Anishinaabe so that he will lead a good life. I too will not be far away. I will be within eye distance when they come needing my gifts.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go ge-niin bezhigon ennadiziyaan, mashkiki owe gaa-bimiwidoowaan owe gii-inaagoziyaan, gii-paa-naaniibawiyaan.
Inga-wiiji’aa ge-niin aw Anishinaabe ji-onji-mino-bimaadizid.
Gaawiin ge-niin waasa inga-ayaasii.
Mii go omaa, mii go omaa besho ge-niin ge-babaa-onzaabiyaan baa-nanaagadawaabamag.

paragraph.text_eng: I will feel it when they are hungry. I shall not run far. I too offer the same gift; I think the same way.

sentence.sent_text: Inga-gikenimaa noondeskaded aw Anishinaabe, mii dash omaa, gaawiin waasa inga-apa’iwesii.
Mii go bezhigon ge-niin enendamaan.

paragraph.text_eng: I too eat grass, little twigs and medicine trees. Also in the water, I eat the roots. These roots are the ones they will make the medicine tea with, our grandchildren that will arrive. I too shall care for the Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go ge-niin enanjigeyaan mashkosiinsan, mitigoonsan mashkikiwaatigoonsan nimiijinan.
Mii go ge omaa nibiikaang, ojiibikensan.
Mii sa go iniwe bijiinag ge-ni-mashkiki iwaabookaadamowaad ogowe waa-dagoshinowaad gozhisinaanig.
Inga-zhawenimaa ge-niin Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: This is my gift, my hide they will have and find a way to utilize it. Eventually he will know how to make use of it.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa ge-niin awe, imbashkwegin ge, oga-ayaan, gegoo go oga-inaabajitoon.
Oga-gikendaan bijiinag ge-inaabajitood.”

paragraph.text_eng: And then that one bear, he too arrived.

sentence.sent_text: Waa mii sa wiin miinawaa bezhig a’aw makwa iizan ge-wiin imaa gii-tagoshin.

paragraph.text_eng: “I too feel the same way as my brothers. Bear is my name.

sentence.sent_text: “Howah mii sa go ge-niin i, mii go ge-niin enendamaan ogowe gaa-ikidowaad niiji-akiiwenziiyag.
Makwa indigo.

paragraph.text_eng: My gift I shall give the Anishinaabe, I carry a lot of grease. This is how they will survive, from my fat I shall give him. They too will use my fat and perhaps they will find a way to heal from it, this grease; I too need to be treated with respect, that is what I need also.

sentence.sent_text: Aya’iin niin omaa inga-miinaa aw Anishinaabe, inga-bimiwidoon owe niibiyo bimide.
Mii dash imaa ge-ondaadizid owe ji-onji-bimidemid omaa inga-miinaa.
Gegoo sa go ge oga-inaabajitoon owe imbimidem maagizhaa ge gegoo maagizhaa-ge ingoding da-gikendam owe ge-izhi-noojimoshkaagod gegoo.
Owe bimide weweni, weweni ge-niin izhi’igowaan, mii go ge-niin izhi-andawendamaan weweni.

paragraph.text_eng: Also my meat is good. And my jacket, my jacket is very warm. The Anishinaabe will find a way to use the jacket to keep themselves warm.

sentence.sent_text: Owe-ge niwiiyaasim onizhishin igo ge owe.
Owe ge nimbiizikawaagan, aapiji giizhooyaa nimbiizikawaagan.
Mii go owe ge-ni-inaabajitood aw Anishinaabe ji-onji-giizhoozid gaye wiin.

paragraph.text_eng: I will not be seen in the winter but I will not be far away. I will be sleeping nearby if Anishinaabe knows how to find me, I will not be far away.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiinoon owe gii-biboong inga-inaagozisii, gaawiin dash wiin igo waasa inga-izhaasii.
Mii go omaa besho ge-nibaayaan giishpin gikendang aw Anishinaabe aaniin ge-izhichiged owe ji-bi-andawaabamid, gaawiinoon waasa ingoji inga-izhaasii.

paragraph.text_eng: Perhaps I will visit him there when he is sleeping. This is where I will tell him where he can find here, where I live.

sentence.sent_text: Maagizhaa-ge ingoding ninga-odisaa omaa gii-nibaad.
Mii imaa ge-onji-wiindamawag aandi, ge-ondinang owe, aandi ge-izhi-mikawid omaa endaayaan.

paragraph.text_eng: Perhaps the Anishinaabe will have a pet. Such as the dog will be their keepers.

sentence.sent_text: Booshke ingoding awiiyag da-ondayiwag maawiin ge Anishinaabeg.
Animoshan oga-ganawenimigowaan.

paragraph.text_eng: Some dogs have spirit teachings. He has teachings to pass onto the Anishinaabe. Here the dog will bark. This is how the Anishinaabe, our grandchildren, will know. This is where his dog will give the teachings.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding idash igo mii owe enaadizid aw animosh mii awe debaajimod.
Mii awe waandamowaad onowe Anishinaaben.
Nashke omaa da-bi-migi da-bi-migi aw animosh.
Mii dash imaa ji-gikendang owe Anishinaabe, goozhisinaan.
Mii omaa ji-ni-wiindamaagod ini odayan.

paragraph.text_eng: If he honors his dog in a good way. He will tell where to find me. This is what I offer. I will care for the Anishinaabe when he arrives.”

sentence.sent_text: Giishpin weweni izhaad onowe odayan.
Oga-wiindamaagoon omaa ge-onji-mikawid.
Mii sa ge niin iye ge-izhichigeyaan.
Inga-zhawenimaa, inga-zhawenimaa dagoshing aw Anishinaabe.”

paragraph.text_eng: And soon, apparently the smaller animals arrived. Such as the beaver, hetoo arrived.

sentence.sent_text: Waa biinish igo gaa-babiiwizhe-iwaad awiiya iinzan imaa bi-da-dagoshinoog.
Ge-wiin awe amik ge mii dagoshing.

paragraph.text_eng: “And then, what else am I to think, as our grandchildren arrive. I will do the same.

sentence.sent_text: “Waa mii go ge-niin owe aniishinaa gegii-inendamaan anishinaa igi gosinaanig ogowe waa-dagoshinowaad.
Mii go gaye niin owe bezhigon ge-izhichigeyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: My meat will cure the Anishinaabe, I too eat this way, those medicine trees by eating the bark, and I go about gathering water lily. So when they eat my flesh, this’S how they cure themselves.

sentence.sent_text: Niwiiyaas oga-minoshkaagon aw Anishinaabe.
Mii go ge-niin enanjigeyaan onowen mitigoog nimbishagaakwamaag ingoding ge ojiibigensan akandamoo ge imbabaa-moozhiginaa.
Mii dash owe miijid aa Anishinaabe owe, niwiiyaasim, mii go imaa ji-noojimoowidizod.

paragraph.text_eng: I do not go far; when you look around in the water, you see my lodge standing there. This is where the Anishinaabe will find me. I will not be stingy with what I have to offer to the Anishinaabe so that he can provide for himself. As for my hide, they will find a good use for.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin ge waasa ingoji inga-izhaasii mii go imaa, mii go imaa ingoji nibiikaang waabandameg mii imaa ji-badakideg owe.
Mii omaa ge-bi-izhi-andonowe-id aa Anishinaabe.
Gaawiin ge-niin wiikaa indaa-zaakitoosiin iye, awe ge-izhi-bamii’idizod aa Anishinaabe.
Nashke ge owe niwayaan ge owe gegoo go oga-inaabaji’aan.

paragraph.text_eng: I too will care for the Anishinaabe: will chew down the trees and as the tree gets dry this is where he will get his dry firewood. I do not eat the wood that is dry. Only the green trees with the bark on them. This is my gift to the Anishinaabe.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii iye ge-niin, inga-zhawenimaa Anishinaabe, booshke ge inga-gawamaag igi mitigoog, inashke idash awe animishiiwaadigoowid mitig.
mii imaa ge-ondininang inim gaa-onji ge-ondinised aw Anishinaabe nibaasod awe mitig.
Gaawinoon gaa-baasowaad mitigoog, gaawiinoon etino’o indaa-amwaasiig.
Ogowe eta go oshki-mitigoog gaa-wanagekowiwaad.
Mii sa ge-niin ge-izhi-wiijitwaayaan.”

paragraph.text_eng: As the gathering gets larger, the rabbit arrives hopping.

sentence.sent_text: Waa biinish igo niibiyo awiiya miinawaa, waabooz iinzan miinawaa omaa bi-bagamibatoo.

paragraph.text_eng: “Here I have something too. I too have something to offer the Anishinaabe.”

sentence.sent_text: “Howa ge-niin, ge-niin gegoo indayaan.
Ge-niin owe indayaan waa-izhi-wiijii’ag aw Anishinaabe.”

paragraph.text_eng: The rabbit was looking at Nenabozhoo.

sentence.sent_text: Oganawaabamaan iinzan ini Nenabozhoon.

paragraph.text_eng: “Who do you think you are? Look at you and how small you are. You don’t even have much meat on you.”

sentence.sent_text: “Awenen da giin na awe, dak sa giin naa?
Shke giin enigiiniyan.
Gaawiin gosha aapichi gegoo wiiyaas gidaayaasiin.”

paragraph.text_eng: “Nope, don’t think of me that way. I will sense when the Anishinaabe is struggling to find food to eat.

sentence.sent_text: “Ooh gaawiin, gego inenimishiken, gego aanawinimishiken.
Nashke ge-niin owe inga-gikenimaa aw Anishinaabe giishpin ingoding gagwadagitood owe gwiinawi-ondinang waa-miijid.

paragraph.text_eng: So if you study what I have to offer, if you look at how tall the trees are, that is how tall my gift will be, that is how much I care about the Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke naanaagaji’iyan, nashke ogowe eyaakwaakosiwaad mitigoog, mii go awe ge-apii-jishinaabaan, mii epiichi shawenimag aw Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: I will not go anywhere. Whenever I see a round snare, that is where I will put my head into. That is how much I care about the Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin wiikaa ingoji indaa.
Nashke ingoji waabandamaan gegoo, wiimbagoodeg nagwaagan, mii imaa ge-izhi-biindigweniyaan.
Epiichi zhawenimag aw Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: When you look at me and my fur, they will get warmth from it. And perhaps they will make something from it, like a blanket. They will know what to do.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ge owe gaa-izhinaagoziyaan, owe niwayaan, oga-giizhooshkaagon ge-wiin iye.
Owe shke gegoo omaa oga-ozhitoon gemaa ge waa-owaaboowaanid oga-ozhitoon.
Oga-gikendaan ge-izhichiged.
