paragraph.text_eng: My eating habits are the same as the others. I go about eating medicine plants. I do not eat from where it is dirty, only from the clean earth. That is the way I am.

sentence.sent_text: Owe ge gaa-inanjigeyaan ge-niin, mii go bezhigon ge-niin.
Mashkikiwaadigoonsan nimbabaa-moozhagandaanan.
Gaawiin wiikaa ingoji bakaan gegoo gaa-wiinakamigaag indawindanjigesii, mii eta go onowen gaa-biinakin.
Mii iniwen.

paragraph.text_eng: When they make soup from me, that is how they will cure themselves. You will hear people say, eat the rabbit, if you are having a hard time. This is where you will get rid of your illness when you make this soup. My body carries medicine.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke dash owe gii-naboobiikaazhid aw Anishinaabe, mii omaa gaa-onji-aad, ge-onji-noojimod.
Nashke sa go giga-noondawaawag bijiinag ji-ikidowaad owe waabooz gidaa-amwaa, giishpin ingoding maanimanji’oyan.
Mii awe ge-ani-onji-minomanji’oyan naboobiikaadaman awe.
Mashkiki owe gaa-bimiwidowaan owe niiyaw.

paragraph.text_eng: There are a lot more, such as my white fur jacket. Anishinaabe will know how to use my gift, like sometimes, somewhere, when they get a skin rash, such as how children suffer with that. They will use my rabbit fur, my hide.

sentence.sent_text: Niibiyo go gegoo, nashke ge owe nimbiiskawaagan owe gaa-waabishkaag.
Gegoo go oga-gikendaan ge-naabajitood aw Anishinaabe, booshke ingojing, ingoding awiiya awe gii-biigwazhesed gii-inind aapich abinoojiinyag maawiin igo izhi-ayaawag.
Mii inowen ge-aabaji’aawaad ini waabooz, niwaaboozowaanan.

paragraph.text_eng: First they will singe it slightly. Then he will rub it onto the rash. This is how he will get well, how he will heal. I will not be stingy with this. I too will care for the Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Akawe bangii oga-banzwaan.
Mii dash awe ge-izhi-zhoobiigiid onowen aandi imaa ezhi-biigozhesid.
Mii go imaa ge-ezhi-mino-ayaad, ge-ini-noojimod.
Gaawiin ge-niin wiikaa indaa-zaakitoosiin owe.
Inga~-zhawenimaa ge-niin a’aw Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: I will not be far away. All they need to do is look around, and they will find my trail; this is where they can get me.”

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin wiikaa ingoji waasa inga-izhaasii.
Mii eta go ji-ba-anda-waabamid imaa ezhi-miikinaakeyaan, mii imaa ge-onji-debinid.”

paragraph.text_eng: And now I will talk about the partridge. And he too came to speak with Nenabozhoo.

sentence.sent_text: A’a miinawaa awe inga-ani-dazhimaa bine.
Mii owe iidog imaa ge-wiin imaa gaa-pii-izhaad wii-pi-gaganoonaad iniwe Nanaboozhoon.

paragraph.text_eng: “I too have something to help the Anishinaabe with,” he says. “As you can see, I have wings and I fly.

sentence.sent_text: “AhawAAAAhaw ge-niin gegoo inga-wiiji’aa Anishinaabe” ikido iinzan.
“Nashke owe gaa-izhinawiyeg, oningwiiganan indayaanan imbimise.

paragraph.text_eng: I will not run away from the Anishinaabe,” he said. “I will sense when he is hungry.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin dash wiin igo wiikaa indaa-aapichi-maajiibay’iwaanaasii aw Anishinaabe” ikido iinzan.
“Nashke owe gikenimag ge-niin owe noondeskaded.

paragraph.text_eng: He will hear me here in the woods when I make the drum sound. This where he will hear me and find me. That is how he will know where I am at.

sentence.sent_text: Ninga-noondaag omaa ingoji noopimiing owe gii-madwewe’oyaan.
Mii omaa ge onji-naanzitawid.
Mii omaa ge-onji-gikenimit aandi eyaayaan.

paragraph.text_eng: Even when I see a snare somewhere I will put my head into it. I too care for the Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ge ingoding nagwaagan ingoji waabandamaan mii go ge-niin imaa ge izhi-biindiweniyaan.
Aaniishinaa inzhawenimaa ge-niin aw Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: When they find my eggs, they can take them as long as they leave me one or two.”

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ge onowe ingoding gii-mikang owe iniwe waawanoosan gii-ikidong, oo gaawiin igo godino debinaak ko maagizhaa bezhig maagizhaa ge-niizh ishkwanimaagoyaan.”

paragraph.text_eng: That is what he said.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog awe gaa-ikidogobanen.

paragraph.text_eng: “I too eat the medicine food; in the winter I eat the buds on top of the trees. In the summer, I eat the leaves. I too carry medicine. I too shall help the Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: “Mii go ge-niin owe ezhichigeyaan, mashkikiwaadigoonsan apane nimiijinan mashkikiwan nimiijinan gii-wiisiniyaan mitigoonsan inakoon wanimakoon nimiijinan gii-biboong.
Miinawaa owe gii-niibing aniibiishensan nimbabaa-moozhagandaanan.
Mii dash igo ge-niin iye nimbimiidoon owe mashkiki, mashkiki nimbimiwidoon.
Mii awe ge-niin ge-izhi-wiiji’ag aw Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: As for my feathers, they will find a way to utilize them, and also my tail feathers, they will find good use for them. That is the way I will help our grandchildren when they arrive.”

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ge ogowe nimiigwanag bijiinag oga-gikendaanaawaan aaniin ge-ani-inaabaji’aawaad ogowe nimiigwanag nashke ge ninashkidiigwanag, booch igo gegoo da-gikendamoog aaniin ge-ani-inaabaji’aawaad.
Mii sa iwe ge-niin, ge-izhi-wiiji’ag owe gozhisinaan waa-pi-tagoshing.”

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh me too,” said the muskrat, as he arrived. “I have something too that I can help the Anishinaabe with. This is what I will do too.

sentence.sent_text: “Oonh ge-niin.” ikido iinzan aw wazhashk, bi-tagoshin iinzan imaa.
“Ge-niin owe gegoo indayaan gaye ge-izhi-wiiji’ag aw Anishinaabe.
Mii go ge-niin owe ge-izhichigeyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: When you look in the water, this is where you will see that I live and that is how you will know that I am close by. If you study my habits as you see me, I eat the stock of the bitter root plant and also grass. So this is how you will know this, when you eat my flesh it is like you are eating the bitter root when you are gathering (the bitter root). This is one way that I too can help the Anishinaabe so that they will be well and havea good life. The bitter root is what I wear.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go imaa nibiikaang, mii imaa ji-waabandameg owe, mii imaa endaayaan, mii imaa ge-onji-gikenimigoyaan, besho imaa ayaayaan.
Nashke owe giishpin ingoding nanaagaji’iyeg, waabamiyeg sa go gaye, mii go apane igiwe aya’aag odabiiwaatigoog.
odabiig indamwaag wiike, mashkosiinsan gaye nimiijinan.
Mii dash imaa ge-onji-gikendamegoban owe, nashke miijiyeg owe niwiiyaas mii go dibishko awe wiike gii-mawanji’ind.
Mii imaa, mii iye bezhig ge-niin ge-izhi-waa-wiiji’ag aw Anishinaabe ji-onji-mino-ayaad, ji-onji-mino-bimaadizid.
Nashke owe wiike gigigishkawid.

paragraph.text_eng: Someday soon we shall see them, and they will sing too. They will have drum too. This is how he will have a clear voice when he eats my meat. Because that is how I eat; I eat the bitter root when I eat. This is how I will help, this flesh of mine that I carry, it tastes very good when someone makes soup out of it. This is how I shall help the Anishinaabe. I will not go far; I will be nearby so that I can see them, care for them.”

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ogowe bijiinag giga-waabamaanaanig awiiya da-nagamowag bijiinag.
Dewe’iganan gaye oga-ayaawaawaan.
Mii dash imaa ge-onji-gizhiiwed awe gii-miijid owe niwiiyaas.
Anishinaa mii awe gaa-inanjigeyaan owe wiike gii-amwak.
Mii iw ge-niin ge-izhi-waawiijitwaayaan booch owe ge wiiyaas gaa-bimiwidoowaan aapichi ge niin, aapichi ge niin minopogwad owe wii-naboobiikaadang awiiya.
Mii owe ge-niin waa-izhi-wiiji’ag aw Anishinaabe.
Gaawiinoon ingoji waasa inga-izhaasii.
Besho igo omaa inga-ayaa, ge-onji-de-waabamag igo.”

paragraph.text_eng: So the duck also came in and landed.

sentence.sent_text: Haw ge-wiin inzan omaa bibooni aw zhiishiib.

paragraph.text_eng: “I too have something that will help the Anishinaabe. For example, when I am around here in the fall and sometimes too in the spring, when I land I come to see all the Anishinaabe. I come to help, to heal, aid in their health, our grandchildren.

sentence.sent_text: “Howa ge-niin sa, ge-niin igo indayaan owe ge-izhi-wiiji’ag gego Anishinaabe Nashke owe gii-bimi-ayaayaan imaa gii-tagwagig ingoding ge gii-ziigwang imbimibooni omaa imbi-waabamag ogo gakina Anishinaabeg.
Imbi-nanaagaji’aag, inga-bi-nanaagaji’aag goozhisinaanig.

paragraph.text_eng: I will also know when they get hungry. I will be nearby. I will not run away too far. And sometimes someone will hit me. This is how they will be able to get me. I will not be stingy. I too love our grandchildren, those ones that are going to arrive.

sentence.sent_text: Inga-gikenimaa ge-niin gishpin noondeskadewaad.
Oooh besho omaa inga-ayaa.
Gaawiin igo ingoji waasa inga-izhi-maajiba’iwesii.
Booshke ingoding awiiya inga-pakitebwaanig awiiya ingoding.
Mii go omaa ge-onji-debinigoowaan gaye.
Gaawiin indaa-zazaagizisii.
Inzhawenimaa ge-niin awe goozhisinaan waa-pi-dagoshing.

paragraph.text_eng: They can use my feathers for something and eventually they will know what for. They also know how to use my bones for something. They will come to know how to make things. This is how I too will help. I shall care for the Anishinaabe that is going to arrive.”

sentence.sent_text: Nashke-ge ogowe nimiigwanimag gegoo ge-inaabaji’awaad ge owe bijiinag oga-gikendaanaawaa aaniin ge-inaabaji’aawaad.
Nashke ge onowe nikanan gegoo go oga-inaabajitoonaawaan.
Baamaa oga-ani-gikendaanaawaa aaniin gegoo ge imaa ji-onji-ozhitoowaad.
Mii ge-niin owe ge-izhi-wiijitwaayaan.
Inga-zhawenimaa awe Anishinaabe waa-tagoshing.

paragraph.text_eng: And then, “Me too,” said the goose as he landed there.” I too will allow myself to be caught even though I travel far, as I look over, as I fly by, even though I see them.

sentence.sent_text: Waa’ “ge-niin” ikido iizan a’a we’we’ gewiin imaa biboonii.
“Ge-niin maawiin ingoding inga-gashki’igoo ji-debinigoowaan ji-debinid awe, aanawi waasa apane indizhaa.
Mii eta go ko bimi-naanaagadawaabamagwaa omaa go gii-bimi-ayaawaan, aanawi go ninde-baabamaag.

paragraph.text_eng: As I go home south for the winter, as in the future, they will learn something. They should not look at me after I pass beyond. As I fly far to the south, do not look after me longingly. It is forbidden to watch because it is the same trail that our ancestors use when they pass on the thunderbird road,” he said. “They will learn more about it as they teach each other.”

sentence.sent_text: Iwedi dash waasa indizhi-giiwe gii-biboong awedi zhaawanong gii-ikidong, mii dash ko imaa owii-gigikendanaawaa maawiin bijiinag oga-ani-gikendaanaawaan gegoo.
Gaawiin sa wiin iwe da-wii-toodanziiyog awe ji-noosawaabamiyaad.
Awedi gii-waasa izhi-giiweyaan zhaawanong gaawiin, gaawiin da-noosawaabamigosiik.
Dibishkoo eta go awe gegoo andawendang ge-wiin ji-wii-ina’adod awe zhaawanong miikana binesi-miikana,” gii-ikidod.
“Bijiinag go oga-gikendaanaawaan ji-ani-gikinoo’amaadiwaad.”

paragraph.text_eng: Stop. Don’t look at them after they pass.

sentence.sent_text: Gego.
Gego noosawaabamaaken owe.

paragraph.text_eng: “Even though I go far away, I shall care for those grandchildren that are coming. I will not hide very far away. I shall be within hearing distance and I shall be heard.

sentence.sent_text: “Booch igo ge-niin ingoding inga-bamii, inga-bi-zhawenimaa awe goozhisinaan inga-bi-waabamaa.
Gaawiin igo ge-niin waasa inga-izhi-gaazosii ingoji.
Inga-de-bitaag ogeng ingojin noondaagoziyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: This is how I eat too, just like the rice that grows on the lake. This is how they will get the rice; it will be transplanted to another lake or river. As I transplant for the Anishinaabe, and so they will occasionally see it there. They shall see the rice growing in other waters. This is how I will help the future generation.

sentence.sent_text: Mii imaa ge onji gikendamiwaad mii go geniin enji’ geyaa owe, nashke ge owe manoomin gaa nitaawiging.
Mii omaa ingoding wenji-ayaawaad gu-miiji’aan nowe manoomin, mii naa’ed da bezhig zaaga’igan izhaa’aan.
Mii idi dibishkoo go ingitigaadaan ingitigi amo angogwe Anishinaabeg, mii eta miinawaa ingoding gii-onji-waabandamowaad owe.
Manoomin ingoji ji-saagibiig awe biigwaj zaaga’iganiisan ingeyaagi.
Mii iw geniin ge-izhi-wiiji’twaayaan.

paragraph.text_eng: All I need is to be respected. Place my bones back in the water; that is what helps me to grow and stay alive. If they follow this protocol, they will never run out of food. Another will recycle from there, another will grow from there if you do it with care, just like the other animals that have already offered.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa eta go geniin ezhandawendamaang gegoo weweni ji-izhi igo waa.
Nashke onawe nikanan ambegish imaa azhebakobii’igaadegin nibiikaang, aanishina mii omaa wendaadiziyaan mii imaa apane denaadiziyaan.
Giishpin weweni izhichigeyeg weweni izhichewaad awe gooshisinaanig waa-bidagoshinowaad gaawiin wiika da jaaksesiiwag inowe wiisiniwin.
Mii go miinaa omaa ge-ani-onoonji’, ozhigitawe bezhig giishpin weweni gegoo weweni izhitowaad nashke ogii-igowe awesiiyag gaa-aazha gaagii-pigaagiigidowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Just like what they said about respecting the remains of animals, they should be placed in a clean ground. Another one shall walk from there. Just as the muskrat said, put my bones in the lake; another one shall swim away from there. That way, you will never kill off the animals.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii iwe gaa-ikidowaad weweni ini izhichigaadenig onowe, okaniwaan ingoji biinakamigong ji-achigaadenig mii go miinaa imaa bezhig.
Ge-noonji dibishkoo oombinaagozid awesii.
Mii go awe waazhashk gaa-ikidod, weweni gegoo bakobii’igaadegin ini okananan, mii go miinawaa imaa ge-ani-oondadigeyaan bezhig.
Weweni izhichigeyok gaawiin wiikaa oga-jaaginaanaasiwaawaa’ iw awesiiya’ awe ge-inanjigewaad.”

paragraph.text_eng: As the seagull come flying in. As he began to talk, he says that he has something to offer to the generations to come.

sentence.sent_text: Ayi’iy iizan miinawaa bibooni gayaashk, Mii go geniin iwe ikido iizon geniin gegoo indayaan ge-izhi-wiiji’agwaa Anishinaabeg.

paragraph.text_eng: “Just like every spring, I bare eggs on the reef on the lake. There are quite a few of us living on the reef. This is how I will help the Anishinaabe that are coming.

sentence.sent_text: “Nashke onawe ayi’iin gii-ziigwong waawanoon indayaanan gii-ziigwang imaa minisaabikong.
Nimbaatayiinomin imaa endaayaang minisaabikong.
Mii dash imaa ge-niin ge-izhi-wiiji’ag Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: It is okay to come and get some of these eggs. All! need is one person to offer tobacco beter picking up my eggs. You don’t just take anything without offering first. All I ask is to offer me tobacco.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin ingodino be-indowaabandang ingoding onowe inwaawanoon.
Miichiit etago geniin ezhi-andawendimaan bezhig owiiya asemaan nowe omaa ji-bagidinaad.
Gaawiin oniwe gegoo bizaan igo gii-izhi-daapining.
Asemaa geniin inandawenimaa ji-bagidinaamaagooyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: As you see how many eggs are in my nest, just as long as you leave me one. I would be happy with that because I know that Anishinaabe is looking for food.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa inowe endasigin ini waawanoon imaa niwasisoning, ambegish ganage bezhig ishkonamawii’eg.
Mii go ge-izhi-minwendamaan aaniishinaa ingikendaan wiiji’ag Anishinaabe wii-wiisinid.

paragraph.text_eng: They will hear me whereever I am at because I am loud and that is how they will find me. As you see the reefs, that is where our nests are, this is where we live, that is where the eggs are. This is how I will help the Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Inga-noondaag aapichi ingiishiiwe ingoji gaa-daayaan mii omaa ge onji-gikendang aandi ge onji-mikawid.
Aapichi go imaa ingoding omaa minisaabikong, mii imaa endaayaang mii imaa eyaagin niwaasisoninaanan, mii dash imaa ezhi-ayaagin niwaawanonaanin.
Mii iwe geniin ge-izhi-wiiji’ag Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: Ocasionally, you shall see me flying about; I shall clean as I see litter. This is how our future world will look like. As they learn to live well, the ones who arrive. I shall clean up, shall clean those. But I also like to be fed by someone, as you throw me something to eat. I too really like fish, as the fishermen throw me their scraps. This is how I am going to help too.”

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding inga-waabamig ji-baabamiseyaan ji-babaa-biinichigeyaan imaa igoding gegoo ingoding awiiya gii-apichi-agwaawebinang.
Mii iwe bijiinag ge-ani-aye-ezhinaagooyak awe aki ji-ani-waabandamowaad.
Ji-ani-bimaadiziwaad ogowe waa-dagoshinowaad Anishinaabeg.
Inga-biinichige inga-biinitoonan inowe.
Idash inga-minwendam geniin igodiing awiiya, gegoo apagibamaagowaan ge miijiyaan.
Aapichi geniin niminwenimaa owe giigo amook, gewiin idash gegoo nindaa-apagidamaag ozhiigozhiganan gemaa gaye gii-giigookewaad awiiyag.
Mii go geniin ge-izhichigeyaan.”

paragraph.text_eng: As the snapping turtle come crawling onto the land.

sentence.sent_text: Gewiin iizan awe mikinaak bii’agwaa’oode.

paragraph.text_eng: “I have something to offer to the Anishinaabe,” he says. “He will also hear me speak. I shall pass something on to give direction to the Anishinaabe. As he hears me speak, I shall give spiritual direction to help live the good life. This is how I shall help the Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Ooh geniin gegoo inga-wiiji’aa Anishinaabe,” ikido iizan.
“Naske gaye bijiinag owe inga-noondaag ji-gaagiigoyaan.
Gegoo ji-waawiindamawag oga-ani-gikendaan owe aaniin ge-izhichiged Anishinaabe.
Inga-noondaag sa go ji-gaagigidooyaan Booshke ingoding gegoo inga-miinaa ge-onji-mino-bimaadizid.
Mii owe gegiin ge-izhi-wiiji’ag Anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: Just as you see my shell, they will find a good use for it. Just like the meat that I am carrying, I shall provide food for them. This is how I will love and care for the grandkids that are coming.

sentence.sent_text: Inashkege gaye owe gaa-ezhi-naagwad iwe nimbikwan, gegoo go owe oga-inaabajitoonaawaa, Booshke gaye owe wiiwaas gaa-bimiwidooyaan, gewiinowaa owe gegoo da-onji-wiisiwag.
Mii geniin owe ge-wiiji’ag, ge-izhi-zhawenimak owe goozhisinaan waa-dagoshing.

paragraph.text_eng: I shall not go far away; I live right here on the lake. He shall see me as I peek where he lives. I do not do this to bring fear.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin igo waasa inga-izhaasii, mii go imaa goji-gii-ayaag zaaga’igan endaayaan.
Inga-waabamig ingoding Anishinaabe gii-maabamag goji-gii-daad.
Gaawiin igo gegoo inga-gagwe-maanenimaasii.

paragraph.text_eng: I have something else to help too. This is what I will do too.

sentence.sent_text: Gegiin gegoo indayaan ge-izhi-wiiji’ag.
Mii go geniin ge-izhichigeyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: I have a lot of eggs to offer. He will find them; he will know where to find them. I also say to save me some of those eggs. Don’t take them all; just take what you need, only that which you can take.”

sentence.sent_text: Aapachi gaye ayaawaan, baatayenidoon niwaawaanoon.
Oga-mikaanaan, inga-gikenimig aandi ge-izhi-atooyaan.
Mii dash geniin ekidoyaan, bangii ishkonamawishin onowe niwaawaanoon.
Gego gakina maajiidooken, debinaak igo ji-debiseyan, minik ge-izhi-maajiidooyaban.”

paragraph.text_eng: “This is the way that I will help too,” as the mud turtle says.

sentence.sent_text: “Mii owe geniin ge-izhi-wiijitwaayaan,” gewiin iizan owe mishkwaadesi.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what he said too, “I shall do the same thing too. I also have food to offer.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go geniin owe ikido iizan, “Mii go geniin owe bezhigwan ge-izhichigeyaan.
Geniin nimbimiwidoon owe wiisiniwin.

paragraph.text_eng: I too carry eggs,” he said.

sentence.sent_text: Geniin nimbimiwidoonan waawaanoon” gii-ikidong.

paragraph.text_eng: “From time to time you shall see me on top of a rock as I watch the Anishinaabe paddling by. He knows where I am; he knows where to retrieve me from. I will always be close by.

sentence.sent_text: “Inashke ingoding imaa giga-waabamim, maagizhaa imaa ogiji-asin Inga-onzaabamaa imaa Anishinaabe gii-bimishkaad.
Ingikenimig aandi eyaayaan, ingikenimig aandi ge-onji-debinid.
Besho omaa indayaa.

paragraph.text_eng: Just like my shell. I know that I will see my shell being used in the future, this boat on my back. They may even make a dish plate out of my shell. This is how I offer mv shell.

sentence.sent_text: Inashke gaye owe nimbikwan, booshke ingodoing gaye giga-waabamaa gegoo ji-inaabajitood, owe nimbikwan ninjiimaan.
Booshke gaye owe giga-waabamaa oga-ani-odoonaaganin maagizhaa.
Anishinaa mii owe geniin ezhi-bagidendamaan ezhi-bagidenimak.

paragraph.text_eng: The Anishinaabe mav use my back for something. As in the future, they will be spiritual leaders who will learn how to use my shell. They will use it for something, and more people will learn how to utilize my shell.

sentence.sent_text: Owe nimbikwan gegoo ge-inaabaji’aad owe Anishinaabe.
Booshke gaye ogowe bijiinag danaagoziwag ogowaa gaye ge-mamaandaawiziwaad.
Gegoo go oga-naabaji’aawaa’, oga-gikendaanaawaa ge-ani-inaabaji’aawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: I shall also be close by peeking; I will not go too far away. This is how I shall help too.”

sentence.sent_text: Besho geniin omaa inga-onzaab, gaawiin igo waasa inga-izhi-maajiibayiiwesii.
Mii owe geniin ge-izhi-wiiji’iweyaan.”

paragraph.text_eng: This is the way I contribute to help the language survive for the next generation. I am passing on my teachings from my grandmother from a long time ago. Thank You.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa owe geniin ezhi-wiiji’agwaa ge-ani-bimaadiziwaad nidaazhawiinamaagen nookomis gaa-gii-miinid gichi-mewinzha.
Miigwech.

paragraph.text_eng: Okay then, now again, shall talk about these trees, what we call them these ones. There are many pine trees here where we live, here at Nigigoonsiminikaaning. Perhaps you probably call them differently. This is why I say this; everybody has different teachings, the way they were raised. This is what I am using, the way they taught me, those elders that raised me, perhaps differently. Someone different, may say it another way.

sentence.sent_text: Ahaw, nashke sa miinawaa ogowe aya’aag, mitigoog inga-dazhimaag, ezhinikaanagindwaa niinawind ongowe.
Zhingobii-waatigoog omaa gii-ayaayaang Nigigoonsiminkaaning.
Maagizhaa ge bakaan giinawaa gidizhinikaanaawaatogenag.
Mii iye ko gaa-onji-ikidoyaan bebakaan, bebakaan awiiya gegoo gii-izhi-gikino’amawaa gii-bi-ombigit awiiya.
Mii eta go ge-niin owe ayaabajitooyaan gaa-izhi-gikino’amawiwaat ogowe gichi-anishinaabeg gaa-gii-nitaawigi’iwaat.
Maagizhaa ge bakaan, bakaan wiinawaa awiiyag, day-ikidowag.

paragraph.text_eng: Now this tree with needles, the one called white spruce; oops, I just remembered. First I need to talk about this. All these trees we see in the bush have Indian names. Nanibosh gave them all Indian names when he made the earth. And that is why, that is what I tell them, people. It is very sacred when someone has a spirit name. That is why we were given Anishinaabe names. The spirit gave these to us. The spirit gave us these names so that we can carry them in a sacred manner. That is why they were so sacred, highly honored. That is why. That is how one receives good life when they take care of or honor their name. This is what my late grandmother told to me. If you think about those trees, they all have spirit names. That is why you have a spirit name. This is what my grandmother told me.

sentence.sent_text: A’awe aya’aa zhingobiiwaatik, sesegaandag gaay-izhinikaaazot.
Aya’ii tagiin omaa akawe niwii-tazhindaan.
Ogowe mitigoog gaa-waabamangwaa omaa noopiming gakina Anishinaabewinikaazowag ogowe mitigoog.
Gakina wiinzowag, gakina ogii-wiinaa’ awe Nanabosh omaa gii-ozhitoot iy aki.
Mii giin ge-izhinikaazoyin, mii iye gaa-inaad.
Mii dash owe gaa-onji-wiindamaawagwaa-ko awiiyag.
Aapiji gichi-apiitendaagwat owe wiinzowin awiiya gii-ayaat.
Mii iwe ge-giinawind gaa-onji-Anishinaabewinikaazoyang.
Gigii-miinigonaan awe.
Manidoo gigii-miinigonaan inowen wiinzowinan gaa-bimiwidamaageyang.
Mii dash owe gaa-onji-gichi-apiitendaakogin.
Mii omaa ge-onji-mino-bimaadizid awiiya weweni kanawendang awiiya owe wiinzowin.
Mii niin, ako gaa-izhit awe nookomisiban.
Nashke qi naanaagadawenimadwaa igiwe mitigook gakina, Anishinaabewinikaazowag.
Mii dash ge-giin gaa-onji-anishinaabewinikaazoyan mii, mii iye gaa-izhitaw nookomisban.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what Nanaboozhoo did, he gave all trees names. That is the white spruce that was named. There are a lot of uses for the white spruce. So he (the white spruce)was asked, “How are you going to help the Anishinaabe when they get here?”

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash iwe gaa-izhichiget owe Nanabozhoo, gakina ogii-wiinaa’ iwe mitigoo’.
Mii awe zesegaandag gaa-inind.
Niibiyo gegoo inaabadizi awe zesegaandag.
Miidog igo gaye wiin gaa-izhi-gagwejimind “Aaniin giin waa-izhichigeyan wii wiiji’at awe, Anishinaabe gaa-wii-tagoshing.”

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh there is a lot they can use me for” he said. “They might even make medicine out of me; they can use my tree-ness and my needles.”

sentence.sent_text: “Oh niibiiyo go gegoo ninga-inaabaji’ig” gii-ikido “Booshke go ingoding oga-mashkikikaagenan inowe, owe nimitigom, owe ge shingop.”

paragraph.text_eng: “Spruce” apparently is what he is called in the English, when one here uses the English language that is what the Canadians call them. And I have this one teaching, one of the ways I use the white spruce when the moose is killed. And this, a certain intestine part of the moose has inside of him, that is what I used. Using white spruce, I shrink it. I turned it inside out, that certain part of the intestine. And then I heated up the intestine. I made a fire. And then I put that spruce there. Then on top of that smoky spruce I put that moose intestine to shrink. Does it ever taste good when you do it this way.

sentence.sent_text: “Spruce” iidog izhinikaazo, zhaaganaashiiwag wemitigoozhiwag ezhinikaanaawaat.
[we wiin igo geniin ingii-izhi-kikendaan aazhaa gaa-inaabaji’ag owe zesegaandag.
Owe gii-nisind aa mooz.
Owe dash eyii, onagish omaa biinjaya’ii gaa-ayaag aa mooz.
Mii awe gaa-aabachi’ag sesegaandag ingii-ondaabiishaan i’i.
Ingii-aabooda’aan iw onagish.
Mii dash omaa ga-izhi-odaabiishamaan ingii-pootawe.
Miish dash omaa gaa-izhi-asag aa sesegaandag.
Miish dash ogidaandag ga-izhi-odaabiishamaan owe aya’ii mooz onagish.
Aapiji minopogwad inakeya’ii gii-izhichigeng.

paragraph.text_eng: And then there is the next one. The cedar tree, that was another one that was asked; “How will you help the Anishinaabe?” Nanabosh asked.

sentence.sent_text: Mii awe bezhik miinawaa.
Giizhikaandak, cedar tree, mii awe iidog aw bezhig ga-kagwejimind.
“Aaniin giin waa-izhi-wiiji’at aw Anishinaabe?” odinaan Nanabosh.

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh there are a lot of ways I can help the Anishinaabe,” he said, “When somebody has a child, when a couple has a child, they will use my wood to make the cradleboard,” he said. “I will give him all the love that I have to offer to the child. I shall bestow many visions onto him for the duration that he is in the cradlebooard. And he shall dream too. The child will have healthy bones, have a straight spine, strong and straight bones just be totally healthy if one uses the cedar. I have many uses that I can give them, when they want to make medicine from my being a tree. When someone is making a canoe, that is one use that will be used to make the strips of cedar on the bottom when someone makes it. They can make a cedar bark covering for their shelter when they want to stay warm during the winter.” That is the one, the cedar bark, that will be utilized fora roof covering. And also these trees they will make other things like rice knockers, how it was said. This is where it will come from. “There are many ways I can help the Anishinaabe, I shall care for them too.”

sentence.sent_text: “Oh niibowa go gegoo inga-izhi-wiiji’aa” ikido iinzan.
Nashke owe gii-ayaat, kii-odabinoojiimit a’a, kii-odabinoojiimiyaat.
“Niin, onowen nimitigooman oga-aabaji’aan ji-ozhitood owe tikinaaagan” gii-ikido.
“Aapiji dash inga-zhawenimaa aw abinoojiinh.
Inga-miinaa ge onowe bawaajiganan minik omaa ge-agwaakwapizod omaa tikinaaganing.
Da-bawaajige ge.
Aapiji ge oda-minogininiwan onowe opikwan ono sa go ezhi-okaanit apichi oda-minogininiwan owe giishpin aabaji’ind awe akikaandag giishkaandag.
Niibiyo sach igo ge gegoo indaa-aan inga-miinag ogowe, ge-onji-mashkikiimiyaat onowen, onowen nimitig ezhi-mitigowiyaan.
Oshke na awe gii-chiimaanikeng mii owe bezhig ge-ni-aabajitoowaat onowen owe giishka’ gii-ozhi’aad awiiya.
Booch ge naa ge apakwaanan owe gii-ozhitoowaat awiiya awe waa-dazhi-giizhoozit awiiya gii-biboong.” Mii owe a giishkanagek mii iniwen oga-pakweyaat.
Miinawaa ogowe a’aag mitigoog oga-ozhitoonaawaan gegoo boosh ke naa iniwe bawa’iganaakoon gii-ikidong.
Mii omaa ge onji.
“Niibiwa go gegoo inga-izhi-wiiji’aa aw Anishinaabe aaniishinaa inga-zhawenimaa geniin.”

paragraph.text_eng: Next I will talk about the jack pine.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa miinawaa owe akikaandag.

paragraph.text_eng: “I will also help.” That whom they call the jack pine, perhaps is what he is called. “Oh me too, I could help out the Anishinaabe. Me too! I have medicine that the Anishinaabe could use.”

sentence.sent_text: “Oh geniin igo.” Okikaandag enind jack pine maawiin izhinkaazo awe.
“Geniin igo awe indaa-wiiji’aa aw Anishinaabe.
Geniin igo indaayaan owe mashkiki ge-aabajitoowaad ogowe Anishinaabe.”

paragraph.text_eng: They will learn more about it. There is something, one thing, I would like to tell about. For instance these certain partridges the ones called spruce hens. It is these boughs that these spruce hens eat. That is where the Anishinaabe looked for them to go get when he wanted to eat the spruce hen, it is said. The spruce hen is very tame.

sentence.sent_text: Baamaa oga-ni-gikendaanaawaa.
Aaniin owe ge-naabajitoowaad ge-naabaji’aawaat iniwe owe okiikaandag.
Aya’iin igo gegoo bezhig indaa-dibaadodaan.
Nashke ogowe a’aag binewag gaa-aya’aag, mishkodese gaa-inindwaa.
Mii onowen gii-amoowaat ogowe mishkodesek.
Mii dash omaa gaa-onji-tebinaad owe anishinaabe wii-amwaat inowen mishkodeseg gii-ikidong.
Aapiji waangawizi aw mishkodese.

paragraph.text_eng: “And that is the way I will try to help the Anishinaabe.” They are easy to snare the spruce hen whenever they use a snare (on a long stick). “That is the way that I shall help the Anishinaabe.”

sentence.sent_text: “Anishinaa mii iwe geniin enendamaan ge-zhi-wiichitwaayaan.’ Mii go bizaan igo ge-izhi-michi-naabigo’oonaawaa owe mishkodese gegoo wiin baabiiginamowaat.
“Mii dash owe geniin ge-izhi-wiichi’ag awe aw Anishinaabe.”

paragraph.text_eng: Then next the balsam tree arrived. It is the balsam tree which is called this way.

sentence.sent_text: Ininaandag iidog omaa gii-pi-tagoshin.
Mii iitog owe balsam tree gaa-inind.

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh me too, I shall help in many ways. For instance, when the Anishinaabe makes camp. They will use my boughs as a floor when they need something to lie on. And for instance these things, the way that I look, it is, if someone pokes at the lumpy pitch, the blister part of that tree, from there they will get medicine. The medicine they will get from here, and they know later on how to use this medicine. There is a reason why I look like this, when the tree has all this sticky pitch. There are many uses for this. They will use this for flooring, and others will use this when they make medicine. They will have dreams as to how to use it, those Anishinaabeg when they arrive.”

sentence.sent_text: “Oh geniin, niibiyo gegoo inga-wiiji’aa.
Nashke owe gii-ozhiget aw Anishinaabe.
Mii onowen ge-apishamod onowen owe ninzhingobiim mii owe gaa-izhi-pishimod.
Nashke-ch ge onowen gaa-ayaagin owe gaa-izhinaagoziyaan owe ii, giishpin baashka’ang awe owe gegoo gii-pikobiit awe mitig.
Mii omaa oga-ondinaan omaa gegoo ini mashkiki.
Mashkiki omaa oga-ondinaan baamaa ogikendaan aaniin ge-ni-aabajitoot awe mashkiki.
Kegoo go owe wenji-izhinaagoziyaan.
Owe gii-babiikobiit owe mitik.
Niibiyo go gegoo da-inaabadizi.
Mii sa iniwen aapiji oga-apishimonikenaawaaa booshke ge aanind oga-aabaji’aawaan owe ezhi-mashkikiwaabooket awiiya.
Bijiinag oga-ni-gikendaanaawaa da-ani-bawaajigewag ogowe Anishinaabeg waa-tagoshinowaad.”

paragraph.text_eng: And there is another one, the next one. The white pine, the one they call white pine, is what they named it. I did not hear of many uses for this tree. However, it burns very well when used as firewood this pine tree.

sentence.sent_text: Mii awe miinawaa bezhig.
Biisaandago-shingwaak mii iidog igo awe a white pine, gaa-inind.
Gaawin igo aapiji awe gegoo ingii-noondanzii aaniin enaabadizid awe.
Aapiji dash a, aapiji dash minokwane awe gii-manisaanin awiiya iniwen biisaandago-shingwaakwan.

paragraph.text_eng: And then the next one, he is like the others, too. He, too, is medicinal. All the trees that grow there, they are all medicinal trees. It is only, someone will come to know how, how a person would utilize this tree, how it be would used. This is what I was told when I was being instructed in something. You will live and learn about it. Now look at this Pine. It is the same this one, when I used to see that tree. When they used to split it up in little pieces, and they would saw it up. We used to make play things out of it when we were children. This is what we did; we would bend the needles to make little snowshoes, little snowshoes just like when a child is a play.

sentence.sent_text: Mii awe miinawaa, mii go bezhigon ge awe gii-mashkikiiwit awe mitik.
Gakina go ogowe mitigoog gaa-badakizowaat gakina mashkikiwaatigoog igi.
Miish sa eta go ji-bijiinag awiiyag gegoo gii-ani-gikendang aaniin ge-ni-aabaji’aad aaniin ini mitigoon ge-ni-aabaji’aat.
Mii iye niin ko gaa-igowaan ge-waawiindamaagowaan gegoo.
Baamaa giga-kikendaan.
Nashke ge owe shingwaak gaa-inind.
Mii go bezhig ge owe, ngii-waabamaa ko owe.
Omisimiiwaat iniwen obiisaga Owaawaan ogo, ogiishgiboonaawaan.
Ingii-ayaamin ako gii-odaminwaagemin gii-abinojiiwiyaang owe.
Ingii-maaminopinaanaanig ogowe a’aag, ingii-aagimesikemin.
Mii iye gaa-izhichigeyang; aagimesag omaa tibishkoo go gii-odaminot aw abinoojiinh.

paragraph.text_eng: Then another one spoke up. “Me too! I carry medicine, Later-on the Anishinaabeg will know how to use me,” the tree said.

sentence.sent_text: Mii awe miinawaa bezhig iidog gaa-ikidod, “Ge-niin nigoo nimbim-miitoon i’i mashkiki.
Baamaa oga-kikendaan aa Anishinaabe gii-ikidogwen.

paragraph.text_eng: And now that white birch tree, he, too, has many uses. This is where a variety of things are made from. For example, as far back as I can remember, I would watch my late father. He would make snowshoes by bending that birch tree, He also made a toboggan. And when he used the bark, he made many things with it. Also the folding birch bark basket, it was said. Also when the Anishinaabe needed something for roofing. do not remember what it is called (wiigwaasabak), when they sew the birch bark together. That is what one would use for roofing material long ago, even nowadays whenever one wants to make a roof. That is the birch tree that I am talking about.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa awe wiigwaasaatik, mii owe ge miinawaa bezhik niibiyo gegoo, inaabadizi awe.
Niibiyo aapiji gegoo omaa onji-ozhichigaate.
Shke omaa, wiin igo geniin eko de-bi-kikendamaan ingii-kanawaabamaa owe gaa-oosiiyaan.
Aagima’ omaa ogii-onji-ozhi’aa’ ogii-waaginaan iniwen wiigwaasaatigoon.
Miinawaa odaabaanaakwan ogii-ozhi’aan.
Miinawaa owe ezhi-onagekod, wiigwaasaatik niibiyo omaa gegoo gii-onji-izhichigaatewan.
Miinawaa ge piskitenaaganan gii-ikidong.
Miinawaa onowen aya’ii ezhi-apakwet aw Anishinaabe.
Gaawiin nimijimendanzii ezhinikaatek (wiigwaasabak).
Gii-maawandoogwaadeg i’i wiigwaas.
Mii iye oda-apakwaanid mewinzha, Geyaabi sa go aapi gii-apakawed awiiya.
Mii awe aa birch tree gaa-inind.

paragraph.text_eng: And now for the poplar tree. Poplar tree is probably the name of it. And he too spoke up.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa awe a’a azaadi.
Poplar tree maawiin izhinikaazo.
Mii go ge awe iidog aapiji gaa-pi-dibaajimot.

paragraph.text_eng: “I too have many gifts to help the Anishinaabe. For example, when the way that my tree looks and even the smaller trees, this is where the Anishinaabe will get medicine from, when they make medicine.”

sentence.sent_text: “Niibiyo ge niin gegoo indayaan ge-izhi-wiiji’ag aa Anishinaabe.
Nashke awe gaa-izhinaagozit awe nimitik.” Aanind ge ogowe ga-babiiwizhe’iwaat mitigoonsag.
Mii omaa ge-ondinamowaad owe ge omashkikiimowaat ogowe Anishinaabeg.”

paragraph.text_eng: I also remember back when I was a child. We would eat the sap from the bark from the poplar tree. We would peel the bark of the tree. This is where we would get it from. Boy, did it ever taste good that one! It was called thick sap. It almost tastes like sugar. That is what we use to go after, later on into the summer. I, we, really liked the taste of it and this is what my late grandmother told me. “You are medicating yourselves when you eat that sap. That is medicine that you are eating” is what she used to tell me. I really liked what she said to me. I would hang out in the woods eating the sap of the tree. There are many uses for that poplar tree.

sentence.sent_text: Owe chi go ge-niin ezhi-minjimendamaan gii-abinoojiiwiyaan.
Ingii-ozibinikaanaanaan ako owe ozaadi ga-inind.
Ingii-bishagaakwawaanaan.
Miich imaa gaa-ondinimaan.
Aapichi onzaam gii-minopogwad awe.
Oziban izhinikaate.
Dibishko gegaa go, gegaa go ziinzibaakwat izhipogwat iye.
Mii dash iye gaa-noojitooyaang gaa-izhi-ishpi-niibing igo.
Aapiji niin, aapiji ningii-minopitaamin mii sa go gaa-ikidod awe nookomisiban.
“Kinoojimoo’idiz iye gii-miijiman owe oziban, mashkikii gaa-miijiyan” ingii-ig ako.
Howah sa ingii-minotawaa.
Mii go apane noopiming gii-pabaa-ayaawaan geniin, babaa-ozibanikeyaan.
Niibiyo gegoo enaabadizi a’a azaadi.

paragraph.text_eng: And then there is the big tooth aspen. I don’t remember hearing any uses for this one. I do remember hearing something from the old time Anishinaabe. It was when spring was approaching. Everyone would wait for the birch bark to be ready to be peeled so they could make their things out of birch bark. There was this one lady, my aunt, that is now deceased, that told me this. You should study the big tooth aspen. When the aspen has finished growing leaves, this is how you will know. That is when the bark is ready; that is when you will go and look at it when the aspen is finished growing leaves; this tree reall has big leaves. I can’t say the name of it, big tooth, something.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa awe maanazaadi.
Gaawiin igo aapiji gegoo awe ingii-noondanzii, enaabidizit.
Owe dash wiin ago ko gaa-izhi-noondawagwaa ogowe kichi-anishinaabeg.
Nashke iwe gii-ani-ziigwang, Gakina awiiya obii’toon owe ji-ayaag, jibwaa baabagoshkaag owe wiigwaas gegoo gii-ozhichigaadeg omaa wiigwaasing.
Mii dash ako gaa-izhit a’a bezhig a’a ingii-onoshe’inan mindimooye-iban, aazha gii-maajaa.
Owe gidaa-naanaagadawaabamaa maanizaadi.
Aapii kiizhibagizit a maanizaadi, mii omaa ji-kikendaman.
Mii ji-baabagoshkaag i’i, ji-baabagoshkaag i’i wiigwaas mii o’apii ge-ando-waabandaman giizhibagizit a’a maanizadi aapji mamaangibagizi etino’o.
[Aspen I guess that’s the name of it,] mii ezhi-zhaaganaashiiwinikaazod.
Wiigobiiwaatik, mii owe miinawaa a’a bezhig.
A’awe minawaa aa, wiigobiiwaatik gaa-inind, wiigop maayiin igo izhinikaazo aw mitik mii owe basswood enind.
Miinawaa awe bezhig aapiji gichi-aabadat owe wiigop gii-baabagonind a’awe wiigobiiwaatig.
Apane go geniin awe noongom indizhichige.
Nashke-ch dash ge awe gii-ayaat gikiizhibaabagonind ginii-biitobiigibinind.
Ingii-naanaagajitoon noongom niibinong ini mitigoon, betinaa sa onzaam naaganoon ini mitigoon.
Aapiji nanaagaakododewan gii-baategin.
Mii dash omaa gaa-onji-ozhitoowaan eyii bawaa’iganaakoon.
Wiingenaa ozaam, naanganoon wiinge ge zhooshkwaakwatoon.
Kaa memwech gegoo ingii-izhikotanziinan.
Mii eta go michipikotamaan aaapiji naangane a’a mitik.
Niibiyo maawiin igo gegoo inaabadizi iidog a’aw mashkikiwaatik.
Gakina mashkikiwaatigoog ogowe aya’aag gaa-tazhimigwaa mitigoog.
Mii owe a’a basswood gaa-inind.

paragraph.text_eng: And there is the speckled alder. It grows in lower brush area that alder. That too has many uses. Someone once told me this to use this tree when something is wrong with a child, when the child suffers from a diaper rash, but I would not go into detail how it is used. There are special protocols before someone does things like making medicine. This is what I was told. Seek out someone’s advice when you do something in a sacred manner, especially when tobacco is offered. Some offer food before cutting down a tree. This one too has its special use. Speckled alder is what it is called.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa awe adoop, tabaskobaang omaa ayaad aw adoop.
Mii go ge iye niibiyo gegoo inaabadad.
Bezhig aazha ingii-wiindamaagoban awiiya, ji ayaabajitowaan owe gii-ayaat, gegoo gii-izhi-ayaat aw abinoojiinh.
Gii-biigozhaandizot, kaawiin dash wiin igo owe indaa-dibaajimosii aaniin awe ezhichigaateg.
Aanishinaa gigootaazimigoomin owe onjigo weweni gegoo ji-izhichigeyan jibwaa ozhitooyan owe mashkiki.
Mii niin ako gaa-igoowaan.
Akawe weweni gagwejim awllya owe dash ke gaa-izhichigeng gegoo gii-bagidinigaadeg asemaa, Nashke ge omaa aanind owiiya wiisiniiwin odabagidinaanaawaa owe jibwaa giishka’ang owe mitik.
Mii awe miinawaa bezhig gechii-inaabadak.
Speckled alder iidog izhinikaazo.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what I was also told about this moon that is called throw-sickness-away-moon. You may have a different name for it. As for me I use the moon that is named the crows-return-moon, That is it how I taught my children as I watched them grow. This is the way I was taught, too. The-throw-away-sickness-moon one, that is when you will use the speckled alder tree. And so you can throw it at the moon when it is night. So it is here that you tell what you are throwing away, “I throw it away.” Choose one that is old and almost falling apart. That is the one that you use to throw with, at the moon that is up in the sky. This is when you tell her, the moon, what you are throwing away. “I am throwing it away.” Sometimes perhaps someone will throw away their sickness, or they could throw away their anger and anything that is plaguing you. This is what they tell the moon, to take the sickness away, “I do not want it to bother me anymore” is what someone will sometimes say. Use the wood that is almost falling apart, that is what I was told. That is what one would throw to the moon, the moon hanging in the sky. It is then that your sickness or your sorrow is taken from you. So that is what one use that I heard how it is used, this one called the speckled alder.

sentence.sent_text: He’enh.
Mii owe miinawaa a’a mii niin ako owe gaa-igoowaan owe webinige-giizis gaa-izhinikaazod.
Awegwen giinawaa.
A’aa niin ingii-ayaabaji’aa ko awe aya’aa andego-giizis gaa-inind.
Mii owe mii kwa apii gaa-bi-izhi-kino’amaawangwaa ge gaa-pi-ombigi’aawasoyaan.
Ge niin sa go gaa-izhi-gikino’amaagowaan.
Webinige-giizis awe, mii apii ge-aabajtooyan awe adoopiiwaatik.
Aapiji go owe gaa-biigijiisagowang.
Mii dash awe ge-apagidamowat a’awe giizis kii-tibikak gaa-agoojiing.

Mii dash omaa wiindamowat awe aaniin wegonen dinowa webinaman “Niwebinige.” Maagizhaa ingoding awiiya, adaakoziwin aetna awiiya ingoding maagizhaa ge onishkaadendamowin owebinaan maagizhaa ge gegoo, gegoo owe gaa-migoshkaasikaagod.
Mii omaa mii wiindamowat a’a giizis ji-odaapinamawig ji-maajiidood “gaawiin geyaabi owe niwii-babaamendanziin” ingoding ako gii-ikidod awiiya.
Aapiji go awe gaa-biigajiisagowid mii niin gaa-igoowaan.
Mii awe ge-apagidamowat awe dibikigiizis gaa-agoojing, mii dash omaa ji-maajiidood owe gidaakoziiwin maagizhaa ge gimaanendamowin.
Mii iwe ni-bezhig gaa-jzhi-noondamaan ako enaabadizit awe adoop gaa-inind.

paragraph.text_eng: Red willow, red willow. This is yet another one, a great medicine tree.

sentence.sent_text: Miskwaa-biimak, miskwaa-biimak.
Miinawaa awe, bezhig gichi-mashkikiwaatig.

paragraph.text_eng: Apparently the red willow said, “The Anishinaabe that are going to arrive will have many uses for me. They will come to know or perhaps they will come to dream of how to use these things.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii iidog gaa-ikidogobanen awe miskwaa-biimag “Aapiji niibiyo gegoo inga-inaabaji’ig owe a’a Anishinaabe omaa waa-tagoshing.
Bijiinag sago, da-ani-gikendamoog, omaa ge maagizhaa gegoo oga-ani-bawaadaanaawaan.”

paragraph.text_eng: And then again as for me I, too, know about this one. This red willow I use when I make little birch bark baskets. I use them to sew on the trimmings, so that it can secure/reinforce around the birch bark basket, also when one makes a winnowing basket or when wild rice is winnowed. That is the part I use, the willow part. It bends nicely, it bends very well when one uses it.

sentence.sent_text: Minik igo idash wiin igo ge-niin ezhi-gikendamaan awe miskwaa-biimagoons indaabaji’aa gii-ozhitoowaan onowe wiigwaasi-naaganensan.
Mii awe egwa’agimaa ge-onji-siito’ayaag owe wiigwaasi-naagan.
Mii sa go ge nooshkaachinaagan owe gegoo gii-ozhitood owe manoomin gaa-izhi-nooshkaachigaateg.
Mii awe ko aabajiag [miskwaabiimagoons].
Apiji miinwaagishkaa, gegoo aapiji minwaagishkaag gii-aabadizid.

paragraph.text_eng: The hazelnut tree. This one is the same as all of them; they are all medicine trees. This is one thing that I know of, the way that I used to use it when I was a child. This tree had hazelnuts growing on them. They are ball-like nuts. Probably hazelnut is what they are called in English. We used to gather them when we were children, and we ate them by breaking open the shell. This is how we got our food, how we ate by going around collecting hazelnuts. There is a lot of ways that you can use that. I’ve heard of many ways of how the medicine people use this tree. They use it in a lot of ways. That is why it is called hazelnut tree because hazelnuts grow on there.

sentence.sent_text: Bagaanimizhiig.
Mii go ge awe bezhig a’a, mii maawiin igo gakina ayaawaad mashkikiwaatigo-iwaat igiwe.
Aya’ii dash ko geniin bezhig nindizhi-gikendaan gaa-inaabaji’ag Owe sago abinoojiiwiyaan.
Bagaanag omaa gii-nitaa-wigiwag gii-ani-tagwaagig.
Babiikwaadaminagiziwag igiwe bagaanag, hazel nut iidog izhinikaazo zhaaganaashiiwinikaazod.
Mii dash iko igiwe gaa-maawanji’angidwaa gii-abinoojiiwiyaang mii dash gaa-izhi-amowangidwaa mii go bizaan igo mii sa eta basa’angidwaa.
Mii omaa gaa-onji-wiisiniyaang babaa-ando-bagaaneyaang.
Mii awe miinawaa bezhig niibiyo gegoo inaabadizi awe, niibiyo aazha gegoo o’apii nindizhi-noondam enaabaji’aawaad ogiwe gaa-nanaandawi’iwewaad awiiyag.
Niibiyo gegoo inaabadizi.
Mii owe gaa-onji-izhinikaazod bagaanimizh, bagaanag omaa nitaawigiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: Pin cherry, this too is another one with medicine. There are a lot of berries growing on it. My grandmother used to tell me to gather up the berries. She used to make something out of it. She made it into tea. “Here take a drink of this,” she said to me. This must be her medicine water; however, I did not ask her what it was for. I had a lot of respect for my grandmother, and whatever she told me, that is what I did.

sentence.sent_text: Bawa’iminaanagazh, mii go awe bezhigwan ge-wiin.
Niibiyo omaa gegoo agoodeni omaa ezhi-nitaawiging.
Ingii-ig ako nookomisiban ji-moozhaginamaan iniwen bawa’iminaanan gaa-izhinikaadegin.
Gegoo dash go ogii-ozhitoonan, ogii-gabaatoonan.
“Nashke owe minikwen” indig.
Mii dog omaa, mii iidog owe omashkikiiwaaboom gaawiin-shk ke ingii-gagwejimaasii aaniin enwaadang iwe.
Anishinaa ingii-manaazimaa aapiji nookomisiban.
Mii go gegoo wiindamawid mii iye gaa-mii go iye gaa-ani-izhichigeyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: And then there is the choke cherry tree. That tree has choke cherries growing on it. I have a lot of uses for that tree. Once I made choke cherry jelly with those choke cherries. That jam tastes really good. That tree is also a great medicine tree.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa awe a’a asasaweminaganzh izhinikaazo.
Mii go ge awe, aapiji niibiyo gegoo omaa nitaawiginoon asasaweminan.
Niibiyo go ge-niin aazha gegoo nim-bi-inaabajitoon iwe.
Aabiding ingii-ozhitoon eya’ii baashkiminsigan ingii-baashkiminisaanan iniwen asasaweminan, Aapiji mino-pogwadoon eya’ii.
Mii owe ge bezhig gichi-mashkikiiwaatig.

paragraph.text_eng: Juniper. This is another one of the needled trees. Wherever it is a smooth rocky area is where this can be seen. This is what the white man calls juniper. Again this one has many good uses also. All the trees that we see have many uses for them.

sentence.sent_text: Gaagaagiwaandag.
Mii miinawaa a’a bezhig, zhingobiiwaatig, aya’iing.
Ingoji gii-zhooshkwanaabikaag mii iidinong naagozid.
Mii maawiin iye juniper gaa-izhinikaanaad wemitigoozhi.
Mii go awe niibiyo gegoo, niibiyo gegoo inaabadizi.
Niibiyo gakina, niibiyo gegoo inaabidiziwag ogowe mitigoog gaa-waabamangwaa.

paragraph.text_eng: Sumac. And then there is this other one. This one grows all over the place. As children we would eat the things that grew on this tree, They taste really good. I am not sure what they are called. They look like little red berries. I think the white man calls it sumac. This is where the pipe stem is made from. When someone makes a pipe, this is where the stem is made from.

sentence.sent_text: Opwaaganaatig.
Mii awe miinawaa bezhig.
Miziwe aapiji nitaawigi a’a dinowa.
Eya’ii omaa ingii-miijimin ako gii-abinoojiiwiyaang onowen gaa-nitaawigingin omaa e’iing.
Aapiji minopogwadoon.
Amanji igo ezhinikaategwen owe, indigo miskominensan ezhinaagokin.
Sumac iidog odizhinikaanaawaan wemitigoozhiwag.
Mii dash omaa wenji-ozhi’aawaad.
Wenji-ozhichigaadeg okij okijiiwaatig a’a opwaagan awiiya gii-ozhi’aad.

paragraph.text_eng: We know what to do when we are doing these things. No one should cut down a tree for no reason. Only if one has a purpose for it. That is what I was told not to do. Do not cut down a tree without a purpose. Only if you have a reason to use it like making medicine or if one were to make a pipe stem. It is the same as when you use the alder, Even though the tree is rotten or falling, you should do something for the tree. You should also honor the tree and tell it why you are cutting it down. This is what I was always told; they are someone. All the trees that you see standing, all of them are someone. That is someone that is standing. It also has a name. That is why vou show respect to it. You do not cut it down for no reason. This is what I was told; you should have respect for all things. Thank you.

sentence.sent_text: Anishinaa gigikendaamin owe ezhichigeyang.
Gaa wiikaa awiiya anishaa odaa-giishka’waasiin ini mitigoon.
Onjida igo gegoo ji-inaabadizid awe mitig.
Mii go ge-niin gaa-onji’igowaan.
Gego wiin anishaa go giishka’waakwen igi mitigoog.
Gego eta go wii-inaabaji’ad wii-mashkikikaageyan gemaa ge owe gegoo okij awiiya gii-ozhitood.
Gemaa-ch ge awe aa adoopiiwaatig.
Aanawi gii-biigijiisagowid aw mitig ge weweni gidaa-izhi aa gegoo.
Weweni ge gidaa-gagiizomaa aaniin wiin wenji-giishkiga wad a’aw mitig.
Mii iye niin ako gaa-izhi-wiindamaagowaan.
Awiiya go ogowe.
Awiiya igiwe mitigoog ingoji gii-waabamad badakizod aw mitig.
Awiiya owe gaa-niibawid.
Wiinzowin ge odayaan.
Mii dash wenji-manaaji’ad.
Gaawiin anishaa gigiishkiga’waasii.
Mii niin ako iye gaa-izhi-waawiindamaagowaan gidaa-manaajitoon gegoo.
Miigwech.

paragraph.text_eng: One thing I heard the elders say is that, “Someday the world will end.” I didn’t know the reason for them saying that.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go bezhig gaa-noondawagwaa ingiw chi-aya’aag gii-ikidowaad, “Booch igo ingoding da-ishkwaa-akiiwan.” Gaawiin ingikendanziin awegonen aaniin gaa-onji-ikidod iko.

paragraph.text_eng: “The Chimookomaan is going to ruin the Earth,” they would say. You see they started knowing that a long time ago. And that is what we see today how the Chimookomaan is ruining our land, the Creator’s land, that we live on. We don’t own the land, the Creator does.

sentence.sent_text: “Mii aw Chi-mookomaan ge-nishwanaajitood o’ow aki.” gii-ikidowag.
Nashke mewinzha ogii-maajii-gikendaanaawaa iw.
Mii dash noongom azhigwa waabandamang i’iw keyaa ge-izhi-nishwanaajitood aw Chi-mookomaan iw gidakiiminaan iw Manidoo odakiim o’ow anishaa gidabiitaamin o’ow.
Gaawiin gidibendanziimin o’ow aki, manidoo odibendaan.

paragraph.text_eng: See they have taken all the trees, every single different kind of tree. The trees give us life. And also our lakes, the Chimookomaan is ruining them too. He spills in many harmful things, and all over our fish now too, are feeling the effects of the Chimookomaan’s ways of spoiling them.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke, mii akina azhigwa ingiw mitigoog azhigwa mamigaazowaad bebakaan akina ingoji ingiw mitigoog.
Gi-bi-maaji’igonaanig ingiw mitigoog.
Miinawaa gaye gizaaga’iganiminaanin, onishwanaajitoonaawaa iniw zaaga’iganan ingiw Chi-mookomaanag.
Niibowa imaa oziigwebinaan mayaanaadadinig, akina go ingoji miish ingiw gigiigoonyiminaanig zhigwa ge wiinawaa azhigwa, moozhitoowaad iw ezhi-nishwanaajichiged aw Chi-mookomaan.

paragraph.text_eng: Now over there in the place called Bad River, over there, they want to dig a big hole to dig up some kind of metal. And there is the lake, in which the toxins will run into, and the Anishinaabeg over there will be unfortunate, by the fish that they eat being infected with toxins.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ge iwidi Mashkiziibiing ezhi-wiinjigaadeg mii iwidi, wii-chi-waanikewaad miinawaa wii-moona’amowaad awegodogwen dinowa biiwaabik.
Miish imaa zaaga’iganiing ge-izhijiwang i’iw maanaadadinig, mii ge-wiinawaa iwidi akeyaa anishinaabeg da-inigaazowaad, da-miikoshkaagowaad iw maanaadadinig ingiw giigoonyag ge-wiinawaa emwaawaajin.

paragraph.text_eng: See, these unknown creatures, the ones that are coming into our river, from Lake Superior and some come from the ocean, whatever kind of insects they are. That is how they kill our fish. They go around there on the sea, and also some of them from overseas, they stick onto their boats and that is what brings them over here. And also the big river, called the Great St. Lawrence Seaway, that is where now they drive the ships in, that is where the ships come in at. And that is where they detach, and then they crawl around and eat our fish, like when they suck the blood out of the fish, that is what they do.

sentence.sent_text: Shke go ge ongow mayagi-manidoog ba-izhaajig omaa giziibiiminaaning, chi-gamiing wenjibaajig aanind gii owidi chi-agaaming onjibaawag ingiw wegodogwen dinowa manidoonsag.
Mii ezhi-nisaawaad ingiw, iniw gigiigoonyiminaanan.
Mii imaa baa-ayaawaad iw chi-agaaming ingiw chi-mookomaanag miinawaa ingiw wenjibaajig oodi chi-agaaming, mii ezhi-agokenid imaa ojiimaaniwaang iniw, mii dash imaa ba-izhiwinaawaad.
Nashke ow gichi-ziibi, chi-anishinaabe-ziibi “Great St.
Lawrence Seaway” izhinikaadeg, mii imaa azhigwa bi-biindigebizowaad bi-biindigemagak iniw chi-jiimaanan.

Miish imaa mii omaa bakwazikaawaad ingiw, mii dash ezhi-baamoodewaad miish ezhi-amwaawaad iniw nigiigoonyiminaanan, dibishkoo go ingiw giigoonyag omiskwiimiwaa wiikwanjigaadeni mii ezhichigewaad ingiw.

paragraph.text_eng: Everything is changing, different things are happening. That is why those elders said, “Someday the world will end, then Chimookomaan is ruining the Earth.”

sentence.sent_text: Akina gegoo aanjisemagad, bakaan izhiwebad.
Mii iw gaa-onji-ikidowaad ingiw chi-anishinaabeg, “ingoding da-ishkwaa-akiiwan aw chi-mookomaan onishwanaajitoon o’ow aki.”

paragraph.text_eng: We re seeing it now, and I too see it. You see, recently I had a birthday; I am 65-vears-old and now, I see what those elders were talking about. Those elders knew everything.

sentence.sent_text: Mii azhigwa waabandamang ge-niin igo niwaabandaan.
Nashke imaa noomaya ingii-tibishkaa ningodwaasimidana-ashi-naano-biboonagiz noongom azhigwa mii zhigwa waabandamaan i’iw gaa-tazhindamowaad ingiw chii-aya’aag.
Ogii-kikendaanaawaa akina gegoo ingiw chi-aya’aag.

paragraph.text_eng: They also dreamt, those Anishinaabe had a lot of dreams. They didn’t make up what they were telling about, I believe them. That is what those elders said, Someday you will see it; someday you will know it.” And I see it today; we see it, how the Eearth is being ruined.

sentence.sent_text: Ogii-pawaadaanaawaa gaye, niibowa ko ingiw anishinaabeg gii-pawaajigewag.
Gaawiin anishaa ogii-michi-giizhitoosiinaawaa iw gaa-tibajindamowaad, indebwetawaag.
Mii iw gaa-ikidowaad ingiw chi-aya’aag, “Ingoding giga-waabandaan ingoding giga-gikendaan.” Mii dash noongom waabandamaan, giwaabandaamin ezhi-nishwanaajichigaadeg iw gidakiiminaan.

paragraph.text_eng: Even the lakes, that are here, like Mille Lacs Lake, and now our quota is being cut as to how many fish we can take. The Chimookomaan takes many, and he wastes a lot.

sentence.sent_text: Wawaaj ige imaa zaaga’iganan eyaamagak shke ge ow Misi-zaaga’igan, mii azhigwa noongom azhigwa giishkizha’amaagooyang minik ge-mamangwaa ingiw giigoonyag endaso-ziigwang.
Niibowa aw chi-mookomaan omamaan, niibowa ge onishwanaaji’aan iniw giigoonyan.

paragraph.text_eng: See even now what is happening outside, it doesn’t snow very much anymore in the winter. After all, over there too, way up north, those glaciers that float around, they too are melting. That is where the water flows from up there.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke gaye o’o wawaaj igo shke agwajiing ezhiwebak biboong gaawiin geyaabi chi-zoogiposinoon.
Anishnaa owidi gaye iwidi, giiwedinong akeyaa chi-waasaa ingiw chi-mikwamiig iko egonjingig, miish gaye wiinawaa azhigwa ningizowaad.
Mii imaa ba-izhijiwang iw nibi.

paragraph.text_eng: The Earth is now drying up, that is what I heard the Chimookomaan say that it is already drying up. It is gradually getting hotter. See it’s been a long time, about 20 years now since it really snowed a lot. Long ago it really snowed and snowed. Indeed the snow was deep, three or four feet deep. Not anymore, there is barely any snow here today.

sentence.sent_text: Mii azhigwa baatemagak i’iw gidakiiminaan indazhi-noondawaag ingiw chi-mookomaanag iko ikidowaad zhigwa baatemagak.
Eshkam igo ani-gizhaatemagad.
Shke mewinzha ingoji go niizhtana daso-biboon azhigwa gaa-ako-gichi-zoogipog.
Mewinzha igo gichi-zaazoogipon.
Geget gii-ishpatemagad azhigwa go nisozid, niiwozid gii-apiichishin aw goon.
Gaawiin geyaabi agaawaag omaa bimi-ayaa goon noongom.

paragraph.text_eng: And also the animals are being ruined by them. They don’t know what is happening to them, now it gets warm too early, they come back when it’s too cold and some freeze to death, And all of these ones outside you see, those rabbits and deer, they are all starting to taste differently now, the fish too. And see the Chimookomaan farmer, he uses many different kinds of things when he farms, to sprout, he uses fertilizers adding them in so that what he plants grows well. This animals eat this and that is what makes them sick. They too have various types of sicknesses.

sentence.sent_text: Mii ge ingiw neshwanaaji’igowaajin ingiw awesiinyag.
Gaawiin ogikendanziinaawaa aaniin akeyaa ezhiwebadinig, mii zhigwa noonde-aabawaag mii zhigwa bi-azhe-giiwewaad miinawaa zasikaa izhi gichi-gisinaamagak miinawaa mii gawajiwaad gaye aanind.
Ingiw gaye akina omaa agwajiing ingiw nashke ingiw waaboozoog miinawaa ingiw waawaashkeshiwag, bebakaan azhigwa gaye wiinawaa ani-ayipogoziwag giigooyag gaye.
Nashke aw chi-mookomaan aw gitgiewinini niibowa bebakaan odabajitoonan gitiged imaa, ezaagakiinig mashkikiinsan odaabajitoon odagonaanan imaa da-nitaa-maajiiging ingiw getigaadang.
Mii miijiwaad ingiw awesiinyag mii ezhi-akoziishkaagowaad, Anooj ezhi-inaapinewaad ge wiinawaa.

paragraph.text_eng: I see that too.

sentence.sent_text: Mii waabandamaan ge iw.

paragraph.text_eng: Indeed those elders speak the truth, they told the truth when they told of the Chimookomaan ruining the Earth, The end of the Earth is probably near.

sentence.sent_text: Geget debwewag ingiw chi-aya’aag gii-tebwewag gii-tibaajimowaad da-nishwanaajitood aw chi-mookomaan o’ow aki.
Geget ganabaj beshwendaagwad iw da-ishkwaa-akiiwang.

paragraph.text_eng: I wish the Anishinaabe, the young Anishinaabe, would hurry to know how to properly offer tobacco, to pray someday and to speak.

sentence.sent_text: Begish ingiw Anishinaabeg oshki-anishinaabeg wewiibitaawaad da-gikendamowaad nitaa-asemaakewaad, da-gaagiizitaagoziwaad ingoding da-gaagiigowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: See it was the manidoo who gave our language to the Anishinaabe. He can’t hear the Anishinaabe now, only a very few speak Ojibwe. Long ago everyone spoke Ojibwe. All of the manidoo heard them. Nowadays, only every once and awhile someone speaks.

sentence.sent_text: Shke aw Manidoo gaa-miinaad iniw Anishinaaben iw gidinwewininaan.
Ogwiinitawaan iniw Anishinaaben azhigwa, bebangii eta go awiya ojibwemo.
Mewinzha ko akina awiya gii-nitaa-ojibwemod.
Akina ingiw Manidoog ogii-noondawaawaan.
Noongom dash apaapii eta go awiya gaagiigido.

paragraph.text_eng: I hope the new speakers can offer tobacco, I hope they can speak for the tobacco to get help. That’s all.

sentence.sent_text: Begish nitaa-asemaakewaad begish nitaa-apagizomawaad iniw asemaan da-wiidookaagoziwaad ingiw noongom weshki-ojibwemojig.
Mii iw.

paragraph.text_eng: Indeed it is important that people use this Ojibwe language. You see, there is a lot of things we do and when we give names as well as when we offer our tobacco, when we have our dances, our Mide lodges, sweat lodges, at funerals, everything.

sentence.sent_text: Geget apiitendaagwad i’iw aabajitood awiya ow Ojibwemowin.
Nashke, niibowa gidizhichigemin gegoo gaye ge-wiindaawasoyang miinawaa gaye asemaakeyang, niimii’idiiyang, midewiyang, madoodooyang, maajaa’iweng, akina gegoo.

paragraph.text_eng: See, there aren’t a lot that do this, they are few. See long time ago they fasted in order to know things. Some of them were taught by their parents a long time ago,

sentence.sent_text: Nashke gaawiin niibowa ayaasiin aw ge-izhichiged gegoo, bangiishehnwagizi.
Ke mewinzha ko gii-kii’igoshimowag da gegoo da-gikendamowaad.
Miinawaa aanind ge ogii-kikingoo’amaagowaan iniw ogitiziimiiwaan mewinzha.

paragraph.text_eng: See this naming ceremony, when someone is given a name, I was eleven years old when I was spiritually given the right to give someone their name. But I didn’t know. See after I saw a manidoo, I wouldn’t be able to forget him. I didnt tell anyone about it until after I got out of the service was when I told those elders about it

sentence.sent_text: Nashke o’o shke bezhig iw wiindaawasowin awiya miiniind odizhinikaazowin, ingii-asho-bezhigo-biboonigiz, gii-miinigooziyaan iw awiya da-miinag odizhinikaazowin.
Gaawiin dash ingii-gikendanziin, shke gaa-waabamag manidoo, gaawiin niwii-poonenimaasiin.
Gaawiin ge ingii-tibaajimosiin baamaa go gaa… baamaa go gaa-ishkwaaj-zhimaaganishiiwiyaan apii gii tibaajimotawagwaa ingiw chi-ayaa’aag.

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh, you’ve been given something.There is a reason you saw him. Oo, he didn’t tell me anything.”

sentence.sent_text: “Haw gegoo…gegoo gigii-onji…gigii-miinig.
Gegoo gigii-onji-waabamaa.” “Oo, gaawiin ingii-wiindamagosiin gegoo.”

paragraph.text_eng: So when I was about forty, that’s when I took an offering to a medicine man, a bundle, that’s why I went to see him and I said to him, “What was the reason for me seeing him (the manidoo)?”

sentence.sent_text: Ingoji go dash gaa-niimidana-daso-biboonagiziyaan mii apii gii-o-bagidinamawag aw nanaanda’iwewinini obagijigan aandi gaa-onji-waabamag aw, “Aaniish gaa-onji-waabamag wa aw?” ingii-inaa.

paragraph.text_eng: “Come over tomorrow and I’ll tell you.”

sentence.sent_text: “Bi-izhaakan waabang ga-wiindamoon.”

paragraph.text_eng: On the next day I went there to go see him.

sentence.sent_text: Wayaabang gaa-izhi-izhaayaan gii-o-waabamag.

paragraph.text_eng: “Oo I had a dream of him; he gave you something.”

sentence.sent_text: “Oo!
Ingii-pawaanaa aw, gegoo gigii-miinig.”

paragraph.text_eng: “Ahaw, who, what is it he has given me?” I said to him.

sentence.sent_text: “Ahaw, wenesh, awegonesh gaa-miizhid?” indinaa.

paragraph.text_eng: “No, I shouldn’t tell you; someday you will know.”

sentence.sent_text: “Gaan, gaawiin indaa-wiindamoosinoon giin, ingoding giga-gikendaan.”

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what those elders always said, “You’ll know someday.” So you see it wasn’t until ten years later that I knew the reason why I saw the one I saw.

sentence.sent_text: Mii apane ikidowaad ingiw chi-ayaa’aag “Ingoding giga.” Nashke baamaa gaa-midaaso biboonagak apii gii-kikendamaan iw gaa-onji-waabamag aw gaa-waabamag.

paragraph.text_eng: That’s what those men said, those old men that I sat with, “You got a name from their names. Oo.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish iw gaa-ikidowaad ingiw waadabimagig ingiw ininiwag akiwenziyag, “Izhinikaazowin imaa gidoondinaan izhinikaazowinan.” “Oo.”

paragraph.text_eng: So that’s how I too am able to give someone their name, from my vision I had. And since I started, I now dream a lot about my dream spirits. So that is why I am able to help out my fellow Anishinaabe. Indeed it is hard to do; he is busy; they keep him busy the one who does it.

sentence.sent_text: Mii ge niin wenji-gashkitooyaan da-miinag awiiya odizhinikaazowin, ow gaa-inaabanjigeyaan.
Miinawaa gaa-ako-maajitaayaan, azhigwa niibowa zhigwa nibawaajige nibawaajiganag.
Mii ge niin iw wenji-gashkitooyaan da-wiidookawag aw niij-anishinaabe.
Geget zanagad a’aw gegoo da-izhichiged ojaanimizi…ojaanimi’aa a’aw ezhichiged.

paragraph.text_eng: See my one cousin who lives close by here, the one named Obizaan, they keep, that little old man busy. He is hired to do all sorts of things, he does it skillfully too. And he teaches me. He is the one I sit with and help when he is doing something. See even when he does funerals, it takes a long time. I sit with him when he does it. I listen to him.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke aw bezhig niitaawis omaa besho eyaad Obizaan ezhinikaazod ojaanimi’aa a’aw akiiwenziins.
Anooj inanoonaa da-izhichiged, wawiingezi ge gegoo izhichiged.
Aanigikinoo’amaag ge gegoo.
Mii aw waadabimag waadookawag gegoo izhichiged.
Nashke ge wawaaj iw maajaa’iwed, giiwenzh azhigwa izhichige i’iw.
niwiidabimaa ge ezhichiged.
Imbizindawaa.

paragraph.text_eng: See the one that taught him, it was in the late 1800s that, that elder who raised him, the one who taught him was born. I can’t deny what my cousin says. I listen to him carefully.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke aw gaa-gikinoo’amaagojin in the 1800s…late 1800s gii-ondaadiziwan iniw chi-ayaa’aan gaa-nitaawigi’igojin gaa-gikinoo’amaagojin.
Gaawiin indaa-aagonwetawaasiin gegoo ikidod a’aw niitaawis.
Weweni imbizindaawaa.

paragraph.text_eng: I hope that these new Ojibwe speakers today, more pursue to learn the culture of the Anishinaabe. When something is wrong with someone, asks for a name, a funeral, everything. I wish more would pursue it, that they help their fellow Anishinaabe. Yeah it’s hard, it isn’t enough for someone to speak good Ojibwe when they help their fellow Anishinaabe when something happens to them. Then indeed it will be more important.

sentence.sent_text: Begish ingiw weweni noongom weshki-ojibwemojig, nawaj igo biminizha’amowaad gagwe-gikendamowaad iw keyaa ezhitwaad aw Anishinaabe.
Gegoo izhiwebizid gego nandodang izhinikaazowin maajaa’iwewin akina gegoo.
Begish nawaj biminizhang o’o, mii ge-onji-wiidookawaad iniw wiij-anishinaaben.
Geget zanagad iw, gaawiin go debisemagasinoon iw awiya da-nitaa-ojibwemod wiidookawaad iniw wiij-anishinaaben gego izhiwebizinid.
Mii iw geget ge-apiitendaagwak nawaj.

paragraph.text_eng: That is as much as I’m going to tell you guys for now. I don’t know everything; I know only a little bit, but those elders told me what I have talked about here. If some challenge me by saying, “Your lying,” then those elders that raised me must have been lying too. That’s enough.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iw minik omaa ge-izhi-wiindamoonagog noongom.
Gaawiin gakina gegoo niin ingikendanziin bangiishehn eta niin gegoo ingikendaan ow dash go debaajindamaan ingiw chi-ayaa’aag ingii-wiindamaagoog.
Giishipin awiya ge-aagonwetawid, “Gigiiwanim” izhid, mii go gii-kiiwanimowaagwen ingiw chi-ayaa’aag gaa-nitaawig’ijig.
Mii iw minik.

paragraph.text_eng: Long ago it was the custom for the young boys befor e they became young men they were put out to fast. I heard it like this. It was in the early morning; I think charcoal ash was put on their faces, maybe, I’m not sure if it was charcoal, something was used. It was here that they were told to go fasting.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha ko ingiw gwiiwizensag azhigwa, dabwaa-oshki-ininiwiwaad igo gii’igoshimo’aawag.
Ingii-izhi-noondam.
Chi-gigizheb ko, ganabaj akakanzhe omag oshitigwaaniwaang gii-ganabaj namanj akakanzhe gegoo gii-aabajichigaade.
Mii oma, gii-wiindamawindwaa da-gii’igoshimowaad

paragraph.text_eng: Ido not know where they went, far into the woods to fast. See when someone went fasting, they can’t drink water; they cant eat anything; they can’t put anything in their mouth when they are fasting, is how I heard it.

sentence.sent_text: Dibi-sh gaa-izhaawaagwen di megwayaak waasa gii-baa-gii’igoshimowaad.
Nashke gii’igoshimod awiiya, gaawiin gegoo odaa-minikwesiin nibi miinawaa gaawiin gegoo odaa-miijisiin, gaawiin gegoo odaa-atoosiin omaa odooning gii’igoshimod, ingii-izhi-noondam.

paragraph.text_eng: I do not know how long they were to go out fasting, maybe two days, three days, four days, however long they were able to. And then when they finished their fast, I don’t know, maybe when they had began to dream, maybe they dreamt while they were fasting, maybe someone came to them. I dont know, maybe they were finished when someone came to them, or perhaps when they had dreamed. They received something in a spiritual way.

sentence.sent_text: Namanj igo minik gaa-ayaawaagwen gii-paa-gii’igoshimowaad, maagizhaa niizhogon, nisogon, niiwogon namanj minik igo ge-gashkitoowaad.
Mii dash iw gaa-ishkwaa-gii’igoshimowaad, namanj igo apii azhigwa gii-maaji-bawaajigewaad maagizhaa ge megwaa gii’igoshimowaad gii-paawaajigewag, maagizhaa awiya ogii-pi-odisigowaan.
Namanj igo maagizhaa, wiikaa gaa-ish… gaa-kiizhiitaawaad mii apii maagizhaa awiiya gaa-pii-odisigowaagwen, maagizhaa gaa-pawaajigewaagwen.
Gegoo Sa go gii-miinigooziwag.

paragraph.text_eng: It is from that the Anishinaabe came to know things. See, those healers fasted long ago; someone came to them, pitied them. That is how they came to know the way to do their doctoring. And those medicine men, the ones who know all about the medicine were shown (in a spiritual way)the way the medicine was to be used, how it looked sprouting out of the ground, to be useful.

sentence.sent_text: Mii aw Anishinaabe gaa-onji-gikendang gegoo.
Nashke gii-kii’igoshimowag ingiw mewinzha nanaandawi’iwewininiwag, ogii-pi-odisigowaan awiya, ogii-pi-zhawenimigowaan.
Mii gaa-onji-gikendamowaad keyaa da-nanaandawi’iwewaad.
Miinawaa ge ingiw mashkikiwininiwag, akina gekendangig gegoo mashkiki waabanda, waabanda’igooziwag iw enaabadak iw mashkiki aaniin ezhinaagwak iw zayaagakiig da-aabajichigaadeg.

paragraph.text_eng: And some were blessed with the way to name children, to give someone a name, or maybe more than one name. It is from fasting that it (the ability to give names)comes from.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa gaye aanind gii-shawendaagoziwag akeyaa da-wiindaawasowaad, da-miinaawaad awiya izhinikaazowin, maagizhaa izhinikaazowinan.
Mii imaa gaa-onzikaamagak gii-kii’igoshimod.

paragraph.text_eng: The Anishinaabe was spiritually given everything when he fasts—medicines, doctoring, naming, everything that the Anishinaabe does. hunting, and even the ability to be skilled at crafts, he was spiritually given.

sentence.sent_text: Akina gegoo gii-miinigoowizi a’aw Anishinaabe gii’igoshimod, mashkikiwan, nanaadawi’iwewin, wiindaawasowin, akina gegoo ezhichiged aw Anishinaabe, giiyosewin igo gaye wawaaj miinawaa ge nitaa-ozhitood gegoo gii-miinigoowi.

paragraph.text_eng: But these days you see, not very many young men go fasting anymore. That is why we don’t have those traditional healers and eatdictie ane fodee Those young men are busy sitting inside the house, playing things. They no longer spend time outdoors; they no longer go around in the woods; they don’t fast.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke dash noongom gaawiin…gaawiin awiya ganabaj gwech awiya gii’igoshimosiin aw oshki-inini geyaabi.
Mii wenji-ayaawaasiwangwaa ingiw nanaandawi’iwewininiwag noongom mashkiki-ininiwag noongom.
Ondamiziwag ingiw oshki-ininiwag biindig imaa waakaa’iganing namadabiwaad, odaminowaad gegoo.
Gaawiin geyaabi agwajiing baa-izhaasiiwag gaawiin geyaabi ingoji megwayaak baamaadizisiiwag gaawiin gii’igoshimosiiwag.

paragraph.text_eng: That is how the Anishinaabe came to know things long ago. I think I only fasted for only one day. Maybe that’s why I don’t know that stuff.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iw mewinzha gaa-onji-gikendang aw Anishinaabe gegoo.
Ganabaj eta niin ganabaj eta go ningo-giizhig ingii-kii igoshim.
Mii ganabaj niin gegoo wenji-gikendanziwaan.

paragraph.text_eng: The girls did it differently when they became young ladies. But I shouldn’t tell about that. A woman should tell about it, what is said to the girl when she turns into a woman. A woman will tell about that, not a man. That is all I want to tell about fasting.

sentence.sent_text: Bakaan wiin pii-izhichigewag ingiw ikwezensag gii-ikwezensiwiwaad.
Gaawiin dash niin indaa-dibaajimosiin iw.
Ikwe aw ge-dibaajimopan, keyaa gaa-izhi’ind a’aw ikwezens, azhigwa wii-ni-aanjikwewid.
Ikwe a’aw ge-dibaajidang i’iw, gaawiin wiin inini.
Meta go minik waa-izhi-wiindamaageyaan ayi’ii gii’igoshimowin.

paragraph.text_eng: I still hear some say that when turning into men, or old men, some say, “I fasted.”

sentence.sent_text: Aanind wiin go geyaabi noongom azhigwa gaa-ininiiwiwaad aw awi-akiwenziiwiwaad aanind ninoondawaag ikidowaad iw “ingii-kii’igoshim.”

paragraph.text_eng: I don’t know when, I don’t think it is written, how old they should be too fast. I’m not sure. Long ago it was little boys, young men who were told to go fasting. That is as much as want to tell about that.

sentence.sent_text: Namanj ow apii, gaawiin ganabaj ingoji ozhibii’igaadesinoon gii-daso-biboonagizid a’aw gii igoshimod.
Mii go namanj igo apii ganabaj.
Mewinzha wiin go gwiiwizensag, oshkinaweg gii-izhi aawag da-gii’igoshimowaad.
Mii iw minik maa debaajindamaan wiin i’iw.

chapter.eng_title: Why Does He Look That Way?

paragraph.text_eng: I will tell you guys a little bit more. Go ahead and turn that thing on over there.

sentence.sent_text: Minawaa dash igo bangii giga-wiindamooninim giinawaa.
Maano da-dibiskanemagad iwedi go gaye.

paragraph.text_eng: When we were small/young those elders, Iikwez and Ojiiganang lived in a small house. My grandmother and grandfather (who passed on)it was small; in English they say, small house, that they lived in. And as we looked over there in the corner a little bit above he was hanging, the drum. And there when we looked over there in the direction of the corner up above he was hanging there, that drum, the one that they called the Thunderbird Drum.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-pi-agaashiiyeyaang gii-agaasode iw waakaa’igan gaa-abiitamowaad ingiw gichi ayaa’aag Iikwez miinawaa Ojiig-anang.
Nookomisiban minawaa nimishoomisiban gii-agaasatemagad mii iw zhaaganaashiimong ikido a small house na gaa-biitamowaad.
Mii dash imaa inaabiyaang iwedi, iwedi keyaa jaangate bangii go indigo ishpiming gii-agooji mii iwedi gii-agoojid aw dewe’iigan a’aw gaa-izhinikaanaawaad ko aw binesi-dewe’igan.

paragraph.text_eng: I am going to go ahead anyways and tell it.

sentence.sent_text: Maano idash inga-tibaajim.

paragraph.text_eng: When I was small, maybe I was about eight, maybe eight years, well maybe only seven years old. And so over there I seen that drum sitting there over there in the corner over there up a little bit over there he sat always, And what was hanging from his belt it looked like little coins there on his belt, do you guys understand? The belt of that drum the coins that hung there from that drum had over there, he was where those elders lived. That’s what I looked at me and my older brother; we would always look at that, examine that, as I looked at those animate beings. And I went close and carefully looked at it, examined it, hanging. Behold it was that written there, cracker jack. And so there on the other side it was written, “signs of the zodiac.”

sentence.sent_text: Gii-agaashiiyiyaan maagizhaa eta go giin ingii-ishwaaso biboonagiz maagizhaa eta go giin ningii-niizhwaaso biboonagiz.
Mii dash iwedi waabamag aw dewe’igan iwedi namadabid iwedi zhaangateg iwedi ishpiming go bangii iwedi gii-namadabi apane.
Mii dash imaa gii-agoodenig maa ogijipizoning iniw dibishkoo gaa-izhi-naagwakin zhooniyaasag maa ogijipizon gekendaanaawaa ina?
Ogijipizon aw dewe’igan gegoo agoode imaa zhooniyaasan aw dewe’igan iwedi gaa-ayaad ko iwedi gii-taawaad ingiw gichi-ayaa’aag.
Mii dash iwidi gii-kanawaabandamaan iw niin gaye nisaye apane ganawaabandamaang naanigodinong ganawaabamangwaa ganawaabandamaan iniw agoodemagakin.
Mii dash igo ingoding gii-o-kanawaabandamaan besho gii o weweni iwedi besho gii-onzaabandamaan gii-kanawaabandamaan weweni weweni ganawaabandamaan.
Mii dash iw wegwaagid mii iw gaa-aawang gaa-izhibii’igaadeg imaa cracker jack.
Mii dash imaa gii-animikosidooyaan mii dash odi keyaa “signs of the zodiac” gii-izhibii’igaade.

paragraph.text_eng: Yes I didn’t know what I thought. And today I still wonder about it a little bit. And you guys could think about it maybe sometime and you guys will at some point in time know it as time moves on why those things were being worn by the Thunderbird Drum the little things that look like coins. That’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Eya amanj ingii-inendam.
Geyaabi go noongom bangii ninaanaagidawendaan.

Giinawaa dash igo maagizhaa go eta go gidaa-naanaagidawendaanaawaa maagizhaa ingoding o gaye giinawaa gida in gidaa-ni-gigikendaanaawaa aaniin niw aaniin iw gaa-onji-biizikong go a’aw binesi dewe’igan iniw zhooniyaasan keyaa gaa izhinaagwakin.
Mii iw.

paragraph.text_eng: First of all, I’m going to tell about this, what that old man told me about what had happened with the Anishinaabe around here long ago. This is what they said hap-pened to one woman, that woman, who lived among them. See over there, she used to go get water over at the shore. Her little baby, she brought her baby along. That old man that called Agoode around here, this Is what he had told me.

sentence.sent_text: Akawe maa inda-wiindamaage o’ow, aw sa akiwenzii gaa-pi-wiindamawid yo’ow sa gaa-pi-izhiwebizid aw Anishinaabe omaa mewhinzha.
Mii keyaa gii-ikidowag gaa-pi-izhiwebizid aw bezhig aw ikwe, ya’aw, ya aw ikwe imaa gii-taawaad.
Ke iwidi, nibi owii-naadin owii-naadinaaban iwidi jiigibiig.
Aniw-sh biibiiyensiman, ogii-izhi maajiinaan aniw biibiiyensiman.
Mii aw akiwenzii Agoode gaa-pi-izhinikaazod, mii ow gaa-pi-wiindamawid.

paragraph.text_eng: See, she had gone over there to get water. See she had left her baby by the shore when she had come home. This, she had wanted to go get her baby. But see the baby wasn’t there. She didn’t know what had happened to the baby. When she returned to where they lived, they went to look, but couldn’t find that baby.

sentence.sent_text: Ke ya’aw iwidi gii-naadid o’ow nibi.
Ke-sh ogii-naganaan aniw biibiiyensiman imaa jiigibiig gii-ni-azhegiiwed.
Yo’ow sa, miish igo miinawaa gii-wii-pi-naanaaban aniw biibiiyensan.
