Ke-sh gaawiin imaa gii-ayaasiin aw biibiiyens.
Gaawiin ogikendanziin, yo’ow sa go gii-kikendanziin aaniish gaa-izhiwebizid aw biibiiyens.
Gaa-ni-azhegiiwed oodi gaa-taawaad, gii-o-inaabiwaad, mii gaawiin gii-mikawaasiin aw biibiiyens.

paragraph.text_eng: There was an old man there, that asked her, “Why don’t you go give tobacco to a tent shaker?” See, she went and gave tobacco to find out what had happened to her little baby. That tent shaker told an old woman to build a, a sweat lodge. And then when night came, see that’s when the tent shaker would start.

sentence.sent_text: Ke-sh bezhig a’aw, aw akiwenzii imaa, ogii-inaan aniw ikwewan, “Aaniish aw gii-o-miinaasiwad aw asemaa ya aw jiisikewinini?” Ke-sh gii-o-miinaad aniw asemaan, mii sa wii-kikendang aaniin gaa-izhiwebizinid aw biibiiyens.
Ke aw jiisikewinini gii-inaad aniw mindimooyenyan da-ozhitoowaad o’ow, yo’ow madoodooswan.
Ke gii-ni-dibikak, ke mii azhigwa, wii-maajiitaad a’aw jiisikewinini.

paragraph.text_eng: Those manidoog had gone into the sweat lodge. Then the lodge started to move. It is said that the tent shaker was there for a long time, so that they would know what had happened to that little baby See it is there in the lodge that the manidoog had talked to the tent shaker; he asked them where the baby was. “Right here,” he said. “On top of the hill in the ground.” Near the shore, it is here that the baby was.

sentence.sent_text: Ke agiw manidoog gii-piindigewaad imaa aniw, yo’ow sa madoodooswan.
Mii go gaa-izhi-maajiibideg o’ow madoodooswan.
Gonezh imaa gii-ayaa giiwenh aw jiisikewinini, yo’ow wii-kikendamowaad aaniin gaa-izhiwebizid aw biibiiyens.
Ke o’ow, yo’ow madoodooswan ya’aw agiw manidoog gii-kanoonaawaad iniw jiisikewininiwan, gii-inaad aniw, “Aandi aw biibiiyens ayaad?” “Yo’omaa,” gii-ikido.
“Yo’ow iniw ogidaaki yo’ow sa akiing.” Imaa jiigibiig maa, yo’omaa sa gii-ayaad aw biibiiyens.

paragraph.text_eng: See, that tent shaker. he went into the lodge again, and the spirits told him again, “You should dig, right here to find that baby right here on top of the hill. “So then those Anishinaabeg started digging, to find that little baby. That tent shaker had asked the thunderbirds at the time to start raining and make their thundering sound, the thunderbirds. See that tent shaker had told the manidoog, “You should kill whoever took that baby.”

sentence.sent_text: Ke dash aw jiisikewinini, gaa-izhi-biindiged maa miinawaa madoodooswaning, madoodooswan miish igo manidoon gii-inigod miinawaa gidaa-mookii, mookiin yo’omaa mii omaa, da-mikaweg aw biibiiyens, yo’omaa ogidaakiing.
Ke dash agiw Anishinaabeg gii-moonikewaad, da-baa-mikawaawaad iniw isa biibiiyens.
Mii a’aw jiisikewinini gaa-izhi-gagweijimaad aniw, binesiwan ke-sh mii azhigwa, gii-ni gimiwang bi-noondaagoziwaad agiw binesiwag.
Ke aw jiisikewinini gii-inaad aniw manidoon, “gidaa-nisaag agiw ya’aw sa gaa-mamaad aniw biibiiyensan.”

paragraph.text_eng: See it was the spirit in the water that had taken that baby. See it was the tent shaker that told them to kill the spirit that lives in the water. See but those thunder-birds were hitting that spirit in the water, when he hit the one in the water only blood. He saw here in the water when they killed that spirit that lives in the water.

sentence.sent_text: Ke aw manidoo imaa nibiing eyaad, mii a’aw gaa-mamaad aniw biibiiyensan.
Ke dash, ya’aw jiisikewinini gii-inaad da-nisaad aniw manidoon imaa nibiing eyaad.
Ke dash agiw binesiwag gii-pakitewaawaad aniw, aniw sa manidoon imaa nibi eyaad, gii-pakitewaad aniw imaa nibiing eyaajin.
Ke eta go yo’ow miskwi gaa-waabandang yo’omaa nibiing gii-nisaawaad aniw manidoo imaa nibiing eyaajin.

paragraph.text_eng: And then when they told that tent shaker those spirits told him, “You are all looking for that boy, that baby, you will find him, that spirit there that took him.” He didn’t know where that little boy was taken. See when they found him, he had found that baby. They dug here and found that baby.

sentence.sent_text: Ke miinawaa gii-kanoonaad aniw jiisikewiniwan agiw sa manidoog gii-inaawaad, “mii omaa ginandawaabamaawaa aw gwiiwizens, ya’aw sa biibiiyens ke gida-mikawaawaa mii a’aw manidoo maa gaa-izhiwinaad aniw.” Gaawiin ogii-kikendanziin aaniin gii-mamind a’aw gwiiwizens.
Kesh gii-mikawaawaad aniw aniw omaa ke-sh weweni, weweni gii-mikawaad aniw biibiiyensan.
Gii-moonikewag omaa ogii-mikawaan aniw, aniw sa biibiiyensan.

paragraph.text_eng: See it was that old man Agoode, as he was called here, it was him what is said to have happened here with the Anishinaabe long ago. He told me. “Believe what I am telling you. This is what happened here one time,” That’s all wish to say, That’s it, that’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Ke-sh aw akiwenzii Agoode gaa-pi-izhinikaazod, ke mii ya’aw mii iw keyaa giiwenh gaa-pi-izhiwebizid aw anishinaabe omaa mewinzha.
Mii gaa-izhid, “Debwetan i’iw ezhi-wiindamawinaan, mii keyaa gaa-pi-izhiwebak aabiding.” Miish eta go minik waa-izhi-giigidoyaan.
Mii iw, ho Mii iw.

paragraph.text_eng: So be it then. I thank very much that I was given tobacco to speak here today, to visit, and do storytelling. My name is now Naawgaaboge. I come from Manitoulin Island. Minwaankwad, “Clear Sky Woman,” is my name.

sentence.sent_text: Ahaaw.
G’chi-miigwech semaanh gii-miingowaanh.
N’Miigwechwendam geniinh maanda nongwa giizhgad gii-wiikmigowaanh manpii wii-bi-dnaangidoonaanh, wii-nbwaachininigok.
Leona Nawegahbow geniinh n’dizhnikaaz.
Manidoo-mnising ndoo-njibaa.
Ndoo-nishnaabe-noozwin ge’ii Minwaankwad ”Clear Sky Woman” ndizhnikaaz.

paragraph.text_eng: This person I’m going to be talking about, Hunter-man, when he was small what happened to him. He was saying, his father, his mother, his parents came to tell him the value, for an Anishinaabe in the culture, to be able to hunt, to fish, to trap.

sentence.sent_text: Na’aa geniinh nii-dibaajmaa Giiwse-nini, gii-bi-gaachiin’id gaa-bi-zhizhwebzid nii-dibaataan, ge’ii, oosan, ggitziiman, mamaa’iin miinwaa gashwan.
Gashwan, oosan gii-bi-dbaajmotaagwan gaa-zhi-gchi-piitendaagwak Nishinaabe ge’ii giiwsed, giigoonked, miinwaa niiwoged.

paragraph.text_eng: Now this is something that happened. When these white people arrived, the Anishinaabe people were astounded that these people of white skin arrived. They spoke a lot of English amongst themselves, and the Anishinaabe people spoke Nishnaabemowin amongst themselves separately. They were puzzled why they had to stop hunting. They can’t understand why they cannot fish anymore. They can’t understand why they cannot trap anymore. They can’t understand why they cannot harvest blueberries anymore.

sentence.sent_text: Ni’ii gii’enh gii-zhiwebad.
Gii-bi-dgoshnoog gonda ywaabshkiiwejig, Zhaagnaashag gii-bi-dgoshnoog.
Mii dash ni’ii, maamkaadenmoog Nishnaabeg gii-bi-dgoshninid ne’e ywaapshkiiwenjin.
G’chi-zhaagnaashiimoog, wiinwaash Nishnaabemoog.
Esnaa maakaadendmoog, gaa’ii nindwenziinaa’aa wii-naachtowaad giiwse’aad miinwaa giigoonke’aad miinwaa niiwoge’aad miinwaa pkibjige’aad, miinan bbaa-pkibdoo’aad.

paragraph.text_eng: Sothis is what they say, the Federal government brought this piece of paper to be signed. So this is what they said, “You will still be able to hunt; you will still be able to fish; you will still be able to trap; you will still be able to harvest furred animals; you will be able to harvest berries, and you will still be able to pick medicine.” This is what they were promised, this guarantee. So they signed it then. So then the government asked them, “What is it that you want?” The Nishnaabe people answered, “For us to always to be able to hunt, to always harvest berries everywhere, for all time. For us to be able to fish, all of us, and for us to be able to make a fire to stay warm; they want to be able to do that too.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash gaa-kidwaad, gonda pii gchi-gimaa gaa biidood mzina’igan waa-noozwinkaadeg.
Mii gaa-kidwaad, “Geyaabi ka-giiwsem, geyaabi ka-giigoonkem, geyaabi ge ka-gshkitoonaa’aa ji-niigeyeg, ji-pkibjigeyeg mshkiki ge ji-zgaknameg.” Mii gaa-zhi-waawiindmaagaazwaad.
Miish gii-noozwinke’aad.
Mii dash gii-kwejmigaazwaad, “Wenesh nendwendmeg gegiinwaa?” “Pane wii-ni-giiwse aang, pane wii-ni-pkibjige’aang.
Pane ge wii-i-giigoonke’aang, kina go mzowe, miinwaa wii-boodwe’aang, wii-giizhooteg naa endaa’aang ge’ii nindwendaanaa wii-gshkitowaang wi.”

paragraph.text_eng: Now the one with the white skin is saying, “So how long will this paper last?” this white person is asking. So the Anishinaabe people’s representatives have spoken, the council of chiefs discussed amongst themselves, and presented this to the people. This is what they the chiefs had said, “Forever, as long as the sun brings forth sunshine, for as long as the grass shall grow, for as long as the river flows. It shall never end, for us to be able to fish, for us to be able to hunt, and for us to harvest berries, and trap. This is what shall happen forever. Our grandchildren, our great-grandchildren, and those that will arrive, that are not here yet, they will put to good use for all and forever; they will freely be able to enjoy this treaty that is being made.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash ekdad wa Zhaagnaash ywaabshkii’ed, “Aaniinh dash maanda mnik ge-nishing mzina igan?” Mii sa gii-giigdowaad geye gimaak.

Mii dash gaa kidwaad, “Pane gwa, debnaak gwa giizis biidaasged debnaak go miishkoonsan bi-zaakiig, debnaak go ziibi bmijwang, gaa wiikaa da shkwaasesnoo maanda wii-giigoonkeyaang, wii-giiwse’aang, miinwaa wii-pkibjige’aang, wii-niiwge’aang.
Mii maanda pane ge ni zhiwebag.
Nooshenaanig, ngichi-ooshenaanig, miinwaa gwa gee waa-bi-yaajig, miinwaa baadaasmosejig, kina wii-mnowaabjitowaad maanda mzina’igan ezhchigaadeg.

paragraph.text_eng: So then it came to be that this little boy, whose name was Little-Hunter-Boy, was told about this paper. This is what will come to happen, and this is what’s going to happen about fishing. This will always be there; these rights will always be there. We shall never lose that. So then this little boy was instructed on the art of trapping. He was taught everything about trapping the beaver. So his father told him then, “This is what it looks like where the beaver lives. It is partitioned into only two parts, just like us. Where we go to sleep and the place we choose to eat, their home is set up just like ours, but the beaver would use trees and dirt.” Then they went and placed those snares over there so that they can trap, so that they can snare beaver. He was taught, this Little-Hunter-Boy, on how to bring beaver home and what the beaver house looks like, and how it’s partitioned, on one side where they eat, and the other side is where this beaver sleeps. It only has two rooms; it is built to have two rooms.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash maaba gwiiwzens, Giiwse-niniins zhinkaazo, gii-wiindmaagaazad maanda mzina’igan.
Mii maanda waa-zhiwebag, miinwaa giigoonkeng.
Pane da-ni-temgad wi, gaa go wiikaa ka-naachtoosiinaa’aa wi.
Mii sa maaba gwiiwzens gii-kinoomowind waa-zhi-niiwged.
Wii-zhisdoon ne’en mikwan gii-niiwaan.
Mii dash gaa-wiindmowind ne’e oosan gii-wiindmaagoon, “Mii ezhnaagoding amik endaad.

Niizhing go eta aachkinigaade dbishkoo gegiinwi, oo-nbaaying miinwaa waa-nji-wiismiying, mii ge’ii maa amik ezhnaagdinig endaad, miish ii go gii-zhitoon mtigoonsan miinwaa zhashki gii-nakaazan wa amik.” Miish oodi gii-oo-towaad ne’e ngwaagnan, wii-ngwaanaa’aad, wii-debnaa’aad ne’e amikwan.
Gii-kinoomaagaazo, Giiwse-niniins, waa-zhi-biinaad ne’e amikwan miinwaa ezhnaagidnig wa amik endaad miinwaa aachkingaadeg wi oodi mbaneying wiisni miinwaa mbaneying ge oodi e-daningwaang.
Niizhing go eta zhinaagdinini.

paragraph.text_eng: So this Little-Hunter-Boy is very happy to know how to go about trapping to get those beaver. So then over there, this whole river was frozen. His father is in the lead; he’s following his father. His father was running very lightly on the ice. Water is running under the ice, but is iced over here. Ice is over the flowing water, a frozen river, but the water is flowing very fast. So then this Little-Hunter-Boy began to run. Right here he was carrying a backpack, or some kind of bag with a beaver inside, and he was following, running towards his father. Then his father was running towards the shore, and he made it to shore. So this young man, Little-Hunter-Boy, he was running over there and then he went through the ice. Under the water he went, and he was thoroughly soaked. Everything was soaked including his backpack, his beaver catch. Holy cow! There is just ice to be seen.

sentence.sent_text: Esnaa maaba gchi-nendam Giiwse-niniins, gwiiwzens, wii-bbaa-niiwged, gii-debnaad ne’e.
Mii dash oodi ziibi, kina maanda gii-mshkodin ziibi.
Oosan dash oodi ni-niigaaniiwan.
Aapji go ni-naangibatoo wa oosan mkomiing, mbiish naamiying bmijwan mkom, shwii go manpii abi, gwetaak epapiichjiwang wi mbiish.
Miish maaba Giiwse-niniins gii-maajiibtood, manpii bimwidoon wi ni’ii amikwan zhe biizwan, noopnanaad ne’e oosan.
Jiigbiig dash oodi gii-ni-patoo’oon ne’e oosan, gii-de-dgoshin maaba jiigbiig.
Maabash ge’ii shkiniigish Giiwse-niniins, gii-bmiptoo oodi mii sa gaa-zhi-kakishing.
Mbiishing nameying gii-pizo, mii go kina e-zhi-nsaabaa’ed.
Kina gwa gozignini ge’e wi mashkimad amikwan bimwinaad.
Gwetaankamik!
Ooh, debwaamdaan oodi mkomiing binid.

paragraph.text_eng: Meanwhile his father is running along the shore. He then broke the ice, parted the ice by striking it. It is there that the Little-Hunter-Boy popped up. He is just soaking wet. It’s cold, and his bag is very heavy. So then his father built a fire right away; he placed little branches down and made a fire. Then it was there that this boy, Hunter-man, ran too. He went and sat down close to the fire. He was very cold, and he removed the backpack. He put the beaver alongside it, and then it was here that he brought the beaver to. They then removed the meat, and then put it on the fire. So then they dined as the father shared similar life stories with his son, this Little-Hunter-Boy.

sentence.sent_text: Miish wa oosan oodi, jiigbiig oodi bmiptoo wa akiwenziin.
Mii sa gii-biigwaad zhe mkomiin, gii-daashkowaad ne’en mkomiin.
Mii sa zhi’e wa Giiwse-niniins gii-bi-mookbizad.
Gwentaag enaabaa’ed, ksinaa ge’e, miinwaa gzignini ge’e mashkimad.
Mii sa we’iib maaba oosan gii-saad zhi’e mtigoonsan, gii-skowaad.
Gwetaankamik dash shkode.
Miish maaba oodi gwiiwzens, Giiwse-nini, gii-patood.
Gii-oo-nimadibid jiigi-shkode, aapji go biingeji, miinwaa gii-giiskoonind ne’e mashkimad.
Mii dash oodi gii-saa aad ne’e amikwan, shaweying, miish go zhiwe gii-biinaa’aad ne’e nondan na’aa amikwan.
Gii-bmowaad wi wiiyaas, miish manpii gii-towaad mshkodeng.
Miish gii-waawiisni’aad dibaajmotaadwag dibaajmotwaan ne’e maaba ne’e gwisan, maaba sa Giiwse-niniins.

paragraph.text_eng: Eventually he dozed off alongside where his father was. His father is going on telling stories about what will come to be in the coming year, continually. This is what he said, “I shall place some more snares over there. There is an abundance of beaver lodges; they are over there, and over there, and over there.” So this is where they took more snares to trap more beaver. So this little boy is getting bigger, this Little-Hunter-Man. As he got bigger he was able to trap more beaver, and so they took a lot of pelts with them. They were given a lot of money for them; they sold them, and so from the exchange they purchased guns.

sentence.sent_text: Gmaapiich gii-ni-nbaa shaweying maa bapaa’iin yaanid.
Gchi-dibaajmo maaba waa-zhiwebag miinwaa ngo-bboongak, pane gwa.
Mii dash gaa-kidad, “Geyaabi aanind nga-toonan ngwaaganan oodi.
Amikwag e-ni-ndaadaa’aad, gwetaankamik maanda ni-zhi-jiiyaanoon ne’e amikgamigoon.” Mii oodi gii-ni-maajoodoowaad nondan ngwaagnan, wii-debnaa’aad geyaabi aanind ne’en amikwan.
Mii dash maaba gwiizens gii-ni-mbigid, maaba sa na’aa Giiwse-niniins.
Eshkam go ni-mdida niibna gii-gshki’aan amikwan wii-nsaad, miinwaa bkindaagnan gii-oo-maamoog.
Niibnash zhoonyaa gii-miingaazoog daa’e’aad ne’e, mii sa miinwaa baashkzignansh miinwaa gii-giishpnadoonaa’aan.

paragraph.text_eng: “So that is where we shall go,” said he father to Hunter-Man. “I will show you how to shoot deer and moose. If the deer is looking at you, facing you, you cannot shoot it. So after he looks at you, he will be standing broadside. That’s what you are going to be waiting for, and this is where you should shoot it. So if you are able to do that, as in hit it here or here, and the deer will drop right where he is standing when you shoot him.” So began his lessons this Little-Hunter-Boy, and so the boy grew, and it came to be he was successful with his first hunt by getting a small deer.

sentence.sent_text: “Mii oodi ge-zhaaying,” kidash wa maaba ne’aa Giiwse-nini, oosan di-goon.
“Ka-kinoomoon waa-zhi-baashkzod wa waa’aashkesh miinwaa moozoog.
Giishpin biidaasmigaabwid wa waa’aashkesh, gaa maamdaa wii-baashkzowad bi-naabid.
Baamaa oodi shkwaa-gnowaabmigyin wa, mii ji-bmidaakjiised.
Maandash nikeyiing naabid, miish manpi!
Jl baashkzowad.
Giishpin shwii go gshki’ad, manpii ge gnomaanh maa ge manpii shaweying.
Miish go eta ji njibzad pii baashkzwad wa” Mii sa gii-skoonwid maaba Giiwse-niniins, eshkam go ni-mdida.
Mii sa gii-pshki’aad waa’aashkwan ntam e-gaachiininjin gii-debnaad.

paragraph.text_eng: It came to be that they had to stop hunting for the winter because of the snow, “As the snow piles up, when there is snow, that is when you must stop hunting,” his dad says, “because at this time the female deer are carrying or taking care of their young ones; you can’t shoot a deer at that time, when they are pregnant and raising their young.”

sentence.sent_text: Gaash ii gwa, pane ngo-bboonigak aabdeg gii-kowe-boontaawag, “Shkwaa-bboong, ne shpaagnigaag, goon ni-bid, mii ji-kowe-boontaa’iin giiwse’iin” gii-igoon.
“Miinwaa sa go ge’ek na’aag waa’aashkeshiinsag, gaa maamdaa wii-baashkzood wa bmwinaawsad.”

paragraph.text_eng: “Okay then, this is what I shall do,” Little-Hunter-Boy says, “I shall get the meat.” He carries the deer. He gave it to his mother. So then they cooked the deer. All of his family arrived, everyone showed up. They came to eat because that was his first kill, this Little-Hunter-Boy, and so there was a grand feast. The young people arrived—the children, the women, his grandfather, his grandmother also, all of his family arrived.

sentence.sent_text: “Nahaaw” kida dash.
“Mii ge zhichgeyaanh, nga-debnaan wiiyaas.” Mii sa gii-giiwedood, manpii bimwinaan ne en waa aashkeshwan, gii ewnaad ne’en mamaa’iin gii-oo-miinaad.
Gchi-jiibaakwe’oog.
Kina gii-bi-dgoshnoog ndanwendaagnan.
Gii-bi-wiisniwag.
Mii gii-shki-nsaad maaba Giiwse-niniins waa aashkeshwan.
Gii-gchi-wiisniikmagad.
Eshkniigjig gii-bi-zhaawag, binoojiin’ig, kwewag, mishoomsan, ookmisan gaye, kina go danwendaagnag gii-bi-dgoshnoon.

paragraph.text_eng: So everyone is having a great conversation. They had great conversations about how the Anishinaabe people long ago were given permission to hunt freely and to be able to trap, and collect firewood. It came to be that the boy was taught how to be a good hunter and how to be successful with beaver trapping. He collected a lot of beavers and deer. After that he was taught where the moose can be found. So they walked for a far distance and saw a rock; so they climbed up this bluff and then saw a large variety of moose horns. The moose are walking through the wetlands.

sentence.sent_text: Gchi-dibaajmo’oog.
Dibaajmo oog gaa-zhiwebdagbane gii-bagidnigaazwaad Nishnaabeg wiinwaa pane wii-ni-giiwse’aad, miinwaa wii-niiwge’aad, wii-pkibjige’aad, miinwaa msan wii-maawnjitowaad.
Gii-kinoomaagaazo shkiniigish we’eni waa-zhi-giiwsed, miinwaa na’aan amikwan waa-zhi-debnaad.
Niibna amikwan gii-zgaknaan, miinwaa waa’aashkeshwan.
Gaa-shkwaa bezhik gaa-shkwaa-nsaad, mii miinwaa aanind gii-kinoomaagaazad ge’ii moozoog yaa’aad.
Waasa gii-zhi-bmosewag gchi-gidaabig gii-zhaawag, miish oodi gii-ninaabwaad, gii-debwaabmaa’aad.
Gwetaankamik deshknan wa na’aak moozoog bmosewag oodi enji-mbiigmigaak.

paragraph.text_eng: So then this young boy, Hunter-Man, was then shown how to shoot the moose. He is told, “Go gently when you pick up your bullets; do not leave evidence that you were there. Do it without being noticed, and when you pick up that rifle, do not make any noise. Be quiet, be careful, do it without getting noticed. If you make a noise, the moose will run away. You have to be absolutely careful.”

sentence.sent_text: Miisa maaba shkiniigish, Giiwse-nini, gii-kinoomowind waa-zhi-baashkzwaad ne’e.
“Nengaach gaazo pii-daapnaman nwiinsan gaa’ii ka-bmiptoosii.
Giimooj ka-daapnaan wi, miinwaa ji-naashknadoo’iin baashkzigan, gaa’ii gegoo ka-zhi-mdawetoosii.
Nengaach.
Giishpin mdwe’etoo’iin mii go ji-gjibowed wa mooz.
Nengaach aabdeg.”

paragraph.text_eng: So he finally came to see a moose. Very, very carefully he picked up those bullets. He loaded the rifle, and so he came to see the moose. He then waited for the moose to get into position. So the moose stood broadside, and then he pointed at the moose right here, right where the heart is, exactly where the heart is. There was one loud bang and then the big moose dropped. He yelled, “I killed it!”

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa gii-debaamaad ne’e moozoon.
Nengaach gii-daapnang ne en nwiinsan.
Gii-biintood baashkzigning, gii-waabmaan bi-naabnid ne’e.
Mii sa gii-baabii’aad wii-bmidaagsenid nee.
Gii-bmidaakgaabwiwan ne’e, mii sa gmaakpii gii-zhinoowaad, gii-zhinoowaad oodi ne’e, mii’aaw go de’iing.
Mii go ea ngoding gii’mdwe’ezged mii gii-mdwe-bangishing gchi-mooz.
Gii-noondaagzid, “Ngii-nsaa!”

paragraph.text_eng: So they all arrived, his dad and uncle came and helped him. They taught him what to do to clean it up. Then they stored everything away. They put it away in its proper place, even the hooves were hung up in a tree. This was his first kill with the moose, He stored everything he even put the horns away. He cleaned the skull really good, and then he put it away. So they took away large amounts of meat; it was heavy.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa kina pii-bi-dgoshnanid, ne’e oosan, zhishen’iin ge’e, gii-bi-naadmaagaaza.
Mii sa gii-kinoomowind waa-zhichged wii-biinaad.
Kina go gegoo we’eni gii-zgaknaanaa’aa.
Oodi ge zidan gii-maajiijgaadenoon oodi wii-chigaadeg neyaab.
Ka-goodoonan nonda mtigoong ne’e’ gii-gaaza.
Mii gii-shki-nsaad ne’en moozoon.
Kina gegoo gii-zgaknang, deshknan ge gii-zgaknaan.
W’eni gii-biintoon wi ndib, miinwaa gii-oo-zgaknang wi.
Gii-aajiidowaad, gwetaani niibna wiiyaas, gozigwan.

paragraph.text_eng: So they took all of it back home, and then again another feast took place. The whole entire village, his relatives, and the adolescent boys also came to investigate. Everything was stored away. The tongue, the head, they cooked everything the moose has. All the internal organs were put away, stored. So if you don’t cook everything in the feast, you would hang up the remainder from the trees to respect this moose. This is in recognition of how the moose let go of his life.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-maajiidowaad miinwaa endaa’aad, mii sa miinwaa gii-gchi-wiisnikmagak.
Kina gii-bi-zhaa’aad, ngo-oodenwens eyaanjin ndanwendaagnan, miinwaa gewiinwaa shkiniigshag.
Git-bi-dbaamjigaaza maaba mooz gii-nchigaazad.
Kina gegoo gii-zgaknigaade denew gii-mnozaanaa’aa, kina go gegoo wa mooz eyaang ndib, miinwaa go ne en ni’iin ode, kina go gegoo biinjna etenig gii-zgaknigaadeni.
Giishpin kina bwaa nakaazyin ne’e mii dash oodi mtigoong gii-oo-goodoowaad, mnaadenmin maaba mooz ge’ii gaa zhi-bgidniged.

paragraph.text_eng: So this man now offered tobacco. He was very glad for his successful hunt, and he was also very happy that he was given the ability by the Creator to hunt, to be able to feed the entire community. So the father of this Hunter-Man talked, “We are full of respect for this way of life: the trees, the plants, the animals, and the fish.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa maa gii-bgidnaad maaba nini.
Gii-gchi-nendam gii-debnang niibna wiiyaas miinwaa gchi-nendam ge’ii nondandebenjgenjin Gzhe-mnidoon, gii-miingwad wi-gshkitood naa wii-shamaad gchi-ngoodeno Nishnaaben.
Mii gii-dbaatang oosan maaba na’aa Giiwse-nini, “Gegiinwi e-zhi-mnaadendmang mtigoog, zyaakiig, wesiinsag, ge miinwaa giigoon’iig.”

paragraph.text_eng: So it came to be that he was taught everything: how he will trap, how he will hunt, and how he will fish. So they are going to place a net on the ice. They then went about training Hunter-Man how to cut the ice. He drew out a plan with trees and marked their plans on the ice with the little trees. They were out in the open on the ice. It was very cold; there are no more water openings; they have all been frozen over; ice is now there. This is where they put the little trees, for this is where the net is. The anchor was placed, and all along here they erected all of the little trees. Then this net was under the ice, underwater, for two days, this is all ice.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa maaba kina gaa-zhi-kinoomoowind, wii-niiged, wii-giiwsed, geyaabi dash wii-giigoonke.
Sabiin dash wii-saa’aan mkomiing.
Kinoomaagaazash Giiwse-nini waa-zhi-giishkonaad mkomiin.
Mii dash gii-mzinbii’ang wa waa-zhichged, mtigoon dash gii-nakaaznan.
Giji mkoom dash maanda.
Zhaazhi ni-gchi-ksinaa, gaa geyaabi mbiish nsaaksiznoo, miish mkoom bid.
Mii mampii mtigoonsan gii-towaad, mampiish maaba sab bi.
Miish mampii gwezgong gii-chigaadeg, kina manpii mtigoon gii-bdagshimaa’aan.
Miish mampii niizhgwan gii-bi wa sab manpii naambiing mkomiing, mkom maaba kina.

paragraph.text_eng: Then it came to be this Hunter-Man came to get the net. Over here is where he cut into the ice. From this hole he pulled the net, bat everything else beyond the hole was ice. From here the women, the children, and the men watched. All of this was sheltered off because it was very windy and cold. From here is where they landed the fish. This is where this ice hole is. It is from here that they all took fish, and then all the people cooked. It came to be that this Little-Hunter-Boy was successful in his fishing. He got northern pike; a variety of fish were caught. They brought all of the catch over here, and it was from here where all of the people were fed.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash maaba Giiwse-nini wii-bbaa-naanaad ne’en naa’aan sabiin.
Mii mampii gii-giishkonaan ne’en mkomiin.
Miish mampii wii-wiikbinaad ne’e, maanda dash wii gag ii-mshkodin.
Manpii ge gii-nji kwe’oog, binjiin’iig, nin’oog-gii-kowaaboog zhonda.
Kina maanda gii-aachkigaade zaam gchi-noodin, aapji go ksinaa.
Miish mampii giigoon’iin gonda gii-wiikdaabaanaa’aad.
Miish mampii bagonezid manpii maaba mkom.
Mii zhiwe gii-bi-daapnaa’aad ne’en giigoon iin, miish goonda kina mampii gonda bemaadzijig gii-jilbaakwe’aad.
Mii maaba Giiwse-niniins gii-nsaad nonda kina giigoon’iin.
Gnoozhen, nonj go na’aan giigoon’iin gii-debnaa’aad.
Miish mampii gaa-nji-binaa’aad ne’e, kina gonda gii-shanjgaazwaad bemaadzijig.

paragraph.text_eng: This is all that he was taught to trap, to hunt, to fish. Also he now has to accom-pany the women to go out and pick. The women were delegated to harvest berries and to harvest medicines. It came to be that this Little-Hunter-Boy grew into a man. When he was of great age he accompanied the women and the girls when they picked berries and harvested medicine, and also the quills of the porcupine. They went about searching for porcupine. This Hunter-Man was also informed as where to find the porcupine.

sentence.sent_text: Miish gaa-zhi-kinoomowind maaba; wii-niiged, wii-giiwsed, wii-giigoonked.
Geyaabi dash wii-bba-pkibjiged, kwewan wii-bba-naagdawenmaad.
Kwewag gii-miingaazwag wii-miinke’aad miinwaa mshkiki wii-zgaknamwaad.
Miish maaba Giiwse-niniins gaa-ni-mbigid go naa.
Gii-ni-gchi-piitzid mii gii-maajiinaad ne’en kwewan miinwaa kwezensan wii-bba-pkibjigenid, mshkiki gii-bbaa-maawndoonaanaa’aa, miinwaa dash gaawyag.
Gaagoon gii-bbaa-ndine’aa’aan.
Mii dash maaba Giiwse-nini gii-kinoomowind yaanid ne’en gaagwan.

paragraph.text_eng: Very high up on the rock he went. He climbed for a long time, and he sweated. He asked his friends to accompany him. There were three of them; there were three men looking for porcupine. When they got onto this big hill, they could see this big rock over there. So they said, “We should take this rock.” So they got a stick, and this stick is what they used to nudge the rock. They were sweating profusely trying to move this rock.

sentence.sent_text: Gchi-gidaabik oodi gii-zhaa.
Gii-kodaazii oodi gbeying, aapji go gii-bwezo.
Gii-wiikjiiwnaan ne’en wiijkiiwen’iin.
Gii bbaa-nswiwag, gii-bba-nswiwag gonda ninwag, mii ne’en ndane’aa’aad gaagwan.
Miish oodi gaa-dgoshnawaad gchi-gidaaki, mii gii-debwaamdamwaad oodi gchi-sin mii maanda engokwaagwenh wi.
“Esnaa gdaa-gii-maajiidoonaanh wi,” kidoog dash.
Mtig dash gii-naadnaa’aa.
Miish wi gaa-nakaazwaad wi wii-giikwebamwaad wi mtg.
Getin nokiiwag, aapji go bwezwag.

paragraph.text_eng: Eventually, something dark came from over there; it is no longer hot or sunny. So it was then that they saw this big bird which had big feet coming to land. It was under this rock that they hid; they ran for cover under the rock. They laid down in there; they are hiding. Ho-wa! Ihis great huge bird landed where they were; my God the bird is really hot. Meanwhile these three are laying under this rock.

sentence.sent_text: Gmaapiich gii-bi-mkade’aamgad gegoo oodi.
Gaa ii geyaabi gzhaatesnoo.
Mii sa gii-waabmaa’aad gchi-bneshiinyin gwetaan engokzided wa gchi-bneshiinh bi-booniid.
Miish mampii naami-sin gii-powe’aad, gii-zhangishnoog zhi’e, gkizoog.
Gwetaankamig!
Gchi-bineshiinh zhi’e gii-booniid, gwetaankamik epiichi gzhizad.
Miish gonda zhi’e gii-zhangishnowaad naami-sin.

paragraph.text_eng: Oh my, they are scared. At the same time they are sweating a lot; it is hot; holy cow, they are sweating a lot. So this bird spoke, “I am very thirsty,” it says, “I should look for a little rock,” and then he split that rock. So when the bird flexed, this stone made a noise. At this time something flowed towards the earth. This rock is an egg! This Little-Hunter-Boy is astounded; this young hunter realized that this bird owned this egg. “What’s going to happen to us now?” One of the men said, “This bird is going to kill us.” Then the bird flew away. The bird was flying far off into the distance. The three men came up from underneath the rock and went home. They came to the realization that this was a big nest all along, where this egg was in.

sentence.sent_text: Ta’aa, zegziwag.
Bwezoog bekish, gzhide, gwetaankamik, ezhi-bwezwaad.
Mii dash ekdad wa, “Aapji go ngaasnaabaagwe,” kida, “esnaa gegoo siniins ndaa-gii-ndaneyaan,” mii sa gii-gaashkang wi sin.
Miish ow bineshiinh bmaajiid mii maanda gii-mdoweg gchi-sin.
Mii ge gwa bi-njigaamgak gegoo.
Miina gona maanda gchi-waawon yaawang.
Esnaa maaba maamkaadendam Giiwse-niniins, mii sa iidig maaba bineshiinh maanda wiin dibendaan maanda waawon.
“Aaniish naa iidig ge zhiwebziyiing?
Ka-nsigonaanh maaba bineshiinh.” Mii sa gii-maajiibzad wa gchi-bineshiinh neyaab.
Gwetaani waasa gii-nimbizo, mii gonda gii-bzigwii’aad, gii-gjibwe’e’aad, neyaab gii-kodaasiptoo’oog zhiwe aazhbikoong, neyaab gii-ni-giiwe’aad.
Mii na go na iidig maaba wiin awi, gchi-saswin iidig maanda gaa-aawang, zhi’e maanda waawon gii-teg.

paragraph.text_eng: They went and told their story of what happened to them. “We went looking for porcupine quills, but we did not see any porcupine. So over there we saw a big rock, and it looked like an egg, that’s how it looked. We tried to bring it home, and while we were there this big bird arrived. It came down and sat there and we were almost stuck. Then when it left, when it moved away, that’s when we ran away from there. That is why we left from there, that big bird would have killed us. We left because of that big bird. Had we still been there that big bird would have killed us. That is why we returned home without any porcupine quills. If we would have seen any porcupines, we would have brought the quills so you could do quillwork,’ said the hunter.

sentence.sent_text: Miish naa gonda gii-oo-dibaajmowaad gaa-zhiweziwaad.
“Ngii-bbaa-gaawkemi, gaa pwaya gaagoog ngii-waabmaasiinaanig.
Oodi shwii gwa gchi-sin ngii-waamdaanaanh waawon ezhnaagwak, mii ezhnaagwak.
Ndaanwi bi-gii’edoonaanh wi, mii dash epiichi-yaa’aang zhi’e gchi-bineshiinh.
Gii-bi-nimadibi zhi’e.
Gegaa dash ngii-baataashnami.
Miish pii gaa-ni-maajiibzad bbaa-ndane’ang waa-shamgowaang, mii wi gii-bi-gjiboweyaang.
Mii dash oodi gaa-bi-nji-maajaa’aang wi zaam go naanh ndaa-gii-bi-nsigonaanh wa gchi-bineshiinh giishpin yaa’aangiba saswining.
Mii dash nongwi wi gaa-nji-binaasoongdwaa gonda gaawyag.
Giishpin waamangdiba wa gaag, ndaa-gii-biinaanaanig ge ek gaawyag wii-gaayagkeyeg,” gii-kida sa maaba.

paragraph.text_eng: Many times afterwards he went out to pick medicine, where they can search for porcupine, where to fish, where to hunt, and where to trap. So this is what this Little-Hunter-Boy did when he grew up, and from there it started, his teachings, his instruction. So they studied this, the treaty. How long, and how much they could hunt, and where. “For as long as it is hot, for as long as the sun throws forth it’s light, for as long as the grasses grow, for as long as the water flows,” this is what was told to them. Okay.

sentence.sent_text: Niibnanchingsh maaba gii-bbaa-zhizhaa waa-nji-mshkikiikeng, gaagwan waa-nji-ndane’e’aad, waa-nji-giigoonke’aad, waa-nji-giiwse’aad, miinwaa waa-nji-niiwge’aad.
Mii maaba gaa-nankiid na’aa Giiwse-niniins gaa-ni-mbigid.
Miish wi gaa-nj-maajsenig wii-kinoomowind.
Gchi-mzina’igan gii-gnowaamjigaadeg wi ni’ii mnik go giizis ge-zaagii’aasged, mnik go miishkoonsan ge-zaagiik, miinwaa go mnik ge go mbish ge bmijwang,” mii gaa-gaazwaad gonda.
Nahaaw.

paragraph.text_eng: Alright, so I am going to start. Before I start, however, I would like to be thankful. With this tobacco that I hold on my heart’s side, I say thank you Creator, for all that you have placed on earth, animals, all different looking animals, thank you very much, and for having given us this life. For the animals, for their lives, each animal that was placed here, they were also given a road to follow. And so it is the same for Anishinaabe, us too as Anishinaabe, our lives are here and so this is what I am thankful for, for having been given life and for being given another day to see this sun to come shining, so that we will feel good.

sentence.sent_text: Ahaaw, mii go ji-maajtaa’aanh.
Jibwaa maajtaa’aanh shwii gwa, nga-ke-miigwechwendam.
Maaba semaa manpl myignag nde’iing nikeyaa, gchi-miigwech ndi-naa Gzhemnidoo, kina gegoo gaa-bgidnang gidkamig, wesiinyiig, enso zhinaagziwaad go wesiinyiig, gchi-miigwech.
Miinwaa maanda bmaadziwin gii-miingoyiing.
Wesiinyiig ge iinwaa bimaadziwiniwaa, enso bezhik wesiinh gaa-bgidnigaazad ge’ii gii-naaknigaadeni miikaans waa-naagdood.

Miish go naasaab Anishinaabe, gegiinwi Anishinaabewying manpll temgad gegiinwi gbimaadzwininaanh, mii dash maanda gchi-miigwechwendmaanh bimaadziwin gii-miingoyiing miinwaa bgidnigoyiing miinwaa ngo-giizhiik wii-waabmangid maaba giizis wii-bi-mnowaasged, wii mno zhiyaaying.

paragraph.text_eng: I also say thank you for this Anishinaabe language, for having been left for us, this Anishinaabe language is very precious. Thank you also for our parents and our children. We hope that the Creator helps us to help these children that they will come to be raised in a good way, so that they will see how the Anishinaabeg used to live; to hear the Anishinaabeg telling stories how they used to see their parents, their grandfathers, their grandmothers, how they lived, how they saw everything. So I say thank you to you as well for coming to sit here, for inviting us to come and tell stories. We are very thankful to come and help out by coming here. Okay, thank you very much.

sentence.sent_text: Gchi-miigwech ge ndi-kid maanda Anishinaabemwin geniinwi gii-ngadmaagowaang, aapji go gchi-piitendaagwad maanda Anishinaabemwin.

Miigwech ge ngitziimnaanig, miinwaa nda-binoojiiminaanig, nbogsenmaanaa Gzhe-manidoo ji-naadmaagying ji-naadmoongidwaa gonda binoojii’iig we’eni wii-bi-zhi-kognigaazwaad wii-waamdamwaad gewiinwaa wi gaa-bi-zhi-bmaadziwaad Anishinaabeg wii-nondmowaad Anishinaabeg dibaajimowaad ge’iinwaa gaa-bi-zhi-waabmaa’aad gitziimwaan, mishoomsiwaan, gookmiswaan, gaa-zhi-bmaadzinid, kina gegoo gaa-zhi-gnowaamdamwaad.
Gchi-miigwech dash ndi-kid miinwaa gegiinwaa manpii bi-nmadbiiyeg, gii-wiikmigyaang maanda wii-bi-dibaajmoyaang.
Aapji go ngichi-nendaami go geniinwi maanda wiidookaageyaang manpii bi-zhaa’aang.
Nahaaw, gchi-miigwech.

paragraph.text_eng: I will place down tobacco here. And so I will start. First, I will talk about what my name is, my name for real. Ida Rose Trudeau is my name, but this here Trudeau is the name of the person I had married. But before I was married, before I was married my name was Recollet. Also my mother, my father, that was his name. And also this Anishinaabe name. I carried it for a long time, but did not know it until that doctor, Anishinaabe doctor, when I saw him, that’s when he told me that. “Oh I want to ask you to give me an Anishinaabe name,’ I say to him. He looked at me then,“Oh, you already have an Anishinaabe name,” he says to me.

sentence.sent_text: Maaba dash zhonda nga-bgidnaanh semaa.

Mii dash ji-maajtaa’aanh, ntam ni’ii nga-dibaataan maanda go naa genii ezhnikaazyaanh, gegeti go naa noozwin, Ida Rose Trudeau ndizhnikaaz, maanda go naa Trudeau zhinkaaza maaba gaa-wiidgemag, wi shwii go naa jibwaa niibwiyaanh, jibwaa wiidgemaagniyaanh noozwin Recollet ndizhnikaaz, mii geniinh nmamaa, nbapaaba gaa-zhinkaazad.
Miinwaa dash.

Anishinaabe noozwin gchi-gbeying ngii-bmwidoon gaa dash ngii-gkendziin baamaa wa mshkikiinini, nishnaabe-mshkikiinini, pii e-waabmag, mii gii-wiindmowid wi, “Ohn, nishnaabe noozwin kwii-ggwejmin wii-miizhyin,” ndi-naa.
Ngii-gnowaabmig dash, “Ooh, zhaazhi gdaa’aan Anishinaabe noozwin,” ndig.

paragraph.text_eng: “Is that right?” I say to him.

sentence.sent_text: “Mii na go gegeti?” ndi-naa.

paragraph.text_eng: Yes who gave you that name when you were a baby?” he says to me. Well, that’s all I know, Waabningozhiins. “That is your name,” he said to me.

sentence.sent_text: “Enh, wenensh wi noozwin gaa-miingowiin gii-binoojiinswiiviin?” ndig.
Aanzh mii sa eta geniinh gekendmaanh Waabningozhiing “Mii i go wi gda-noozwin,” ngii-ig.

paragraph.text_eng: That is what I carried for many years. Waabningozhiins supposedly is my Anishinaabe name. Waabningozhiins. It is then White dove supposedly. This is what this medicine man told me, this Nishnaabe medicine man, “Waabningozhiins.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash wi gaa-bmwidowaanh maanda gchi-niibna nsa-bboon.
Waabningozhiins gii’enh wi ndanshinaabe noozwin.
Waabningozhiins.
Mii dash wi “White dove” giiwenh wi.
Mii maaba gaa-zhid mshkikiinini, maaba nishnaabe-mshkikiinini, maanda “Waabningozhiins.”

paragraph.text_eng: So I’m from Spirit Island, that which is called Wikwemikong. There are lots of those who speak fluently over there. It is only since birth, at first hearing the language, it was this Anishinaabe language. This is all we heard when we were raised, the Anishinaabe language only.

sentence.sent_text: Manidoo-mnising dash ndoonjibaa, Wiikwemkoong ezhnikaadeg.
Baatiinoog oodi mooshkin eta e nishinaabemjig.
Mii go eta beshki-ndaadziiyaang go, eshki-noondmaang nowewin, mii maanda Anishinaabemwin.
Mii go eta maanda pane gaa-noondmaang, gii-bi-kognigowaang, Anishinaabemwin eta.

paragraph.text_eng: This thing that I want to talk about, I want to talk about this young man first. The Anishinaabe grandfathers, or their fathers, the boys, the youth, were always taught how to hunt, how to go over there in the forest. Absolutely you have to think a lot about it; you have to be thoughtful here, that which is in your head, and here, in your heart. You cannot have angry thoughts if you want to go hunting. What you are thinking has to be clear. There cannot be any hate, jealousy, anger. Here too in your heart, you must have good feelings; you have to look good at your fellow humans.

sentence.sent_text: Maanda dash ni’ii waa-dibaatamaanh, maaba go ntam nwii-dibaajmaanh shkiniigshens, pane go naa Anishinaabe mishoomsag maa ge bapaawaan, gii-kinoomaagaazwag gwiizensag, eshkniigjig, waa-zhi-giiwsewaad; waa-zhi-zhaawaad oodi megwemtigwaaki, aabdeg kwii-ke-gchi-naanaagdawendam, ka naanaagdawendam miinwaa dash maanpii baandeg gidibaang miinwaa zhinda gide’iing.
Gaa’ii maamdaa nshkaadendmowin wii-yaaman giishpin wii-bbaa-giiwse’iin.
Aabdeg wii-biinaagwad manpii mekwendman.
Gaa’ii maamdaa gegoo zhiingendwin, gizhaa’endimowin, nshkendiwin.
Manpii ge gde’iing ka-mno-nendz kwii-mno-gnowaabmaa gwiiji-bimaadiz.

paragraph.text_eng: You will be going hunting I mean to say. You’ll be looking for deer, or some animal that is necessary to feed your children. That is what this Anishinaabe elder says, our grandfather, or our father. Father, that’s how he teaches. Before you go into the bush, you must be thankful. You have to put your tobacco down there, and then you leave. If there is a lot of sadness, dislike, anger, jealousy you will not see anything over there in the forest because there is a lot of bad stuff here, that ugliness. That is why these young people are taught how to get ready. To get ready in their thoughts, heart, and how you view something. Anishinaabeg view things differently. And this is this young man, whom I’m going to talk about.

sentence.sent_text: Gbi-bbaa-giiwse nii naa.
Waa’aashkesh gbi-bbaa-ndowaabmaanh, maa ge wesiinh nendwendaagzid wii-shamdwaa gdabnoojiimag.
Mii maaba gchinshinaabe e-kidad, gmishoomsinaanh, maa ge gbapaanaanh.
Oos, mii maaba e-zhi-kinoomaaged.
Jibwaa jekaakooman, aabdeg kwii-miigwechwendam, semnaa ge oodi ka-bgidnaanh, mii dash bjiinag ji maajaayiin.
Giishpin manpii baatiinag maanaadendmowin, zhiingendwin, nshkendmowin, gzhaa’endmowin, gaa’ii gegoo kwii-waamdaziin oodi megwentigwaaki zaam manpit da-mooshknemgad wi myaanaadag, e maanaadag.
Miish aapji enji-kinoomaagaazwaad gonda shkiniigshag wii-zhiitaa’aad, wii-zhiitaa’aad nendmowining, gde’iing, miinwaa ezhi-gnowaamdaman gegoo.
Anishnaabeg ge mkaan gegoo kina da-zhi-gnowaamdaanaawaa.
Mii dash maaba shkiniigshens, maaba waa-dbaajmag.

paragraph.text_eng: Little Antoine was this young man’s name. His father was good at hunting. Antoine’s father, whose name was Michael, always, always, always went hunting. They always went to the forest. And then this boy always followed his father around, following him around going about hunting. Always. And this Michael, always took him along, his darling son.

sentence.sent_text: Aatwenens gii-zhinkaaza maaba shkiniigish, Bapaa’iin dash maaba gii-ntaa-giiwsewan.
Aatwen ge’ii bapaa iin, Miishen gaa-zhinkaazad, pane, pane, pane gii-giiwsewaag.
Megwemtigwaaki pane gii-zhaawag.
Mii dash maaba gwiizens, pane bapaa’iin gii-bbaa-noopnanaan, bbaa-noopnanaad bbaa-giiwsewaad.
Pane gwa.
Mii maaba Miishen, pane gii-bbaamwinaan nonda gwisenyiin.

paragraph.text_eng: So this boy, he saw everything in the forest. Huh, he heard little birds. Ho, little stick cracked over there; ho, who did that? This Antoine ran over there, trying to see them little animals, a little squirrel or partridge. Antoine very much loved the outside. He loved the forest. That’s where always he went about playing.

sentence.sent_text: Miish go maaba gwiizens, kina gegoo gii-waamdaan megwemtigwaaki.
Huh, bneshiinsan gii-noondwaan.
Ho, mtigoons gii-mdwe-boogshkaa oodi, ho, wenesh gaa-zhichged wi?
Miish ko maaba Aatwenens oodi gii-patood, ggwe-debwaabmaad ne’en wesiinsan, jiidmoons maa ge bine.
Aapjish go maaba Aatwenens gii-zaagtoon gojiing.
Megwemtigwaaki gii-zaagtoon.
Mii oodi pane gii-bbaa-damnad.

paragraph.text_eng: Sometimes he would only just sit there in the forest. He stood still; he closed his eyes, and he would only listen. He listened to everything that he heard in the forest and also up above. That’s the only thing that he did, sometimes.

sentence.sent_text: Naadgondoong go eta go gii-oo-nimadabi oodi megwemtigwaaki.
Gii-bizangwaabi dash, gii-bizangwaabi, miish go eta gw a gii-bizinshed.
Gii-bizindaan kina gegoo e-noondang megwemtigwaaki, miinwaa oodi ishpiming.
Mii go eta maaba gaa-nankiid maaba, naadgondoong.

paragraph.text_eng: He’d go and sit in the forest, and he would listen. A little bird would be singing over there. A squirrel would be getting mad over there. He heard someone walking. The twigs were cracking. That’s what this young man would do.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-oo-nimadabi megwemtigwaaki mii dash bizinshed.
Haaw, bineshiins mdwe-ngamo, Oh, jidmoons ge’ii oodi mdwe-nshkaadzi, Gwaya noondwaan bmosenid.
Mtigoonsag boogshkaa oog.
Miish ko maaba gaa-zhichged shkiniigish.

paragraph.text_eng: So when he got big, when he was fifteen years old, his father bought him a small gun. Just a small gun, the one that’s called a twenty-two. That’s what this boy got, this Little Antoine. He was very happy.

sentence.sent_text: Miish go maanda ni-mdidad, mii dash zhiwe medaaso-shi-naano-bboongizid, mii bapaa iin gii-yaamaagwad baashkzigaans.
Baashkzigaans e-gaaching go naa.
Wi niishtana-shi-niish ezhnikaadeg.
Mii maabaa gaa-debnang gwiizens, maaba Aatwenens.
Aapji sa naa gii-gchi-nendam maaba.

paragraph.text_eng: So Michael says, “Little Antoine, you are not just going to take off running to the forest to use this. You have to kow how to take care of this gun. You have to take good care of it. There has to be respect there. Respect what I am giving you, a gun. You have to know how to take care of it. How to love it, how to clean it, and when to use it. Who? Who will you be able to kill when you are able to use the gun? You will not be able to kill a large animal by using this small gun.”

sentence.sent_text: Maaba dash Miishen, “Aatwenens,’ kida sa.
“Gaa’ii go maanda we’iib kwii-maajiiptoosii oodi megwemtigwaaki wii-nakaazyin.
Aabdeg kwii-gkendaan waa-zhi-naagdawendman maanda baashkzigan.
We’eni kwii-naagdawendaan.
Mnaadendmowin wii-temgad zhi e.
Mnaadendan maanda e-miininaanh, baashkzigan.
Aabdeg kwii-gkendaan waa-zhi-naagdawendman.
Waa-zhi-zaagto’iin wi.
Wii-biichigaadeg.
Pii ge waa-nakaazyin.
Wenesh?
Wenesh ge-gshki’ad wii-nsad pii maanda wii-nakaazyin baashkzigan?
Gaa’ii maamdaa gchi-wesiinh ji-nsadiba maanda wii-nakaazyin egaaching baashkzigaans.”

paragraph.text_eng: So Little Antoine was made to understand all this. Little Antoine was good at listening. He listened well to his father. So he and his father and his uncle always went hunting. They lived in a place similar to the forest. The house was a log house that they had. Little Antoine always followed, always went along with his father and his uncle when they went hunting.

sentence.sent_text: Miish maaba we’eni gii-nsastamoonin maaba Aatwenens.
Aatwenens dash aapji gii-ngachtoon bizindang.
We eni gii-bizindwaan ne’en bapaa’iin, Mii sa maaba pane ne’e bapaa’iin miinwaa zhishen’iin, pane gii-giiwsewag gonda.
Miish go manpii dna’oong gaa-daa’aad ge’e megwemtigwaaki.
Wiigwaam, mtig-gamig gii-yaanaa’a.
Aapjish go maaba Aatwenens, pane gii-noopnanaan, pane gii-bbaa-wiijii’aan bapaa’iin miinwaa zhishen’iin bbaa-giiwse’aad.

paragraph.text_eng: There were a lot of deer heads inside where they lived. Deer antlers, all that were killed by Michael. Michael displayed all of these. These animals were of different kinds. So one time when it was in the fall, when it was around September, when it was starting to get cool, especially in the evening, when the sun went down, when you felt it cooling down, sometimes when it was raining, Little Antoine and Michael, and Michael’s brother, David was his name, would plan.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-baatiinoog biindig gaa-daa’aad gond waa’aashkeshii-ndiban.
Waa’aashkeshii-deshknag, kina gwa gaa-bmi-nsaad maaba Miishen.
Miishen, mii nonda kina gii-mzinchigenan nonda.
Noonj gii-zhinaagziwag gonda wesiinsan.

Mii dash maanda ngoding, pii, mii go maanda ni dgwaagigsh maanda, oohn gnomaa ngoji bnaakwii-giizis, bnaakwii-giizis, bangii go zhaazhi bangii ni-tkeyaamgak, ni-tkeyaamgad, memdige go ni-dbikak, ni-nkiiyed wa giizis, mii wi mooshtoo’iin wi tkeyaamgak, naadgondoong ge gwa gmiwan, mii dash gonda gii-naaknigewaad, maaba Aatwenens, miinwaa maaba Miishen, miinwaa maaba Miishen wiikaane’iin, Debid gii-zhinkaaza.

paragraph.text_eng: So they went hunting. It was a Saturday morning. It was just beautiful out. What it looks like in the fall, when all the leaves have fallen. It’s a good day, just enough coolness. The sun had come out, so they left to go hunting—this David, Michael and Little Antoine.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash gonda wii-bbaa-giiwse’aad.
Kizhebsh maanda Maanii-giizhgadoong.
Aapji go gnaajwan, ni-dgwaagik ezhnaagwak, zhaazhi ge kina niibiishan gii-ndagoodenoon.
Mno-giizhgad, aapji go mno-piichi-tkeyaamgad.
Giizis ge gii-bi-zaagiiye, miish gonda gii-maajaa’aad bbaa-nda-giiwse’aad maaba nDebid, Miishen miinwaa dash Aatwenens.

paragraph.text_eng: Okay, this Little Antoine, this young man was already fifteen years old. So he took his gun that was given to him, and he followed his father and his uncle, Little Antoine who lived in the forest was very much acquainted with where he was going. There was a small lake over there. There were lots of ducks there. Little Antoine was very aware of what the forest looked like.

sentence.sent_text: Ahaa, maaba Aatwenens, zhaazhi maaba mdaaso-shi-naano-bboonigizi maaba shkiniigish.
Mii sa ge’ii gii-maajiidood baashkzigaans e-gaaching gaa-miinind.
Miish bbaa-noopnanaad nonda bapaa’iin miinwaa zhishen’iin.
Aapjish maaba Aatwenens, maanda memgwemtigwaaki gaa-daad, aapji gii ngadendaan waa-ni-zhi-zhaad.
Zaagigaans oodi te.
Zhiishiiben’iig aapji oodi gii-baatiinwaag.
Aapji maaba Aatwenens gii-ngadendaan ezhnaagwak megwemtigwaaki.

paragraph.text_eng: Always, always, he always followed his father around. “I think I could do it,” Little Antoine used to say. “I could go all around over there; I could go to the small lake. I could close my eyes. I could go over there with my eyes closed and come back.” This is how this Little Antoine used to boast of himself.

sentence.sent_text: Pane, pane, pane gii-bbaa-zhaa oodi bbaa-noopnanaad bapaa’iin.
“Megwaach go ndaa-gshkitoon,” gii-kida ko maaba Aatwenens.
“Kina go oodi ndaa’bibaa-zhi-zhaa, oodi ge zaagigaansing ndaa-zhaa.
Ndaa-bzangwaab go.
Ndaa gshkitoon go ji-bbaa-zhaa’aanh oodi neyaab ji-bi-bskaabiiyaanh.” Mii ko maaba gaa-zhi-maamiikwaandizad maaba Aatwenens.

paragraph.text_eng: “I could go over there; I could close my eyes all over the place. I will be able to come back.” This is how sure of himself of going into the forest. So on this here Saturday they left.

sentence.sent_text: “Ndaa-gshkitoon go ji-bbaa-zhi-zhaa’aanh oodi, ndaa-bbaa-bzingwaab go kina ngoji.
Ndaa-gshkitoon go ji-bi-bskaabiiyaanh”” Mii maabaa gaa-piichi-ngadendang wi pane gii-zhaad megwemtigwaaki.
Mii dash maanda pii Maanii-giizhgadoong mii gonda gii-maajaa’aad.

paragraph.text_eng: So Little Antoine’s mother, as he was getting ready, he was getting this packsack ready. Little Antoine’s mother, Sophie, says, “Little Antoine, why don’t you put your raincoat there, and also take the matches that you will use. A hat, and a warm jacket, or a thick shirt.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash maaba Aatwenens mamaa’iin, gashwan, ge’ii maaba Aatwenens bmi-gchi-zhiitaa, maanda bmoonjgan, mii maanda be-bmi-zhiitaawtood.
Miish maaba Aatwenens mamaa’iin, maaba Sapii, mii e-kidad, “Aatwenens, esnaa toon zhi’e ni’ii gmooni-biiskawaagan, miinwaa ni’ii mshkodensan ka-maajiidoonan waa-nakaazyin.
Wiikwaan, miinwaa gaazhoowiigak-gbiiskawaagan, maa ge babgoyaan gepagiigak.”

paragraph.text_eng: So this Little Antoine says, “Oh Mother, not necessary, I’m not going to use it. I’m not going to sleep there; we are coming home.” But they were going to be all day. So Little Antoine didr’t bother to put his coat there. Only his shirt he had on, and no raincoat that was warm, or matches, or to have taken a lunch. Michael, Little Antoine’s father, carried a lunch. And so they left.

sentence.sent_text: Miish maaba Aatwenens, “Oh, nMamaa,” kida sa, “Gaa’ii memkaach, gaa’ii nii-nakaasiin wi,” kida.
“Gaa’ii oodi nwii-nbaasiimi,” kida, “nwii-bi-giiwemi go.” Gbe-giizhik shwii gwa wii-bbaa-yaawag.
Mii sa maaba Aatwenens gaa’ii gii-bbaamendziin wii-tood zhi’e biiskawaagan.
Mii eta maanda babgoyaan baaskang, gaa’ii ge gegoo gmooni-biiskawaagan gaazhoowaag miinwaash mshkodensan maa ge noopwaanens ji-gii-maajiidood.
Maaba Miishen kina bimwidoon noopwaan.
Aatwenens bapaa’iin.
Mii sa gii-maajaa’aad gonda.

paragraph.text_eng: When Little Antoine got there in the forest, he was very anxious. He was in a hurry to look for the deer, and so he says to his father as they went to the edge of the forest, “Oh, Father, I will go on ahead. I will go ahead and I’ll see you on the other side.” “Okay,” says Michael. “Dont go too far.” But Little Antoine says, “Ah, Father, I know all of this place, I know how it looks here.”

sentence.sent_text: Aapjish go maaba Aatwenens pii go ni-dgoshing oodi megwemtigwaaki, aapji go naa gii-gwiiwni-zhiyaa.
We’iibendam wii-bbaa-ndowaabmaad ne’en waa’aashkeshwan.
Mii dash e naad bapaa’iin oodi gaa-ni-jekaakomwaad, “Oh nBapaa, niin nga-ni-niigaanii,” kida.
“Niin nga-ni-niigaanii oodi mbaneyiing ka-waabminim,” kida.
“Nahaaw,” kida dash maaba Miishen.
“Gegwa, gegwa aapji waasa ni-zhaake.” Aapjish go maaba Aatwenens, “Ha, nBapaa” kida.
“Kina nii maanda manpii nagdendaan,” kida.
“Ngii-gkendaan manpii kina ezhnaagwak.”

paragraph.text_eng: So Little Antoine went on ahead. Michael and David went over the other way, and Little Antoine went that way. He was carrying this small gun; he was carrying the small gun looking for deer. Aw, he stopped now and then; he hears birds, and when he stops, he listens to them or he sees squirrels. He just walked, walked. He looked all over the place.

sentence.sent_text: Miisa maaba Aatwenens gii-ni-niigaaniid.
Maaba dash Miishen miinwaa nDebid, oodi gewiinwaa nikeyaa gii-ni-zhaawag.
Maaba dash Aatwenens oodi gii-ni-zhaa.
Miish go maanda baashkzigaans bemwidood, baashkzigaans bimwidoon bbaa-ndowaabmaad waa’aashkeshwan.
Aaw, piichin sa go ni-noogigaabwi, bineshiinsan noondwaan miish noogigaabwid ke-bizindwaad ne’e ma age jiidmoonsan waabmaan.
Miish go eta gii-bmosed, bmose.
Kina ngoji bbaa-ninaabi.

paragraph.text_eng: So this is what he does. These handkerchiefs that he had in his pocket, these handkerchiefs is what he tied to the trees. He tore up the handkerchiefs as if he was tearing paper, is what he did. And so he tied these to the small trees. So he walks and walks around there, and he stops and he ties this to the small trees. He went far. He stops after awhile. He stands there.

sentence.sent_text: Ni’ii dash maaba gii-zhichge.
Gonda mooshweniigaansan gaa-biindaagnowaad, gziijaanewang mii nonda gaa-ni-tkobnaajin mitgoong.
Gii-daashkiigbinaan ne’en mooshweniigaansan dbishkoo go naa maanda mzina’igan daashkiigbijgaadeg, mii maanda gaa-zhichged, Mii dash gii-tkobidood maanda mtigoonsing.
Haa, ni-bmose go miinwaa’aa oodi ni-waawnase, miish go miinwaa ke-noogigaabwid, mii sa go miinwaa ni tkobidood maanda mtigoonsing.
Waasa dash go maaba gii-zhaa.
Gmaapiich noogigaabwi.
Naaniibwi dash zhi’e.

paragraph.text_eng: “My it looks strange there. Oh, I must have gone far,” he thinks. “I walked far.” So he starts walking. He does not have a compass. He didn’t have that. He used the sun for direction. Well, its West that way, the sun is to the West. Well, it must be around two o’clock or three o’clock.

sentence.sent_text: “Gesnaa myegnaagwad zhonda.
Oohn, esnaa iidig waasa gaa-zhaa’aan,” nendamsh maaba.
“Sa waasa ngii-zhigaadese.” Mii sa gii-maajiigaadesed.
Gaa ge daa’aanziin maanda go naanh nonda niiwin nikeyiing kinwaajchigaans.
Gaa’ii gii-yaaziin wi.
Michwe dibaamaan dash go naa nonda giizsoon.
Haa, oodi nikeyaa epangishmok, epangishmok nikeyaa abi wa giizis.
Oo, megwaach go daa-niizho-dbagane’e maa ge daa-nso-dbagane’e.

paragraph.text_eng: So he left, and he went that way. When he got there he saw a big tree. A big tree was standing there, and he ilooks at the tree; “Hmm,” he thinks. “I saw this tree behind aver there” He, Little Antoine, must have just walked around. And he came back around to where this big tree stood. Well, Little Antoine never, ever, thought he’d be lost here in this forest. He didn’t know where he was. “Oh my goodness.” At least he had the gun. He had the small gun. So he left again; he left walking.

sentence.sent_text: Mii sa gii-ni-maajaad miish oodi nikeyaa e ni-zhaad.
Miish gii-bi-dgoshing miinwaa na’aan dash gii-waabmaan gchi-mtigoon.
Ooh, gchi-ninaatig zhi’e gii-bidakshin miish gnowaabmaad nondan mtigoon “Hmm,” nendam sa.

Wesiinh-mshkikii-nini, mii maaba Aatwenens gaa-ni-aawid.
Mii dash go eta pane gaa-ni-nankiid wi.
Gii-ni-nakiitaage wesiinhiig enji-gnawenjgaazwaad.

paragraph.text_eng: Alright, thank you for listening to me. I will rest awhile. Here’s water, my throat is very dry.

sentence.sent_text: Nahaaw, miigwech gaa-bzindowyeg.
Nga-ke-nweb.
Manda mbiish, aapji go mbaate gondaagan.

chapter.eng_title: This is what is going to hellp you have good child bearing years

paragraph.text_eng: Alright, thank you, thank you for the tobacco

sentence.sent_text: Ahaw.
Miigwech, miigwech awe asemaa.

paragraph.text_eng: This tobacco is handed to me. I would never say no when I see tobacco being handed to me. I really honor tobacco. I was always told to have that lead me whenever someone wants to do something or when you are asking for things.

sentence.sent_text: Aaniishinaa Asemaa gaa-niiminimaagowaan.
Gaawiin wiikaa gaawiin indaa-ikidosii owe gii-waabamag awe asemaa gii-niiminimaagoowaan.
Aapichi ningichi-apiitenimaa aw asemaa.
Mii geniin awe apane gaa-igowaan ji biminiigaanii’ag gegoo awiya gii-bimi-ezhichiged gemaa gegii-gagwejimind awiiya.

paragraph.text_eng: For example when one is trapping, you should always have your tobacco lead you like when someone goes hunting. You always put your tobacco down before you start whatever it is that you are doing. That is why I have a high regard for my tobacco.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke awe gii-wanii’iged awiiya, onjida igo akawe ji-niigaanii’aad odasemaan awe ge gii-andawenjiged awiiya.
Onjida ji-bagidinaad awiiya iniw odasemaan jibwaa maajitaad awe waa-izhichiged.
Mii dash iwe wenji gichi apiitenimag geniin aw asemaa.

paragraph.text_eng: I always lived and played in the bush. I was raised in the bush as we lived in the woods, those one that raised me. I have always observed how they hunt and how they trap. This is how we lived and survived, from the animals.

sentence.sent_text: Aapichi geniin apane ingii-pi-ayaa omaa ingii-pi-tazhiike omaa noopimiing.
Ingii-pi-izhi-ombig sa go omaa noopiming gii-pi-endaayaang ogowe gaa-nitaawigii’iwaad.
Apane ge ingii-waabamaag ezhi-andawenjigewaad ezhi-wanii’igewaadge.
Mii sago owe mii sago owe gaa-ondaadiziiyaang owe awesiinyag anishinaa.

paragraph.text_eng: Those are our gifts to provide us with food for our well being and also our warmth. And then there is this one, this one I shall talk about first, the one that is called a moose. I have seen a lot; I myself was privileged to get my own moose.

sentence.sent_text: Aaniishinaa mii-go igiwe gaa-izhi-miinigooziyang ji-bimi-ayiinajigeyang ji-onji-mino-ayaayang sago gaye ji-onji-giizhooziyang gaye.
Aya’a dash awe aya aa niwii-dazhimaa akawe mooz enind.
Niibiyo ge-niin ingii-pi-waabange ge-niin sago ingii-pi-gashkitoon ji-debinag aw ji-nisag aw moonz.

paragraph.text_eng: Long time ago when I was growing up, I was being prepared for this.

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha dash owe gii-pi-ombigiyaan giizhaa gegoo ingii-wiindamaago owe.

paragraph.text_eng: Someday you will be honored to carry a child inside of you; it will grow inside of you as you carry through. This is what they told me.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ingoding gegiin giga-inendaagoz owe ji-bimiwidamaazowin awe abinoojiinh imaa, biinjina imaa da-dazhi-nitaawigi awe abinoojiinh ge-bimiiwinad.
Mii ko gaa-igowaan.

paragraph.text_eng: For instance, the way that the moose looks, study the inside of the moose is what I was told by the one that raised me. She would cut open the moose, such as this, you should have a good look at how it looks.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke dash, onowe minik gaa-izhinaagozid aw mooz nashke naanaagajitoon onowe ingii-wiindamaag sago awe gaa-gii-nitaawigi’id.
Obagojiinaan ni moozoon, nashke owe naanaagajitoon ezhinaagwak owe.

paragraph.text_eng: The woman looks the same in the inside, especially the female moose.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iwe bezhigwan ezhinaagozid awe biinjaya’ii ayikwe, nashke awe noozhemooz.

paragraph.text_eng: I have also seen the unborn moose how it lays inside the womb and wrapped up in the birth bag. The woman looks exactly the same inside as the moose when a woman carries a baby. This is what they told me.

sentence.sent_text: Ingii-waabamaa ge a moozoons ezhi-aabit imaa biinjimisad miinawaa omaa ezhi-biinzod awe.
Mii dash igo iwe bezhigwan ezhinaagozid awe gii-bimiwinaad ni abinoojiiyan mii go gaa-bimi-egowaan.

paragraph.text_eng: There are two things in there. There is this first stomach, and it is large, perhaps it is the same size as a volleyball; it is much like a bag.

sentence.sent_text: Niizh idash gego omaa ayaawan, Nashke awe bebiitoos izhinikaade bezhig e’ii aapichi mangibii eyii maagizhaa, maagizhaa 'volley ball' gaa-inikokobiig mashkimod igo.

paragraph.text_eng: So she would cut it open and shake off the food from it. Not only the female should eat this, but anyone can, ecauiee it is very good to eat and you get healing from it.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash imaa gaa-izhi-ayaad gaa-izhi-bagojiizhang ezhi-bapaawiwebinang.
Mii awe bezhig emiijid ayikwe onjidago, gaawinoon eta go aw ikwe awegwen igo odaa-miijin owedinowa, aapichi onishishin owe awiiya ji-miijid anishinaa nanaandawi’idizo

paragraph.text_eng: And then there is another one about the same size as the other one. This one is called second stomach, and that is another one. This is very good for the woman to eat. You can eat it anytime not only during pregnancy. Sometimes girls start eating this at a very young age.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa go bezhig mii go miinawaa gegaago enigokokwaag aw bezhig eninigokobiig.
Mii sa owe ogidagimod enind mii go awe miinawaa bezhig.
Aapichi wenizhishing ji-miijid ay ikwe.
Amanj igo apii gaawinoon eta go iwe gii-gigishkawawasod awiiya.
Booshke ge ingoding geyaa gii-ikwezensiwid awiya mii go apii maawiin maajii-miijid.

paragraph.text_eng: “This is what is going to help you have good child bearing years,” is what I was told. You will have a healthy pregnancy when you are blessed to carry a child.

sentence.sent_text: “Mii sa awe ge-wiiji’igoyan ji-mino-gi’aawasoyan” mii niin ako gaa-igowaan.
Aapichi giga-minogi’aag ogowe ingoding inendaagoziyan ji-gigishkawad aw abinoojiinh booshke ingoding awiiya.

paragraph.text_eng: Sometimes someone will even carry two babies, and that is why the moose is respected and honored. To give thanks to the moose for giving these two, the first and second stomach, so the woman will have good child bearing years.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding awiiya niizho ogigashkawaa’ abinoojiinha’ mii dash owe wenji weweni izhi-ind aw mooz.
Miigwechiwi’ind sago owe gii-miigiiwed onowe niizh bebiidoos ogitagimod ji-onji-mino-gi’aawasod ay ikwe.

paragraph.text_eng: Those are the teachings I was told and that is what I did.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iwe ko gaa-miizhi-waawiindamaagoyaan geget idash igo ingii-izhichige iwe.

paragraph.text_eng: And I did have good child bearing years, and I even had twins born at one time. So I really thought highly of that moose.

sentence.sent_text: Geget idash igo ingii-mino-gi’aawas boochige aabading gii-niizhiyog ogowe indabanoojiimag aa gaa-bi-nitaawigiiwaat.
Aapichi idash ingii-gichi-apiitenimaa aw mooz.

paragraph.text_eng: Even now that I am past seventy years old; I still eat the same way that I was told to eat while being raised that way. I would never leave the traditional food that I was told to eat.

sentence.sent_text: Geyaabi go aapii naa awashime niizhwaasimidana noongom indasobiboone, geyaabi o’apii mii go enanjigeyaan awe gaa-pi-izhi-ombigii’igooyaan, gaa-apii-igowaan ji-bimi-ayenanjigeyaan.
Gaawiin wiikaa bakaan indaa-boonitoosiin minik gego gaa-bi-izhi-waawiindamaago ji-bimi-ayeninjigeyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: This too she told me, they told me. When you are carrying a child, the things that you do when you are carrying your child, that is the way your baby will be too. This is what I was told again.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ge owe gaa-pi-waawiindamawid eh ee he ndamawiwaad.
Owe gigiigishkawaad awiiya onowe abinoojiiyan, ezhichigeyan igo iwe owe gigishkawad gidabinoojiiyim, mii go iye ge-inaadizid apii ondaadizid a gidabinoojiiyim.
Mii ko gaa-bimi-ayegooyaan miinawaa.

paragraph.text_eng: It was true, I did try that already. I was pregnant seven times. I did challenge, and lived the teachings that I was taught. One of my sons was born past midwinter, Then it was in the fall. I would always go about setting rabbit snares. I did catch rabbits. And today that son of mine is over fifty years old. That’s it, that one is a good rabbit catcher every year. He’s always been that way; he is good at catching rabbits. He too really likes to eat the rabbit.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash igo geget ingii-pi-gagwejitoon igo aazha iwe.
Niizhwaaching ingii-gigishkawaa aw abinoojiinh.
Ingii-bi-gagweyitoonan idash igo geget onowen gaa-gikinoo amaagowaan.
Bezhig awe ngozis baamaa ge-ani-giiwebiboong gii-nitaawigi mii dash iwe gii-dagwaagig.
Mii go apane gii-ayaa-aan gii-babaa-agoodoowaan aa waaboozoo-nagwaaganan ingii-babaa nibaagoodoonan.
Ingii-nisaag sago aa waaboozoog.
Mii dash awe ingozis noongom awashime naanimada daso-biboonigizi.
Mii sa awe, mii sa awe aapichi wenji’aad onisaa’o waaboozoo’endasobiboon.
Apane go pi-inaadizi owe onitaa-nagwaanaa’o waaboozoo’.
Aapichi sa go ge-wiin ominwenimaan amwaad iniwe waaboozoon mii-sago.

paragraph.text_eng: He always gives us some to eat so we will eat the good food. This is one of them that said. “If someone ever feels sick, he is the one you should make rabbit stew,” it was said.

sentence.sent_text: Nimaamiinigonaan ge-niinawiind ge yaa ge-ezhi-mino-wiisiniiyaang amwind aw owaabooz.
Anishinaa mii awe miinawaa bezhig gaa-ikodod awe.
“Giishpin wiikaa awiya maanimanji’od, mii awe waaboozoon naboob gidaa-ozhitoon.” gii-ikidooban.

paragraph.text_eng: The rabbit says this when he was asked by Nanabush, “How are you going to hellp the Anishinaabe when they get here?”

sentence.sent_text: Gii-ikido iinzan a waabooz gii-mi-gagwejimigod ini a’aan Nenaboozhoon aaniin giin waa-izhi-waawiiji’ad aw anishinaabe gii-bimi-ayiinind?”

paragraph.text_eng: Well, that’s one more; thank you.

sentence.sent_text: Ahaw sa miinawaa iye, miigwech.

paragraph.text_eng: My name is Baadwewidan. I am an Ojibwe Indian. I am a full blood. I am not of any other nation. I am all Ojibwe. Bullhead is my clan. My father was called Jiigogiizhig-akiwenzii. He too was of the bullhead clan. And my grandfather was called Aazhawaa. He was really an old time Indian.

sentence.sent_text: Niin dash Bawdwaywidun indizhinikaaz.
Ojibwe-Anishinaabe indaaw.
Mooshkinebii nimiskwiim.
Gaawiin gegoo bakaan indaawisii.
Mii eta go Ojibwe-Anishinaabe aawiyaan.
Awaazisii indoodem.
Nibaabaa-iban Jiingogiizhig-akiwenzii izhinikaazo.
Awaazisii odoodeman gii-aawi.
Miinawaa gaye nimishoomisiban aazhawaa gii-izhinikaazo, Geget gichi-gete-Anishinaabe gii-aawi.

paragraph.text_eng: Also I remember my great grandfather. He was called Chi-Binesii. He lived to be over a hundred years old. His wife’s name was Waadookose. My grandmother was called Ozaawaandib. She was from Mille Lacs.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa nimikwenimaa gaa-anikoobid nimishomisiban.
Chi-Binesii gii-izhinikaazo.
Awashime ingodwaak endaso-biboon gii-izhi-bimaadizi.
Aniwe ikwewan gaa-wiijiiwaajin Waadookose gii-izhinikaazo.
Miinawaa nookomisiban Ozaawaandib gii-izhinikaazo.
Misi-zaaga’iganiing gii-onjibaa.

paragraph.text_eng: And my mother’s name was Aanikoo-gaabawiikwe. Her father’s name was Naazhoogwan. Jim Heart was his name. He fought for the white man over in Europe. He went to help in World War One. He brought with him a lot of the ways of a man. He associated with people there in Lac Courte Oreilles. The lady was called Waabanang. And here is where I am from too.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa gaye nimaamaayiban Aanikoo-gaabawiikwe gii-izhinikaazo.
Obaabaayibanen Naazhoogwan gii-izhinikaazo.
Jim Heart gaye gii-izhinikaazo.
Gii-miigaadiwaad ah chi-mookomaan iwidi agaaming.
World War One gii-awi-wiidookaazo.
Niibiwa ogii-piidoon gaye wiin i’iw ezhiwebizid inini.
Miinawaa gaye wiin gaa-wiijii’aawaajin imaa Odaawaa-zaaga’iganing.
Waabanang gii-izhinikaazo ikweban.
Mii dash niin omaa wenjibaayaan.

paragraph.text_eng: I was born in a wigwam. I was not born in a hospital. The natural way of birth for the Anishinaabe is the way that I was born. I did not see the white man doctor. I did Not hear anyone speak English. That is the way that I was raised as a child. I did not go to school until I was nine years old. When I started school me too, that is when I learned to speak English. All I heard was the Ojibwe language. That is the origin of the teachings that I carry. Sacred teachings, songs, origin stories, Mide-teachings is what I know. This is what I heard as a child. I never heard anyone speak English where we lived. It wasn’t until I was seven years old that I saw a white man for the first time.

sentence.sent_text: Wigiwaaming ingii-ondaadiz, Gaawiin aakoziwigamigong niin ingii-ondaadizisiin.
Naasaab gaa-izhi-ondaadizid aw anishinaabe mii gaa-izhi-ondaadiziyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: Over there is LCO is what I am talking about is where I was born. That is where it originates from, these things that I carry. The seven sacred teachings that are called, that is where I heard the elders give teachings. They were not the only ones that I heard it from. Everybody that took part in ceremony, they all spoke the same way, they knew the same thing about what they were given, these seven teachings.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin mashkikiwinini gaawiin chi-mookomaan-mashkikiwinini ingii-waabamaasii.
Gaawiin ingii-noondawaasii awiiya zhaaganaashiimod, Mii geyaabi, mii awe gaashii’id awe oshki-bimaadizid gii-aawiyaan.
Gaawiin naa gikinoo’amaadiwigamigong ingii-azhaasiin, baanimaa gii-zhaangashoo zhaangaso-biboonagiziyaan.
Gii-maajii-gikinoo’amaagoyaan gaye niin da-zhaaganaashiimoyaan.
Bizhishig ojibwemowin ingii-noondaan.
Mii iwidi wenzikaamagak gaye niin iwidi dekonamaan giigidowinan.
Mide giigidowinan, nagamonan, aadizookaanan, mide-waajimonan niinawind indazhi-gikendaan.
Mii iw gaye niin gaa-izhi-noondamaan gii-agaashiiyaan.
Gaawiin wiikaa ingii-noondawaasiin awiiya zhaaganaashiimod niinawind gaa-taayaang.
Baanimaa gemaa gaye gii-niizhwaaso-biboonagiziyaan mii nitam ingii-waabamaa owaabishkiiwed inini.

paragraph.text_eng: As the Anishinaabe was told before the white man arrived. There were seven spirits that came to tell the Anishinaabe about what was going to happen with the coming of the white man. These are the teachings that were given that I am going to talk about, The Anishinaabe did not walk away from it. They gathered all the Mide teachings, the objects they used such as our Grandfather Drum, our rattles, Mide items and all that is used for the Midewiwin. They lifted their sacred items, and they all left from there together before the Menominee Indians left, the ones that are known as such; they were given the rice, the sacred rice that is called; the Anishinaabe was told to travel towards the west. As you arrive where it stands, where it lays in the water that sacred rice. This is where you will know the land that is for the Indian will be, This is what they were told. The Menominee were the first to bring the rice. It was in a sack, as we know of it. Then in birch bark and the songs, spirit songs and the wild rice bird that is called.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iwidi ezhinikaadeg Odaawaa-zaaga iganiing, mii owidi dibaajimoyaan gaa-ondaadiziyaan gaa-izhi-nitaawigiyaan geniin.
Mii iwidi gakina gegoo wenzikaamagak gaye niin ezhi-dakonimaan.
Niizhwaaswi midewaajimonan ezhinikaadeg mii idi gii-noondawagwaa gete-anishinaabeg gii-dibaajimowaad.
Gaawiin dash eta go wiinetawa ingii-noondawaasiig.
Gakina awiiya gaa-midewid imaa naasaab izhi-gaagiigidowag naasaab ogii-gikendaanaawaa anoo niizhwaaso gaa-miinind anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: That wild rice bird, that same one that flew up with the spirits as they were leaving. As they come and check it out, looked at it. And this is how we still know it. This sacred food, the spirit put it here for the Indian, for the Ojibwe, for the Potawatomi and the Odawa and the Menominee and the Shawnee that are called. And also the Kickapoo Indians that are called as such. This is spirit food that was given by the spirit. This is where it came from, you will not find anywhere else, that which was given to the Anishinaabe. The Anishinaabe was told to take care of the rice, and the rice will take care of you. The rice will never disappear as long as you take great care of it. And also offer your tobacco before you get into a canoe. Someone will speak to the spirit, that spirit that is in the water. This is the one that you speak to before you get into the canoe.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa gaye o gaa-izhi-wiindamawind aw anishinaabe o’apii dabwaa-dagoshing aw gaa-waabishkiwed.

paragraph.text_eng: As we proceed to pick rice, you shall respect all things. This is what we were told. Always remember the spirit; never forget the spirit.

sentence.sent_text: Niizhwaaso gii-tagoshinoog ezhi-manidoowaadiziwaad gii-wiindamawindwaa anishinaabe aaniin keyaa ewiiyan ezhi-wii-ezhiwebak ingoding wii-tagoshin waayaabishkiiwed.
Mii iwidi gii-wiindamawindwaa ya’o waa-tibaadidamaan.
Gaawiin gii-ozhimosiiwag anishinaabeg.
Ogii-maamiginaawaan gakina izhi-miinindwaa midenid, midewinid ayaabajitood owe ge gimishomisinaan dewe’igan, zhiishiigwanan, midewayaanan gakina gegoo ayaabajichigaadeg midewind anishinaabe.

Mii gaa-izhi-ombinigaadeg mii dash gaa-izhi-maajaawaad imaa keyaa gii-pii-onaawinidiwaad idash dabwa-bi-maajaawaad dash aw manoomini-anishinaabe, manoomini-anishinaabe noongom ezhi-gikenimind mii agiwaa gii-miinaawag yo’oh manoomin, manidoo-manoomin ezhinikaadeg omaa manidowaadad…gii-wiindamawaan anishinaabe iw wapii odi keyaa ningaabii’anong ezhaayan.
Baanimaa dagoshinan iwidi badakideg, agoondeg agoondeg iiwo manidoo-manoomin.
Mii imaa, mii imaa ajiwaa da-gikendameg gaye giinawaa gidandishinaabe-akiimiwaa gaa-ayaamagak.
Mii gaa izhi-wiindamawindwaa.
Wiinitamiwaa dash agiw manoominini-anishinaabeg, mii o gaa-pi-dakonamowaad.
Mashkimod igo dibishkoo mashkimod izhi-gikendamang.

paragraph.text_eng: ’The Creator is the one that put this rice to be growing here on earth. That is why we offer tobacco so that we carry on these sacred teachings. To know these teachings, not only to think about it but to know it, not any old way, not to think about them in any ole way, but to really know the teachings, this is what we were told. That is why tobacco is used before the rice is picked. This where we give our thanks for the sacredness of the rice, as we give thanks. This where we give our thanks to take care, of and to make it. We are not doing enough to take care of it; we don’t give enough voice to it. We do not waste any of it; we take great care of it, so that we can feed our children, so that we can feed the ones that are hungry.

sentence.sent_text: Wiigwaas idash i’ii miinawaa nagamonan, manidoo-nagamonan miinawwa gaye awiiya bineshiinh manoominkeshiiyen ezhinikaazod.
Mii ya’aw, mii ya’aw odaa naasaab gaa gaa-pazigwaa imaa gaa-pagizigwa’od i’iw apii gii-pamid gii-pi-maajaawaad manidoog.
Manidoo-manoomin gii-pi-nanda-waabandamowaad.
Mii dash geyaabi ezhi-gikendamang.

Manidoo-wiisiniwin, manidoo ogii-pagidinaan i’iw manoomin onjidaa anishinaabe, onjidaa giinawind ezhi-ojibwemoyang ezhi-boodawaadamiig gaye miinawaa manoom miinawaa odaawaag miinawaa manoominiig miinawaa gaye giinawaa ozhaawaanii ezhinikaazowaad.
Miinawaa gaye wiinawaa gaa-kikapoo gaa-izhinkaazowaad anishinaabeg.
Mii’yenh mii gaa-izhi-miinindwaa yo manidoo…manidoo-wiisiniwin ezhi-manidoowaadak i’iw manoomin.
Mii imaa wenzikaamagak gaawiin bakaan, gaawiin bakaan gaye gidaa-mikanziimin i’iw mii iw i’iw manoomin gaa-izhi-miinind Anishinaabe.
Mii dash i’yo gaa-izhi-wiindawind Anishinaa weweni ganawendaman yi’o manoomin miinawaa naasaab gaye giin ezhi-ganawenimigoyan.
Gaawiin wiikaa da-maadaasinoon i’iw ezhi-manidoowaadizid imaa nibiikaang.
Mii ya’aw ge-noonind dabwaa dabwaa-boozid awiiiya omaa jiimaaning.
Da-wii-maaminigaadeg i’iw manoomin weweni weweni pane da-manaajitooyan kina gegoo.
Mii gaa-izhi-wiindamaagoyang.
Pane da-mikwendamind, gego wiikaa wanenimaaken aw manidoo.

paragraph.text_eng: As I give these teachings, I want this to be carried on so that the Anishinaabe will know that this was given, as we take care of the sacredness of the food.

sentence.sent_text: Aw manidoo gaa-pagidendang yo omaa akiing da-biijikaamigak manoomin.
Mii dash iw wenji-asemaakeyang geyaabi bimiwidoodyang yo’o midewaajimon.
Geyaabi da-gikendamang, gaawiin eta go da-mikwendamang da-gikendamang gaawiin naasaab i’iw debinaak, gaawiin debinaak da-minikwendamang, da-gikendamang mii ezhi-wiindammengoyang.

Mii dash a’aw asemaa giishpin asemaa weweni aabaji’ aabaji’ang i’iw dabwaa-mamooyang yi’iw manoomin, Mii imaa wiindamawigeyang ezhi-miigwechiwitaagoziyang geyaabi o ezhi-manidoowaadak manoomin da-miigwechiwitaagoziwin.

Mii omaa ge gii-wiindamaagemin weweni wii-kanawendamang weweni wii-izhitooyang gaawiin gidaa-manaajitoosiimin, gaawiin gidaswewebitoosiimin Gaawiin gaye giwebinanziimin weweni giga-ganawendaamin da-wiisiniyang da-ashamang a’aw giniijaanisiminaang da-ashamang gaye a’aw bekaded anishinaabe.

paragraph.text_eng: We lead a good life when we remember the sacred teachings that we were given. I wish my teaching to be carried on to those that hear this. I do not do this for nothing. And I am not trying to step over the boundaries of other’s teachings. I give my teachings with respect to all the young people and the future generation. I give thanks whenever I finish a teaching. I say this to the spirit.

sentence.sent_text: Weweni idash ezhi-wiindamaageyaan nimisiwendaan iwidi keyaa niigaan da-gikendang anishinaabe yo, yo gaa-miinind gaa-miinigoyang da-ganawendamang ezhi-manidoowaadak yo’o, yo’o wiisiniwin.

Geget…geget gi-mino-ayaamin gi-mino-bimaadizimin gikendamang ano giigidowinan gaa-izhi-miinigoyang gaye’ii midewaajimon, Weweni dash nimisawendaan geget weweni da-noondang y’ow ezhi-naajimoyaan gaye niin.
Gaawiin anishaa ni-izhichigesii.
Miinawaa gaawiin, gaawiin ninagowenimaasii awiiya niin.
Weweni nimiinaa ya’o ezhi-dibaajimoyaan kina oshkinaj-anishinaabe.
O niijaanis miinawaa ongow anishinaabeg owid keyaa niigaan waa-ondaadizijig.
Miigwech yi’o taagozi dash ishkwaaj niin dibaajimoyaan.
Miinawaa naasab pane izhi-ganoonag manidoo.
Aazhiwenimishinaam gizhe-manidoo, aazhiwenimishinaam gizhe-manidoo, aazhiwenimishinaam gizhe-manidoo, zhawenimishinang gizhe-manidoo.
Niikaniganaa.

chapter.eng_title: Respect Those Who Dwell in the Water

paragraph.text_eng: I’m going to talk about my grandmother, Zhaabokiijiwanook, today. It’s there where I was raised on the Leech Lake reservation.
