That Mindimooyenh would set nets, and also she would always feast those that live in the water. Firstly, she fed the fish, the water beings, and the different spirits that live there in the water, so that she could make a good catch. And the spirit of the fish, it was like they supported her. It is there that I use to go with her; she was teaching me what I would be doing in the future.

sentence.sent_text: Aaniish naa mii noongom ji-dazhimag gii-bagidawaad ko nookomisim Zhaabokiijiwanook gii-izhinikaazo.
Mii iwedi Gaa-zagaskwaajimekaag ishkoniganing keyaa ge-niin imaa gii-nitaawigi’igoowaan.
Gii-bagidawaa ko aw mindimooyenh, mii dash igo pane gii-ashanged imaa nibiikaang ongow go gaa-ayaawaad igo.
Giigoowag naa go naanibaanawag, naanibaanawag igo niigaan gii-ashamaad miinawaa go bebakaan ingowe eyaawaad imaa manidoog nibiikaang imaa ji-debinaad da ge-wewiim.
Aaniish naa ge waawiindanan giigoowag ogii-naasaab ogii-bami’igoon.
Mii dash imaa geyaa ingii-wiijiiwaag ko wiijiitwangwaa ingii-wiijiiwaag, gikinoo’amawid ge-niin niigaan nagakeyaa ge-ni-izhichigeyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: And so then it was my turn. “You should feast them,” she said. You should feast those spirits who are masters of the water, who look after it. They do not own anything, those here, who look after the water and our land. And it was there that I saw that which was amazing, the one time the lake started up (to develop whirlpools).

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash iw niinitam, maamo-nitam, “Gidaa-ashange ko” gii-ikido.
Gidaa-ashamaag ogowe ogow manidoog ge-dibendamowaad ge-ganawenjigewaad.
Gaawiin dibenimaasiiwag ingiw geganawenjimaad omaa nibiikaang miinawaa go gidakiiminaang.
Mii dash imaa iko gii-ganawaabamag a’a maamakaaj iko gaa-waabandamaan, aaniish naa wewiin aabiding ko gaa-ani-maajiijiwang o’ow agaming.

paragraph.text_eng: She forgot to do a feast, firstly for the Mermaids. It was there that she did not put a feast dish down and that is when it started (the whirl pool), and it was then that we nearly tipped over. We were close there to the reeds, that is where we came to an abrupt stop, and there I really used a paddle to push that boat backwards. And I think perhaps it was some spirit who helped us move when we got stuck. And so we were able to go back to the landing, where we started from.

sentence.sent_text: Ogii-waniike wii-ashamindwaa kawe oo aw nenibaaniwag.
Mii iwidi gaawiin nitam ogii-atoosiin onaagan miijim mii dash gaa-izhi-maajiijiwang mii dash niinawind imaa gegaa go gii-izhi-ditibiseyaang.
Besho dash imaa mashkosiing imaa gii-ayaayaang mii dash imaa gii-nooshkaachi’ang, mii dash imaa geget azhaa abwiin azhaa gaa-zhi-aabajitoowaan azhekwashkamaan iw jiimaan.
Mii dash ganabaj go awiiya ko gii-wiidookaagewind indinendam imaa ge baataaseyaang.
Mii dash i’iw gii-gashkii wewiziyaang go ji-maajiishkaang miinawaa, mii dash iwidi amanji go niwanendam go landing ezhinikaadeg, mii ge gaa-dazhi-boogiziyang.

paragraph.text_eng: And we went back, and so that is where my grandmother chose to stay. “I will go and put the dish down, and I will talk carefully to the spirits who dwell in the water,” she says. And she really went over there. It was nearly dark when she came back. And she did all of everything (ceremony-wise). She did not want to use cloth; she only wanted to use birch bark and food. She made a circular cut in the birch bark; it is there where she put the food. And she was always gifted from the spirit of the fish. Her actions helped her to be gifted.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash imaa gii-azheshkaamaang go mii dash imaa nookomisiban iwidi mii maa eshkwiid.
“Niin eta go inga-o-atoon iniw onaagan weweni ji-gaganoonagwaa manidoog maa eyaawaad imaa agaaming, ikido.
Mii dash geget gii-izhaad iwidi.
Gegaa naa dibikaaginaagok, mii dash gaa-gii-izhi-bi-azhegiiwed.
Mii i’w kina gegoo gii-izhichiged.
Gaawiin wiin gidagiigin owii-aabajitoosii mii etaa go bizaan igo wiigwaas, wiigwaas wii-aabajitood miinawaa wiisiniwin.
Gii-waawiyebimaagizhkizwaad a’aw wiigwaas mii dash imaa gii-atood iw wiisiniwin miijim wii-ashamaad igo manidoog maa.
Maa apane mii gii-gegizod.
Aaniish naa mii gii-zhawenimigod mii dash imaa geget niigaan gaa-izhi-ni-bami’igod giigoowag.
Aaniish naa gii-meshkwadoonaajige ge-wiin weweni gaye wiin ji-debidood i’iw gaa-noondesed.

paragraph.text_eng: And for certain my grandmother taught me, and I saw a lot of what she did when I helped, when I was with her, as she was my elder. And her nets, she first soaked in cedar water. Before she netted, before she even started, she had a feast. Whatever she did she had a feast, and beforehand she gave tobacco, and she placed the tobacco near the water. My home is no longer there.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash imaa geget gii-gikinoo’amawid miinawaa niibowa gegoo gii-o-ganawaabamag ko gii-wiidookawag gii-wiijtlwag aaniish naa ge-wiin zaziikizi a’aw nookomisiban.
Mii dash ge odasabiin gaye aaniish naa piizhikaandag ko ogii-boodaakwebinaan.
Jibwaa-onasabiid, jibwaa-maajitaad sa go weweni ge-gii-ashange wii-maajitaad wiin igo.
Anooj igo waa-izhichiged mii go gaye kawe gii-ashanged, asemaa gaye omiinaan niigaanizid aabaji’aawaad, miinawaa go gemaa besho gii-eta gii-asaa agii’aa asemaa jiigibiig.
Gaawiin-sh geyaabi imaa ge-abiitamaan gaawiin geyaabi maa gidagesii.

paragraph.text_eng: And then, what is that name? Jeez, I lost it, that Wenabozho, how that stick became colored, the kinikinik there I used; when Wenabozho made it, when he had a bloody rear, the story of the color of red willow. I get excited when I hear this; I did not just tell a sacred story; that finished up awhile back.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash iw, aaniin da naa ezhinikaadeg?
O, umm hay’ mii gii-wanendamaan, a’aw Wenabozho, go gaa-wenji-inaandeg i’iw mitigoonsan, kinikinik maa gii-aabajitoowaan gii-ozhitoowaad Wenabozho gii-miskwiwijiidid?
Red willow giiwenh ondinigaadeg.
Nijiikendam ko noondamaan i’iw gaawiin dash ingii-aadizookesii mii bijiinag, mewinzha wiin gii-ishkwaasemagad.

paragraph.text_eng: And so she used that tobacco she made. She also dried it and baked it. It is there she put down ne ners It was later that they went there to the store to buy tobacco. They only made this long ago, but perhaps today we do not do these things. Too much, too much of a hurry, we run over there to the store to buy tobacco.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash iw gaa-aabajitoowaad a’aw asemaa gii-ozhitoowaad.
Miinawaa-ge gaa-baaso-atoowaad ge maa, iw jiibaakwewaad gii-ombizowaad igo.
Mii dazhi-atoowaad a’aw asemaa.
Mii bijiinag wii-naagaji imaa gii-adaawewaad imaa adaawewigamigong iw semaa.
Wiin eta go gaa-ozhitoowaad mewinzha gaawiin dash, gaawiin ganabaj noongom gidizhichigesiimin.
Onzaam, onzaam jajepiimagad, iwidi adaawewigamigong ji-apatoowang ji-adaaweyang asemaa.

paragraph.text_eng: Thus she prepares her net after she finishes cleaning and drying it. Only two, not very big, perhaps three feet by 100 feet, I don’t know how I would say that. Not over there, only by Ball Club Lake she would go set nets. They do it differently over there in Red Lake. She did not put cloth in the water, only a dish and tobacco. My grandmother used birch bark (dish)in the process of retrieving nets. She first did this before setting nets. This is what they must have done.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash iw gii-oninasabiid gii-ishkwaa-giziibiiginaad miinawaa ko gii-baasowaad asabiig.
Niizh eta go gaawiin wiin i iw gii-michaasii, ganabaj igo 3 feet by 100 feet gaawiin ingikendanzii ge-ikidoyaambaan iw.
Gaawiin idi keyaa baaga’adowaaning mii eta go zaaga’iganing awi-naadasabiid.
Bakaan idi Miskwaagami-zaaga’iganing izhichigewag.
Mii dash wiin imaa go gaawiin ogii-bakobiiwebinaasii iw biisikaniganan, mii eta go onaagan miinawaa asemaa.
Naa wiigwaas gaa-aabajitood a nookomisiban e-naadisabiid.
Bwaa-bakobiiwebinaad asabiin.
Mii sa maa kawe gaa-izhichiged nawaj igo gaye ge-izhichigewaagwen.

paragraph.text_eng: When I became engaged over in Red Lake, they did it differently before starting. First they placed their things, what they wore there in the water as well as tobacco ties. They do things differently, they were taught to do these things by their elders. Before they set nets, this is their priority in Red Lake. There is a slight difference between everything we do.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-nangabii’aan gaye Miskwaagamiwi-zaga’iganing, bakaan wiinawaa izhichiged bwaa-maajitaawaad.
Mii kawe odayi’iimiwaan yo’ow biizika’igewaad mii imaa ezhi-bakobiiwebinaawaad imaa agaaming semaa gaye dakonibinaawaad.
Geget bakaaniwaa izhichigewag aaniish naa wiinawaa mii gaa-gikinoo’amaagoowaad ogitiziimiwaan.
Bwaa-wanasabiiwaad ge baa kina gegoo baa-izhichigewaad mii ezhichigewaad Miskwaagamiwi-zaaga’iganing.
Mii dash niinawind bakaan ge-niin bangii.

paragraph.text_eng: And when we picked berries and did what we do, we feasted. Before we left for anywhere, when we received a gift, or anything we might need, we had a feast.

sentence.sent_text: Naa go ge ayi’ii mawinzowang ko naa ge gaa-izhichigeyang wii-ashangeyang.
Jibwaa-maajaayaang naa go, debidooyang gaa-izhichigeyaang miish ge-zhi-ashangeyaang weweni ji-debidooyaang naa gaye weweni ji-jiibaakwe’igeyaang miinan.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what my grandmother did; she cooked and dried the fish. She used to can and dry fish. She always caught sturgeon. The sturgeon tore up the nets, only two were caught, but they tore up the net. And thus, we did sew and repair the nets; it is there that I started to sew and repair the nets.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash ko gaa-izhichiged a’aw nookomisiban gii-gibaakwa’ige mii dash miinawaa go gaye ogii-baasaan giigoonyan.
Mii dash a’aw name pane gaa-debinaad.
Mii dash gaa-izhi-niigobinaad ko asabiin, niizh ko gii-ayaa niizh eta go ogii-dasoonaan, mii dash gaa-zhi-niigobidoowaad asabiin.
Mii dash miinawaa gii-gashkigwaasowaang miinawaa ge gii-ana’enangwaa iw o asabiig.
Mii dash imaa ge gii-maajii-gashkigwaanagwaa gaye niin asabiig naaniibaawishige.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what I was told. Long ago, when my grandmother was a girl, my grandfather caught one mermaid, a mermaid there in the net. And so,he pulled up his net retrieving her. “Please release me; you will come with me if you don’t release me,” and so he listened, and let the mermaid go from his net. And at the same time, the weather was bad all day long. Perhaps that’s why the weather was bad. The old man said “Things don’t happen for no reason.” He spoke to the spirits there in the water, first to calm them so we could go get our nets, and then we could start again. So they calmed down, the weather calmed and the lake settled down. They got their nets, and it started up again.

sentence.sent_text: Mii gaa-zhi-wiindamaagooyaan.
Mewinzha ko gii-ikwezensiwid nookomisiban naa go nimishoome gii-debinind a bezhig nenabaanawe, nenabaanawe imaa go asabiing.

Mii dash gaa-izhi-wiikobinaad igo aw gaa-onasabiid sa go ogii-debinaan “daga bagidinishin giga-ani-wiijiiw iishpin bagidinisesiwan,” mii dash iw gaa-pizindang, ganabaj igo omaa gaye gaa-izhi-bagidinaad iw nenaabaanawe aaniish omaa gaye odasabiing mii imaa gii-debinaad.
Naanendaa ge-wiin mii gaa-izhi-niiskaadad gabe-giizhik imaa mii gaa-onji-niiskaadak ganabaj.

Mii gaa-ikidod akiwenzii mii ge-wiin, “Gaawiin anishaa izhiwebasinoon noongom.” Mii dash gaa-izhi-gaganoonaad iniw manidoowag imaa aagaming eyaawaad gaganoozh, manidoo, ayaa ji-bizaan-ayaawaad, kawe inga-o-naanaanaan wa’aw indasabiinaan, mii dash imaa mii dash miinawaa gidaa-maajiikamigizim.
Mii sa go geget gii-bizaan-ayaawaad, bizaan-ayaamagak agaaming mii dash miinawaa gii-ishkwaakamagiziwaad.
Gii-odaapinaawaad odasabiimiwaan, mii dash miinawaa gii-maajiikamigak o’o.

paragraph.text_eng: And then there was this one who caught a mermaid in his net who nearly drowned. He was barely able to make it to shore. The spirits had empathy for him; that’s why they released him to the shore of the lake. And it was much later that the old man would set his net; as the story goes, he did not feast, he did not feast (the Spirit the Lake)in the proper way; he did not show respect, so today he does.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash a’aw gaa-debinaad a’aw nenaabaanawe gegaa go naa gii-debizh gibwanaabaawazo, Agaawaa go ogii-gashkitoon maa ji-goopiid gegaa go.
Gii-zhawenimigod gaa-onji-bagidinigod ji-goopiid imaa agaaming.

Wiikaa miinawaa gii-onasabii akiwenzii aaniish naa gaawiin ogii-ashangesii giiwenh mii gaa i’iw gaawiin ogii-ashamaasiin weweni agaaming eyaawaad manidoog gaawiin igo ogii-manaaji’aasiin, mii dash noongom.

paragraph.text_eng: That is why we have these feelings of loss, for we no longer do these things of properly feasting, and making tobacco offerings. We don’t pay attention to our teachings, and thus all. will soon be lost; we will lose it all. Perhaps long ago we started losing this. Today our path is different. Our children and great grandchildren do things differently; they do not know they should first feast the spirits who take care of us, and our earth, and all who reside there, and those who reside in the lake. I don’t know if this is happening.

sentence.sent_text: Mii wenji-metisiwininaan o’ow gaawiin geyaabi gidizhichigesiimin o’ow weweni ji-ashangeyang weweni ge ji-asemaakeyang.
Miinawaa go geyaabi gaawiin gibizikendanziimin oo ezhitwaayang, mii dash wii akina gegoo ji-wanising wayiiba kina gegoo ji-wanising.
Ganabaj igo mewinzha gii-maajii-wanising iw.
Bakaan hoongom gidizhitwaamin.

Bakaan giniijaanisinaan miinawaa aanikoobijiganan bebakaan wiinawaa izhichigewag gaawiin ogikendanziinaawaa weweni kawe wiinitam wiinatamawaa ji-ashamindwaa ongow manidoog e-ganawenimaawaad miinawaa gidakiiminaan naa go eyaawaad imaa zazaaga iganing eyaawaad.
Nooj namanj noongom ezhiwebak.

paragraph.text_eng: They do not know that they should use cedar-water to heat and clean their nets, to cleanse them, to purify them. They do not know this process. It is sage that is only known nowadays. How is it that sage, sweetgrass, and tobacco are forgotten?

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin ogikendanziinaawaa ge giizhikaandag ji-aabajitoowaad ji-jiibaakwaanaawaad giziibiiginaawaad odasabiiwaan go ji-abaabasawaa ge odabaabasiwaan.
Gaawiin eta, gaawiin igo ogikendanziinaawaa.
Mii eta ge mashkodewanzh iye gekendigaazod noongom naa go owe gaye.
Aaniin danaa ezhinikaadeg mashkodewanzh, wiingwashk , asemaa gaye gegaa waniikeng i’iw?

paragraph.text_eng: I no longer see anyone carrying tobacco. “Oh, first let me go to the store, I will get my tobacco,” I hear them say. And at Big Drum, nope. This should be used. Not all Anishinaabe carry their tobacco, but they still help each other. It’s only when they pay attention.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin geyaabi niwaabamaasii awiiya ji-baa-dakonaad asemaa.
“Ooh kawe adaawewigamigong inga-izhaa ji-o-naanag asemaa,” mii ekidowaad igo noondawagwaa awiiya.
Miinawaa go ge niimi’idiing ge gaawiin.
Mii go aabaj’aa, gaawiin igo akina anishinaabe gaawiin baa-dakonaasiiwan asemaa, mii go ge-izhi-wiidookodaadiwaad ko gaye.
Mii eta go maa bizikenimaawaad bijiinag.

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh I too should have had my tobacco;” they would forget it, then they realize when they come in.

sentence.sent_text: “Ooh indaa-gii-ayaawaa ge-niin asemaa,” weniban ko, weniban ko ayaawaad, mii bijiinag iwidi mikawisewaad biindigewaad.

paragraph.text_eng: “Oh do you have any tobacco?”

sentence.sent_text: “Ooh asemaa na gidayaawaa?”

paragraph.text_eng: “No. No,” some say.

sentence.sent_text: “Gaawiin, gaawiin ko,” ikidowag aanind.

paragraph.text_eng: Sometimes they will sell their tobacco. And so, this offering is becoming lost; we lost it long ago.

sentence.sent_text: Mii ge-wiin adaawaagewaad wii-aabaji’aawaad asemaa.
Mii sa go gaye mii go maajii-wanising gaye gii-wanitaasowang iw mewinzha.

paragraph.text_eng: When my late husband was still in Red Lake, “Redby” as it is called, three boys drowned. One of the men was his grandson. And his relative went with my husband’s son, this is when they drowned. You see they were using too many nets. And certainly it’s because they were using fifty-six nets out on the water. It is vast on the lake, and thus they did not reach their landing, they had too many fish in the nets and those boys drowned in that water.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-ayaad ko geyaabi naabemiban Miskwaagamiwi-zaaga’iganiing “Madaabiimoog” ezhinikaadeg, gaa-izhi-gibwanaabaawewaad igiw niswi gwiiwizensag.
Mii dash bezhig; naabem, oozhisheyan.
Miinawaa go odinawemaaganan naa go wiiji-kiwenzii ogozisan mii gaa-izhi-gibwanaabaawewaad.
Aaniish naa niibowa ge-wiinawaa asabiin ogii-aabaji’aawaan.
Mii dash iw aaniin danaa aabadeg naanimidana-ingodwaaswi asabiig ogii-aabaji’aawaan naawij dash wiin iwidi agaaming zaaga’iganing michaamagad.
mii dash gaa-izhi, gaawiin gii-debidoosii de-izhaasiiwag iwidi zaamikamig.
Giigoonh gaa-ayaawaad mii dash iniw gaa-izhi-debinigowaad asabiin aw naa go gaye a nibiikaang gii-kibwanaabaawewaad ingiw gwiiwizensag.

paragraph.text_eng: It was more than sixteen days that those boys were searched for. One was found right away; it was his father’s net that he used; the one they found, the one that was found, and one on the eighth day, my husband’s son, his grandson. But firstly he (my husband)went to search out the shaking tent to talk with those spirits who reside in Red Lake to let him go. The elder talked about all things carefully so the lake would release the grandson, just like there on the other side of the shore.

sentence.sent_text: Mii go di ashi-ingodwaaswi di awashime giizhigak gii-andawaabamindwaa ingiw gwiiwizensag.

Gaabige aw bezhig ogii-mikawaawaan, mii dash, obaabaayan dash odasabiin ogii-aabajitoon mii dash a bezhig gii-mikawaad, mikawind, mii dash a bezhig nishwaasogon mii aw naabemiwan ogozis, oozhishenhyan.

Kawe dash ya’aw e-jiisikiid ogii-wananaandamaanaan ji-ganoonaad agow manidoog maa eyaawaad iw Miskwaagami-zaaga’iganing ji-bagadinigod ogowe gichi-onigod maa agaaming kina gegoo ogii-dazhindaan akiwenziiyiban weweni ji-bagidinigod ji-bagidaakwa’ond dibishkoo maa agaaming.

paragraph.text_eng: And this happened early in the morning. The water, and lake were still menacing So one boy was released early in the morning there, but still there was one more being held back; he was held back for 16 days. Therefore that elder came and spoke with them; they addressed him. The mermaid did not have a husband, she was lonely, she missed having a husband. She did not have anyone to be her partner. That is why those boys were drowned; she needed a partner; she needed to be with someone.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash imaa geget gaa-izhiwebak waasa gigizheb.
Mii geyaabi maa nichiiwikamigiziwaad agow nibi miinawaa zaaga’igan.
Mii dash imaa gaye gigizheb gii-bagidakwa ond aw gwiiwizens geyaabi dash bezhig maa gii-ayaa gii-gichiwanaa mii dash a’a bezhig ashi-ingodwaaso-giizhigak mii imaa minik gaa-gichiwinind.
Mii dash gii-bi-ganoonigod, ganoonigowaad aw akiwenziiyiban mii maa nenabaanawag gii-noondesed onaabeman ogii-metisinimaan, metisinimaan sa go onaabeman.
Gaawiin awiiya ogii-wiijiiwaasiin owiijiiwaagan.
Mii dash gaa-onji-gibwanaabewaad ongow gwiiwizensag gii-noonde-wiidige miinawaa noonde-wiiji-ayaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: That is why some, two of those boys were kept back. Who will she marry? That is what happened there, that’s what the elder said, but no one listened. “Properly feast the lake, those that take care of the water there in Red Lake, the spirits who dwell there.” That’s what the elder said, but nobody listened.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash gaa-onji-gichiwinaad aaniind, niizh gwiiwizensan.
Awenen ge-wiidigemaad?
Mii dash imaa gaa-onji-izhiwebak, mii gaa-ikidod akiwenzii na.
Mii gaawiin gii-bizindawaasiin.
“Weweni dash ji-ashamindwaa ogow Miskwaagamiwi-zaaga’iganing e-ganawenjigewaad imaa agaaming nibiikaang manidoog imaa ayaawag.” Mii gaa-ikidod akiwenzii gaawiin dash gii-bizindawaasii.

paragraph.text_eng: And thus, that is when the fish left. They thought they came back there to Red Lake after ten years or so. Perhaps they will remember to feast those fish and spirits who take care of the water there on Red lake. But still, nobody does this. And also on Bowstring Lake, close to where I was raised, they still do not do this. I have not heard of anyone setting nets, not yet. The men, they no longer hunt anymore, they only play at the casino.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash maa gaa-izhi-webinigoowaad agow giigoonwag.
Mii bijiinag midaaso-biboon awashime mii bijiinag, gii-inendamowaad ji-bi-azhegiiwewaad imaa Miskwaagamiwi-zaaga’iganing.
Ganabaj miinawaa ge ji-mikwendamowaad weweni ji-ashamindwaa ongow giigoonyag miinawaa go manidoog maa e-ganawenjigewaad imaa agaaming imaa Miskwaagamiwi-zaaga’iganing.
Mii go gaawiin awiiya ganabaj izhichigesii geyaabi.
Miinawa go gaye iwidi Chaachaabaaning, besho maa ayaa gaa-nitaawigi’igoowaan gaye mii gaawiin geyaabi ge-wiinawaa izhichigesiiwag.
Gaawiin wiikaa ninoondanzii maa awiiya ji-onasabiid gaawiin geyaabi naa.
Gaawiin igo aapiji geyaabi ge giiyosesiiwag ininiwag mii ge-wiinawaa mii eta go biinjwebinigewaad imaa baa-odaminowaad nooj igo.

paragraph.text_eng: Well then, it is perhaps that my grandmother and I, we did not have containers to prepare for when we set the nets. I don’t know, when we got off the boat it was probably to use that ol’ car hood that they had, that sled, a car hood. We used that to haul the fish and nets. And yes, we were poor too. The car hood was used as a sled, It was necessary to use it to be able to prepare the nets and dry them, also we had to clean, clean the fish.

sentence.sent_text: Aaniish naa mii ganabaj, ganabaj iw gaawiin ge ingiw makokosagoon ge ingii-ayaasiimin gii-oninasabiiyaang ko nookomisiban.
Amanj igo, ge gii-goopiiyaang ko mii ganabaj igo gaye ingii-aabajitoomin igo gaye 000 yay odaabaanag awe gaa-ayaamowaad miinawaa go gaye zhooshkodaabaanens miinawaa gaye car hood.
Ingii-aabajitoomin wiikobinangwaa giigoonyag asabiig inzhooshkoshinaan.
Mii ge-niin i’iw aaniish naa ingii-gidimaagizimin ge-niinawind.
Car hood aabaji’ang zhooshkodaabaanens aabajitoowaang.
Mii sa go ge mii booch igo gii-gashkitoowaang gii-onasabiiyaang miinawaa gaye ji-baasod baasangwaa iw asabiig booch igo ge ingii-biinichigemin, biini’angwaa giigoonhyag.

paragraph.text_eng: There were always people who needed to be fed, and my grandfather and grandmother always fed them the fish they had. Today I know what they would do, perhaps buy fish, I don’t know if anyone nowadays knows how to mend nets when they are torn, to be repaired. Perhaps they throw them away to have different ones. My mother, grandmother, and grandfather sewed those nets when repairing them. They smoked the fish. We always had smoked fish.

sentence.sent_text: Apane go imaa gii-ayaawaad gaa-noondesewaad imaa mii go ge gii-ashamindwaa gaye nimishoomis nookomisiban gaye apane gii-ashanged giigoonh gii-ayaawaad.
Amanj igo noongom ge-izhichigewaad ganabaj adaawewag giigoonhyag.
Amanj igo ge noongom ge awiiya ge-nitaa-gashkigwaanaad asabiig biigoshkaawaad ge gaawiin da-nanaa’in, nanaa’inaawaasiwaan.
Ganabaj igo ji-webinaawaad bakaan ji-ayaawaawaad.
Apane wiinawaa nimaamaa, naa nookomis, nookomisiban miinawaa go nimishoomis gii-gashkigaanaawaad iniw asabiig gii-nanaa’i’aawaan.
Gii-ozaawaakozaawaan i’iw giigoowag mii go pane.
Gii-ayaawangwaa ogow gaa-ozaawaakizwaawaad.

paragraph.text_eng: I remember my uncle, he too smoked fish there, but he was a drinker, and thus he would fall asleep over doing it.

sentence.sent_text: Nimikwenimaa ge nizise, ge-wiin imaa gii-ozaawaakiziged, aaniish naa gii-minikweshki, mii dash gaa-izhi-nibaad onzaamichiged.

paragraph.text_eng: “What’s going on? You’re burning the fish,” my mother says, “and you’re sleeping there. Are you still falling down drunk?”

sentence.sent_text: “Aaniin da naa?
Gijaagizwaag gosha ongow giigoonyag,” ikido nimaamaa, “gaye giin nibaayan imaa gigawibii’in.
Enange geyaabi na?”

paragraph.text_eng: “I’s cooking the smoked fish. Ask me again,” he says.

sentence.sent_text: “I’s cooking the smoked fish.
Ask me again,” ikido.

paragraph.text_eng: He made her upset when he sobered up. He over smoked the fish.

sentence.sent_text: Onishki’aan gii-aatebiid.
Gii-onzaamichiged gii-ozaawaakiziged a’aw.

paragraph.text_eng: You see, I worked a lot for my grandmother and grandfather. My grandfather taught me about the things I see there nowadays. I remember when he feasted them. He was always feasting; he feasted the spirits. He feasted those who looked after them; also feasted those trees, the wild rice, the flowers, the mosquitos, the pine on the shore, and also the spirits who dwell there, the three foremost spirits that live in every lake. You see they are related to each other there.

sentence.sent_text: Aaniish naa, mii iw nawach iw pane go ingii-anokiitawaag nookomisiban miinawaa nimishoomis.
Nimishoomis sa go ingii-gikinoo’amawig kina gegoo imaa gaa-izhi-ganawendamaan, noongom.
Mii gaa-minjimendamaan iw gii-ashamaad.
Gii-ashanged pane, ashamaad igo manidoowag.

Ashamaad e-ganawenjigewaad; ashamaad igo gaye ongow mitigoog, manoomin, waabigwaniin zagimeg, zhingwaak agaaming, gaye imaa eyaawaad manidoog, nisowag imaa e-naaniigaaniziwaad manidoog maa eyaajig imaa endaso-zaaga’iganikaag.
Aaniish naa inawendiwag maa.

paragraph.text_eng: Subsequently, no one there knows what their names are, I hope they recapture their names, those lead spirits who dwell in the waterways. They offer tobacco and feast them, to know these, our Anishinaabe names. This is always being discussed over there in Ponemah. My father never forgot those spirits in the water, those who watch over as we set our nets, and when they hunted ducks. Some Anishinaabe people are forgetting all those who reside in the water there. And the deer, when they go out hunting for them, they do not feast them, they do not make tobacco offerings. I hope they return to doing this, our teachings, so that they pay attention to our spirits; this is what I too want.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash imaa gaawiin aapiji awiiya ogikendanziinaawaa aaniin ezhinikaazowaad, Apegish azhewidebidoowaad agow ezhinikaazowaad ongow e-naaniigaaniziwaad manidoog imaa zaaga’iganing eyaawaad.
Asemaakewaad naa ashangewaad ongow Gidanishinaabeminaan wenji-gikendamowaad.
Mii go pane iwidi gaa-izhi-dazhindamowaad ongow iwidi Obaashing eyaawaad.
Mii ge-wiin nibaabaayiban gaawiinsh gaawiin wiikaa ogii-wanenimaasiin ongow agaaming, e-ganawenjigewaad oninasabiiyaang, minawaa go gaye zhiishiibag nandone’waawaad.
Akina igo omaa eyaawaad igo agaaming mii imaa anooj gii-wanenimaawaad ongow aanind Anishinaabeg.
Miinawaa go waawaashkeshi, baa-nandonewaawaad ge mii gaawiin, gaawiin ashangesiiwag, gaawiin asemaakesiiwag.
Pegish igo azhe-mamigaadeg o’ow izhichigewin, gidizhitwaawinaan, ji-bizikendamowaad bizikendamindwaa ge gimanidoominaan mii go geniin igo ezhi-misawendamaan.

paragraph.text_eng: I can no longer find anyone who does these things. My parents, and my grandmother, and my grandfather, they did these things. Today, no more. We did hunt, but I no longer do this. I do not go out with anyone to get food to feed us, my children, and my grandchildren. We no longer do this; I no longer do this. Perhaps this is enough for my story. Thank you for listening.

sentence.sent_text: Mii kina gaawiin geyaabi niganawaabamaasii awiiya gaa-izhichigewaad ko.
Nigitiziimag, naa ninookomis, miinawaa nimishoome, gaa-izhichigewaad.
Noongom, gaawiin geyaabi.
Ingii-giiyosemin ko eyanh’, mii gaawiin geyaabi niin igo ge-niin indizhichigesii.
Gaawiin awiiya niwiijiiwaasii geyaabi ji-ashamangwaa, niniijaanisinaanig miinawaa ninoozhishenaanig.
Mii gaawiin geyaabi indizhichigesiimin iw gaawiin niin indizhichigesii.
Mii ganabaj iw minik ji-waawiindamaageyaan.
Miigwech bizindawiyeg.

paragraph.text_eng: One time Wenabozho was out hunting; then he killed a deer. He cleaned it, built a fire, and then cooked the deer. “Howah,” He lay down there and waited for the deer to cook. He heard the tree, “squeak, squeak.” Okay he didn’t like the sound of that. He climbed up the tree, slipped, and got caught, He looked around. He hung there for a long time. The wolves were running, “Heeyyy wolves go run the other way!” Those wolves stopped running. The alpha male, “By golly Wenabozho has something over there. Let’s go see.” They started running then ate up the meat. After they finished eating, then they ran off. I don’t know why he bothered those wolves when they were running there.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding Wenabozho baa-giiwased gaa-izhi-nitaaged waawaashkeshiwan.
Gaa-izhi-bakonaad imaa, gaa-zhi-boodawed, naa giiziswaad ini waawaashkeshi, “Howah?” Gaa-izhi-gawishimod imaa baabii’aad iniw ji-giizizonid intw waawaashkeshiwan.
Gaa-izhi-noondawaad ni mitigoowan “squeak, squeak.” Oyay odanagayendaan iw.
Gaa-izhi-akwaandawed imaa mitigong, gaa-izhi-ozhaashkoshing, nagwaakojing di oo inaabid di.
Ginwenzh agoojing imaa.
Ma’iinganag bimibatoowag, “Heeeey ma’iinganag awas dibi di apa’idig!” Nagaabatoowaad ingiw ma’iinganag.
Naagaanizid ma’iingan “Tayaa hay’ gegoo odayaan a Wenabozho.
Inaabidaa!” Maajiibatoowaad gaa-izhi-gidaamowaad di wiiyaas.
Gaa-kiizhi-wiisiniwaad gaa-maajiibatoowaad.
Namanj naa gaa-izhi-baamenimaagwen ni ma’iinganan babaamibatoonid.

paragraph.text_eng: One time when Wenabozho went out walking he saw a big rock sitting there. He circled the rock here, “Hey rock, I would beat you if we raced.” The rock paid no attention to him. He circled him again and kicked him too. “Rock I could beat you if we raced.” The rock paid no attention to him. Finally fed up with him, he told him, “Okay Wenabosh roll me up that hill over there.” Struggling, Wenabozho pushed the rock up the hill. When they got to the top of the hill, “Okay Wenabosh, give me a push.” He pushed the rock, He was running back and forth screaming. He was in the lead, then he fell down, and the rock ran over him. I wonder why he bothered the rock when he was sitting there.

sentence.sent_text: Wenabozho aabiding o-baamosed gaa-zhi-waabamaad imaa abinid chi-asiniin.
Aa gizhibaashkawaad omaa, “Hey chi-asin ga-chi-naganin gapwejikanidiyang.” Obaamenigosiin ni chi-asiniin.
Gizhibaashkawaad miinawaa dangishkawaad ge, “Chi-asin ga-chi-naganin gagwejikanidiyan.” Obaamenigosiin ni chi-asiniin.
Ingoding go asiniin chi-asiniin odigoon, “Daga wenabosh oodi ogidaakii chidaabaanishin.
Gaa-dazhiiwid, Wenabozho ogidaakii odaabaanaan ni chi-asiniin.
Dagoshinowaad ogidaakii, “Haw wenabosh, gaanjwebinishin.” ogaanjwebinaan.
Naanoondaagozi wenabosh aazhoobapatood.
Niigaanii gaa-izhi-tibiskaagod gaa-aazhi-bisk bangishing gaa-zhi-tibiskaagod ini chi-asiniin.
Namanj naa gaa-izhi-baamenimaagwen imaa ni abinid.

paragraph.text_eng: One time Wenabozho, it’s fall now, all the ducks and the birds had left. He’s freezing; he’s walking; as he’s crying, he arrived there. He looked out on the lake. The lake was full of ducks. As he was watching them, he thought of what he was going to do. He went out and got some basswood bark. He made some rope. Then he made a basket and dove into the river. He went around tying the ducks legs. “Heyyyy!” The fall ducks took off to the south. Wenabozho left too. I don’t know when this was. I also wonder where he got the basswood bark and how he made a birch bark basket, Well then, he is a spirit.

sentence.sent_text: Aabiding Wenabozho, dagwaagig azhigwa, mii akina gii-maajaawaad ingiw bineshiinyag miinawaa zhiishiibag.
Gawaji-ige, bimose, mawid gaa-zhi-dagoshing imaa.
Gaa-izhi-inaabid imaa agaaming.
Mooshkinebiiwag imaa?
zhiishiibag.
Ganawaabamaad gaa-zhi-mikwendang ge-izhichiged.
Gaa-baa-izhi-naadid wiigob.
Biminikwaanensan gaa-izhitood.
Makak gaa-izhitood gaa-izhi-googiid imaa ziibing.
Baa-dakobinaad imaa kaadensan zhiishiiban.
Ooo aaniish naa heeeeyyyyy!
Gaa-maajiibizowaad inishibag apane shaawanong.
Mii ge Wenaboozhoo gii-maajaad.
Mii sa namanj apii.
Namanj ige gaa-ondinamogwen ni wiigob miinawaa i’iw makak gii-izhitood iw wiigwaas.
Aaniish naa manidoo iidog aw Wenaboozhoo.

paragraph.text_eng: A long time ago Wenabozho stayed here with his grandmother; it was really cold too; she covered him up. “Grandmother, did we used to have fire?”

sentence.sent_text: Mewinzha Wenabozho omaa ogii-wiijiwaan okoomisan.
Ani-gisinaa gaye gawazhewaad.
Wenabozho, “Nookomis, gigii-ayaamin ko ishkode?

paragraph.text_eng: “Yep, the old man took it with him. He lives there across the lake.”

sentence.sent_text: “Uh-huh ogii-maajiidoon akiwenzii.
Agaaming imaa ayaa.”

paragraph.text_eng: “What is fire?”

sentence.sent_text: “Wegonesh dinowa iw ishkode.”

paragraph.text_eng: “It’s like the sun. It gets bigger and hotter.”

sentence.sent_text: “Dibishkoo go chi-oshkaabewis.
Eshkam igo michaa gizhide.”

paragraph.text_eng: “By golly,” said Wenabozho. “I’ll go get that.”

sentence.sent_text: “Ayay,” ikido Wenabozho, “Indaa-naadin goya”

paragraph.text_eng: “The old man won’t let you take it.”

sentence.sent_text: “Gaawiin gidaa-bagidinigosiin aw akiwenzii ji-maajiidooyan.”

paragraph.text_eng: “Now I’ll go get it,” said Wenabozho. “Where does he live?”

sentence.sent_text: “Mii go indaa-naadin,’ ikido Wenabozho.
“Aandish eyaad?”

paragraph.text_eng: “He’s right across the lake.”

sentence.sent_text: “Mii oodi agaaming ayaa.”

paragraph.text_eng: Wenabozho went on his way. His grandmother told him, “That old man has two daughters. Those girls are pretty. He observed them fishing.

sentence.sent_text: Ani-maajaad Wenabozho ogii-wiindamaagon ge iniw okoomisan, “Akiwenzii niizh odaanisan odayaawaan.
Onizhishiwag ingiw ikwezensag.
Wah geget ani-dagoshin di ozhiwewebanaabiiwag ikwezensag.

paragraph.text_eng: “What am I going to do?”

sentence.sent_text: “Oo awegonen ge-izhichigeyaan?”

paragraph.text_eng: Then he changed himself into a rabbit. When the girls saw him they said, “Ooo what a cute little rabbit. Let’s take him home.” They took him home. “Can we bring this little rabbit in?”

sentence.sent_text: Waaboozong gaa-izhi-aanji’idizod.
Ikwezensag waabamaad “Oyay sa-go wenizhishid waaboozens.
Ani-giiwenaadaa.” Wah mii idi gitwenaawaad.
“Gidaa-biindiganaanaan na waaboozoons?”

paragraph.text_eng: “Daga naa take care of him. Watch him closely.”

sentence.sent_text: “Daga naa ganawenimik.
Weweni maa ganawaabamik aw.”

paragraph.text_eng: While Wenabozho was watching the old man and girls go to sleep, he jumped into the fire. He started running across the lake. He was on fire. He stole that fire. That’s why the rabbit looks the way he does today. His tail burned. That’s why the rabbit looks the way he does today.

sentence.sent_text: Wenabozho omaa ganawaabamaad ini gaa-izhi-nibaanid akiiwenziiyan ikwezensag gaa-zhi-gwaashkwanid imaa ishkodeng, gaa-maajiibatood agaaming.
Howah ani-zakizod ishkode.
Mii noongom wenji-izhinaagozid waabooz gii-jaagizod aw ozowens.
Mii noongom wenji-izhinaagozid aw waabooz.

paragraph.text_eng: Now when I was small that old man, my grandfather, when he begins to tell a traditional story, maybe when all the snow is gone, that old man tells a traditional legend. “Haw! Wenabozho, when he was around and about.” “Don’t,” that elder woman said. “Don’t tell legends to those kids,” she said. And then that elder man stopped the legend he was telling. That elder lady said, “Don’t tell those children legends, the Americans won’t like them if they know it. Don’t; bad things will start to happen. It’s not nice if they know it.”

sentence.sent_text: Azhigwa gii-pi-agaashiihnyeyaan azhigwa akiiwenzi aw mishoomisiban azhigwa wii-ni-aadizooked maagizhaa mii gakina gii-maajaad aw goon weweni aadizooked aw akiwenzi.
“Ho!
Wenaboozhoo, gii-babaa-ayaa,” mii aw mindimooye ikido.
“Gego!
Gego aadizookamowaaken ingiw abanoojiihnyag,” ikido.
Gaa-zhi-noogishkaad aw akiwenzi wii-aadizookepan.
Mindimooye ikido, “Gego aadizookamawaaken ingiw aabanoojiiyag.
Gaawiin oga-minwendaziin aw chimookomaan giishpin gikendamowaad i’iw.
Gego, da-ni-maazhisewag.
Gaawiin iw da-onishishinzinoon giishpin gikendamowaad.”

paragraph.text_eng: And I often thought about it. Me, myself, I would think long ago, when I was in the process of growing up over there, and in the future, I often thought about it. I don’t know why they did that, when they didnt tell me legends when I was young. And that is what I thought. I thought too many bad things happened with them; they had a tough time when they were Anishinaabe. Just like they understood the American man wanted to cover it up, to stop being Indian and not be around anymore. That’s it, because of the suffering of those elders.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash iw moozhag ningii-naanaagidawendaan.
Niin igo, ningii-naanaagidawenim mewinzha gii-ni-nitaawigeyaan ingoji go odi niigaan moozhag ningii-naanaagidawendaan.
Namanj iw gaa-onji-izhichigewaad iw gii-aadizookesigwaa gii-pi-agaashiihnyeyaan, gii-pi-aadizookamaagoosiwaan, gii-pi-aadizookamaagoosiwaan gii-agaashiiyaan.
Mii dash iw gaa-inendamaan.
Ingii-inendaan onzaam niibowa gii-gagwaadagisewag, wiinawaa gii-gagwaadagiziwag iw gii-Anishinaabewiwaad.
Dibishkoo gii-nisidotaanaawaa ochimookomaan mii iw waa-agwanang mii waa-ishkwaataatood gaawiin geyaabi owii-ayaawaasiin iniw Anishinaaben.
Mii iw, wiinawaa gaa-onji-gagwaadigitoowaad igiw gichi-ayaa’aag.

paragraph.text_eng: And now, it becomes time when the children will learn. They thought and decided they would not be there to teach them; after all, they thought that is why those children will have bad things happen. If they think Indian, they learn Indian. The white man won’t help; that’s why those children will have a tough time. And that’s why I think they didn’t teach those legends when I was small. That’s what I think. Those elders had a tough time because they were being Anishinaabe.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash iw azhigwa gii-apii-wang da-gikinoo’amaawindwaa ingiw aabanoojiiyag.
Gaawiin gii-inendanziiwag da-gikinoo’amaawaad aniish naa gii-inendaanaawaa mii iw ge-onji-maazhisewaad ingiw aabanoojiiyag.
Giishpin Anishinaabe-inendamowaad Anishinaabe-gikendaasowaad.
Mii iw chimookomaan ogaawiin odaa-wiidookawaasii mii iw ge-onji-maazhisewaad wiinawaa gaye ingiw aabanoojiiyag.
Mii dash iw gaa-inendamaan mii iw gaa-onji-gikinoo’amaagoosiwaang iw iniw aadizookaanag gii-pi-agaashiiyaang.
Mii iw niin gaa-inendamaan.
Gii-gagwaadigitoowaad ingiw gichi ayaa’aag iw gii-Anishinaabewiwaad sa go.

paragraph.text_eng: Now, its ok if you teach those children, to tell those children legends long ago. If we do that here, if we are able to be successful at becoming Anishinaabe, then we will be able to teach the children.

sentence.sent_text: Noongom da-onishishin gikinoo’amaawindwaa ingiw abinoojiihnyag, keyaa gaa-izhi-bi-aadizookamawindwaa ingiw aabanoojiiyag mewinzha.
Giishpin omaa izhichiceng iw, giishpin gashkitooyang Anishinaabewiyaang, da-ni-gikinoo’amawindwaa mii ingiw aabanoojiiyag iw akeyaa.

paragraph.text_eng: I wish very much, that we’re all successful at speaking the Anishinaabe language. If every one of those Anishinaabeg knew how to speak Anishinaabemowin, It would be nice. But I don’t know if it would happen. I don’t know; it was hard for me to be a fluent speaker when I was 19 Truly, my fellow Indians, you guys, I did not how to speak the Anishinaabe language very much. I remembered I was given a lot of this responsibility, but I did not know how to speak the Anishinaabe language very well. And that’s wwhat I thought until I was 20 years old. I want to do that; I want to do that the one thing, to speak the Anishinaabe language well. That’s what I thought. I had my mind made up.

sentence.sent_text: Pegish naa go geget gashkitooyang niibowa da-ansihinaabemoyang wech gakina ingiw Anishinaabe da-nitaa-Anishinaabemowaapan mii iw daa-onishishing.
Namanj idash igo giishpin daa-izhiwebak.
Gaawiin niin gikendaaziin, gii-zanagad gaye niin gii-gaewe-nitaa-Anishinaahemoyaan gii-ashi-zhaangaso-biboonagiziyaan.
Geget niij-Anishinaabedog, giinawaa, gaawiin aapiji ningii-nitaa-Anishinaabemosiin.
Aanawi

paragraph.text_eng: And then I did everything. I tried to do everything; you see, I lived. I always tried to do things more to know how to speak the Anishinaabe language, and also always speak more. I went over and visited those ones, that knew how to speak the Anishinaabe language. And went over there to Midewin. And I went to the dances. The ones who were involved with that old Anishinaabe language, Anishinaabe cultural practices, I always went over and approached them, those Anishinaabeg. I always tried to go and help them, go and see them, when they were doing something. And that’s what came with me, what helped me, to try to help my fellow Anishinaabe friends. I didn’t do this by myself. Together I helped my fellow Anishinaabe friends, and that’s why I got helped.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash akina gegoo gaa-izhichigeyaan.
Akina gegoo gaa-gagwe izhichigeyaan, aansh naa ningii-bimaadiz.
Go gaye gaa-gagwe-izhichigeyaan pane ningii-wiikwajitooyan nawaj da-gikendamaan iw Anishinaabemowin, nawaj go gaye da-nitaa-gaagiigidoyaan apane.
Miinawaa go ningii-o-maawadiswaag ingiw gaa-nitaa-Anishinaabemojig.
Minawaa go ningii-izhaa owidi midewin.
Miinawaa owidi ingii-izhaa niimii’iding.
Ayaawaad ingiw dezhiikamowaad iw gete-Anishinaabemowin, Anishinaabe-izhitwaawinging, mii ingiw apane gaa-o-naazakawagwaa miinawaash igo ingiw Anishinaabe.
Apane ningii-o-gagwe-wiidookawaag, ningii-o-izhaa gii-waabamagwaa gego izhichigewaad Anishinaaben keyaa.
Mii iw gaye niin gaa-pi-wiidookaagooyaan, gaye niin gii-gagwe-wiidookawagwaa niwiij-Anishinaabeg.
Gaawiin go niin gii-izhichigesiin.
Maamaawi wiidookawagwaa niwiij-Anishinaabe, mii iw gaye niin gaa-onji-wiidookaagooyaan.

paragraph.text_eng: And maybe that’s all I am going to say. I don’t know how they will be used, these markers (recorders), this sound maker and that camera. Maybe sometime I will talk some more using the Anishinaabe language, which way am I going to help my fellow Anishinaabe friends to use our sound that was given to us. You guys, Niiyo Giizhig and Anangookwe, thank you for giving me tobacco and asking me to speak a little in Anishinaabe here today. I really like that I was asked to speak in the Anishinaabe language. I only knew a very little something. Maybe good things will happen here with all our fellow Anishinaabe speakers, That’s all, Thank you all for listening.

sentence.sent_text: Mii eta go dash igo minik igo maagizhaa ge-ikidoyaan.
Maagizhaa go gaawiin igo ingikendaziin aaniin ge-aabadak ono akawasijiganan, o’o medweweg minawaa iw mezinaatesemagak.

Maagizhaa go naawaj igo ingoding miinawaa ninga-gaagiigid o’ sa Anishinaabemowin da-aabajitooyaan, aaniin keyaa ge-zhi-wiidookawagwaa niwiij-Anishinaabeg aabajitooyaan o’ isa gidinwewinaan gaa-miinigooziyang.
Giinawaa dash, Niiyo Giizhig, Anangookwe, miigwech miizhiyeg asemaa gagwejimiiyeg da-anshinaabe-gaagiidooyaan omaa bangii noongom.
Geget niminwendaan gagwejimigooyaan ji-Anishinaabemoyaan imaa.
Giishpin igo gegoo bangiishens gikendamaan.
Maagizhaa mii omaa ge-onji-minosed gakina giwiij-Anishinaabeminaanig.
Mii iw.
Miigwech bizindawiyeg.

paragraph.text_eng: I am asked to respond to the way that they were in the process of doing things, Only those Indians, that I know that came forward in time, that used tobacco. Not that Indian, not those Indians who practiced Christianity, I was not ever taught that way, only the Indian way. Those Anishinaabe, the ones who use their tobacco, those ones that taught me a little bit, that I would be intelligent, that I would know a little bit about the Indians’ belief system.

sentence.sent_text: Gagwejimigooyaan da-nakwetamaan keyaa 0 Anishinaabe keyaa Sa go gaa-izhi-izhichiged.
Ingiw eta go niin gekenimagwaa ingiw Anishinaabeg, ingiw gaa-pi-aabaji’aawaad iniw asemaan.
Gaawiin wiin, ingiw Anishinaabe gaa-anama’ejig, wiikaa niin keyaa ningii-izhi-gikinoo’amaagoosi ingiw Anishaabe da-ni-gikendamaan gegoo, mii eta go iw keyaa Anishinaabe.
Ingiw Anishinaabe keyaa gaa-ni-aabaji’aawaad niw odasemaawaan, mii ingiw gaa-kikinoo’amawijig bangii naa go nibwaakaayaambaan, bangii sa go ji-gikendamaan keyaa aw Anishinaabe ezhi-debweyendang.

paragraph.text_eng: Now see a real long time ago those Indians did not dance very much, although they did participate in Midewin. It was very much desired by the white man that the Indian become Christian. Look at the time when my dad and my grandfather were still around, when they worked on those Indian drums, and there is where they were in the process of using their tobacco. They were always asking their spirits to help them, so that they could be helped in their pitifulness/poverty, those Indians, as they are without things in this life.

sentence.sent_text: Shke dash chi-mewinzha gaawiin aapiji gii-niimii’idiisiiwag ingiw anishinaabeg, nashke aanawi sa go gii-midewiwag.
Mii dash igo apiji wayaabishkiiwed ogii-nandawenimaan da-anama’enid.

Shke dash igo wapii go nindedeyiban miinawaa-sh igo nimishoomisiban gii-babaa-ayaawaad, gii-tazhiikawaawaad iniw anishinaabe dewe’iganan, mii dash imaa gaye gii-ni-aabaji’aawaad iniw asemaan asemaa odasemaawaan imaa.
Pane, pane gii-nanaandomaawaad iniw omanidoomiwaan sa da-naadomaagowaad naadamaagoziwaad imaa ezhi-gidimaagiziwaad ingiw anishinaabeg izhi-maneziwaad sa go o’o sa bimaadiziwin.
Ke dash gii-pi-dazhiikawaawaad iniw gii-pi-dazhiikawaad ingiw…anishinaabeg odi keyaa wenjiiyaan iniw dewe’iganan.

paragraph.text_eng: One time they went over there to Wisconsin. They went somewhere over there in town. Odanah it is called, maybe Bad River Reservation over there. Those Anishinaabeg, the ones from the Anishinaabe village, from where I am from, it is called Minisinaakwaang, old Minisinaakwaang, not new Minisinaakwaang village, old Minisinaakwaang that village was there over by the lake. Today they are not there anymore. They were removed out of the way somewhere around 1940 Those white men kicked out the Anishinaabeg, And so, when they were over there at the old Minisinaakwaang, when they went over there to Bad River Reservation, Odanah its named that Indian village.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding dash gii-izhaawag owidi Wiskaansing.
Dibi go owidi oodena gii-izhaawaad.
“Oodena” izhinikaadeg iw owidi, ganabaj Maji-Ziibii ishkoniganing owidi keyaa.

Ingiw anishinaabeg keyaa owidi wenjiijig anishinaabe oodena owidi keyaa niin keyaa ayaayaan, gaa-izhinikaadeg Minisinaakwaang, gete-minisanaakwang, gaawiin wiin iw oshki-minisanaakwaang oodena, iw gete-minisinaakwaang owidi zaaga’iganing gaa-ayaamagak iw odenawens.
Noongom gaawiin geyaabi owidi ayaasiiwag gii-ikonaawag goji go 1940 gii-okonaazhiwaawag zaagiji-basikawaanaan iniw chi-mookomaanan aniw anishinaaben.
Ke dash owidi gete-Minisanaakwaang gii-ayaawaad, mii odi apii gaa-izhaawaad oodi Maji-Ziibiing ishkoniganing iw, ooden izhinikaade anishinaabe oodenawens.

paragraph.text_eng: And so over there, that’s where they took that drum. For sure, that Bad River Anishinaabe was joyful to see that drum. And so, those Anishinaabeg had a really good time in that way, when they were together there, while they danced together, occupied together, in the way that it was spiritually practiced, by those Indians at the time. And now, for awhile, here they were as they are with them, these Anishinaabeg from over there where I am from, and over there, those ones that occupy the land over there. And so at some point, they thought now is the time for us to go home. And now those ones over there are going home, those Indians from over there, from where I am from. And now they are taking that drum with (home). “Aahh,” those Odanah Anishinaabe said, “Please don’t leave yet. You all stay here awhile longer.” And so then they stayed for awhile, and those ones there they always ate well. They always were careful when they did things. They thought it was time for them to leave there. They wanted to go home; they were thinking. “Ooh,” they say, those Anishinaabeg from Bad River, “But don’t you all leave yet.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash odi gii-izhiwinaawaad iniw dewe’iganan.
Wayaa geget aw Maji-Ziibii anishinaabe ogii-minwendaan gii-waabamaawaad iniw dewe’iganan.
Miinawaash igo gii-minawaanigoziwaad ingiw anishinaabe keyaa gii-wiiji-ayaawindiwaad imaa megwaa go niimii idiwaad dazhiikamowaad keyaa sago gaa-izhi-manidoowichiged aw anishinaabe iw apii.
Zhigwa dash noomag omaa gii-ayaawag gii-ni-wiiji-ayaawaawaad ingiw anishinaabeg oodi keyaa wenjiiyaan miinawaash owidi keyaa ingiw eyaajig owidi keyaa gaa-abiitamowaad owidi keyaa.
Mii dash iw ingoding gii-inendamowaad mii zhigwa da-giiwewaad.
Mii zhigwa awedi giiwewaad ingiw anishinaabeg odi keyaa wenjiiyaan.
Zhigwa wii-ni-maajiinaawaad iniw dewe’igan.

“Aahh,” ikidowaad ingiw Oodena anishinaabe, “daga gego mashi maajaakegon, geyaabi maa ajina gidaayaam.” Mii dash iw geyaabi ajina maa gii-ayaawag weweni go gaye apane gii-wiisiniwaad, apane weweni gegoo izhichigewaad.
Zhigo dash minawaa wii-ni-maajaawaad inendamowaad Wii-ni-maajaa, wii-ni-giiwewaad indendamowaad.
“Ooh,” ikidowaad, ingiw odena-anishinaabeg, “gego indaawaj mashi maajaakegon.”

paragraph.text_eng: And that’s the way it was told to me by my father. They left that drum over there behind. They only took a little bit of him home with them. And there they made that drum from that small part. And that’s the one they used over there in Minisinaakwaang. And over there, that’s where they left him, over there, in the town where those Indians make their town. And they never ever heard, we never heard what happened to that drum over there. Maybe he is still over there someplace. It’s only this much that I am telling so you guys can think about what happened to that very old drum. Its unknown where he went. They left him over there that one. And they said, “You guys could take care of him.”

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash igo gaa-izhi-dibaajimotaagooyaan niin indedeyiban.
Mii go dash giiwenh gaa-izhi-naginaawaad iniw aw dewe’igan owidi.
Bangii eta go ogii-kiiwewinaawaan owidi.
Mii dash imaa gaa-onji-ozhi’aawaad iniw dewe’iganan.
minawaa owidi gaa-ni-aabaji’aawaad odi keyaa Minisanaakwaang.
Miinawaa-sh owidi ogii-naganaawaan owidi dibi go owidi oodena, owidi anishinaabe keyaa ezhi-odeniwitoowaad.
Gaawiin dash wiikaa gii-noondanziiwag, ingii-noondanziimin sa go aaniin gaa-izhiwebizid aw dewe’igan iwidi.
Maagizhaa geyaabi ingoji owidi ayaadog.
Mii eta go minik igo ezhi-dibaajimotooninagog naanaagadawendamegiban aaniin gaa-izhiwebizid aw gichi-gete-dewe’igan.
Dibi gaa-izhaagwen.
Ogii-naganaawaan odi bezhig.
“Giinawaa gidaa-ganawenimaawaa” gii-ikidowag.

paragraph.text_eng: Maybe that’s as much as I will tell about them, the old drums, probably. It won’t be thought about as anything negative, that only the good things will come from it (this story), only the good things, that will be thought of as good. And that’s the way I wish, when I was given tobacco. In a good way I make an offering of tobacco to those who accept it from me. That’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Maagizhaa eta go minik eni-dazhimagwaa gete-dewe’igan, maagizhaa.
Gaawiin go gegoo da-inendaagosinoon eta go gakina go gegoo wenizhishing imaa ge-onji-inendaagwak.
Mii iw keyaa iw misiwendamaan gii-pi-miinigooyaan asemaa.
Weweni go gaye mino-asemaakawagwaa ingiw wedaapinigetamawijig.
Mii iw.

paragraph.text_eng: Thank you for this tobacco that you gave me. I shall talk about this. I can only talk about the way that I was raised. I would never imitate someone else’s teaching. I can only use my teachings. And I don’t disbelieve anyone’s way of teaching.

sentence.sent_text: Miigwech awe asemaa gaa-gii-miizhiyan Owe sa inga-dazhindaan.
Onowe eta go gaa-dazhindamaan gegoo mii iwe nakeya’ii gaa-pi-izhi-ombigi’igooyaan.
Gaawiinoon awiiya wiikaa ninaabanootawaasii.
Ningikinoo’amaagoowinan eta go indazhindaanan gaawiin-ge awiiya indaanwetawaasii aaniin wiinawaa gaa-izhi-gikinoo’amawindwaa.

paragraph.text_eng: As a child, this is what I was always told, do not go out at night. Do not go anywhere when it is night.

sentence.sent_text: Owe dash ayi’ii gii-pi-abinoojiiwiyaan, mii go apane gaa-igoowaan, gego niibaashkaaken, Gego ingoji izhaaken owe gii-tibikak.

paragraph.text_eng: So when you think about when it gets dark and the sun sets. It is at this time that the birds stop making their sound, especially the day time birds. This is what I was told, they have settled into sleep. And so was told also not to go out at night (just like the birds). You will run into something but you will not know what it is.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke naanaagadawendaman gii-ani-gashkii-dibikak gii-ani-bangishimod sa go awe giizis.
Mii zhigo gakina ishkwaa-noondaagoziwaad ogowe bineshiinyag gii-giizhigak gaa-noondaagoziwaad.
Mii ko iye gaa-igowaan, aaniishinaa na’iiwag ando-nibaawag.
Mii dash igo ge-niin iye gaa-igowaan, gego, gego niibaashkaaken.
Gegoo giga-bitaakoshkaan giishpin niibaashkaayan gaawiin dash giga-gikendanziin.

paragraph.text_eng: My grandmother was very abrupt with her words. Just when you run into something this is where you begin to not think straight. This is what my grandmother said to me.

sentence.sent_text: Aapiji, aapiji go gii-mamaandaawigiizhwe owe nookomisiban.
Nashke ingoding gegoo bitaakoshkaman mii go ge-ani-izhi-giiwanaadiziyan.
Mii ko gaa-izhid a nookomisiban.

paragraph.text_eng: I would always listen and adhere to her teachings. I would always think carefully about this, why she would say it that way.

sentence.sent_text: Aapiji dash igo ingii-pinzindawaa, ingii-pizindawaa owe gegoo enaajimotawid.
Weweni sa go ingii-naanaagadawendaan iwe, aaniin wenji-ikidod.

paragraph.text_eng: “Later on you will see why I say it this way,” she would say to me.

sentence.sent_text: “Nashke bijiinag giga-ni-waabandaan gegoo,” ingii’ig sa go.

paragraph.text_eng: Take these vehicles, for example, these vehicles that you see, and when you watch them, when you study people (in their cars travelling at night). Then something happens to someone, and maybe they will go off the road. And it is here why something may go wrong.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke ge ogowe aya’aag odaabaanag, odaabaanag gaa-waabamangwaa naanaagajitooyan gegoo naanaagaji’ad sa go awiya.
Mii iwe apii ingoding gegoo ezhiseg owe gemaa-ge bakebizo awiiya.
Mii dash imaa gegoo wenji-maazhi-ayaad ingoding.

paragraph.text_eng: Sometimes, someone may get hurt or bump into someone. I guess this why it is prohibited to travel at night. The bad spirits travel at night time. You do not know when you will bump into that something.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoding wiisagishin awiiya ingoding-gaye obitaakoshkawaan awiiya.
Mii dash iwe iidog gaa-onji-onji iding ji-niibaashkaang.
Maji-aya’aawish babaa-ayaa gii-dibikak.
Gaawiin dash gigikendanziin omaa gii-pitaakoshkaman gegoo.

paragraph.text_eng: Eventually you will begin to get an uneasy feeling. “Why do I feel sickly?” some-one might say to himself. That is why it is said, “Do not travel at night.” There are a lot of beings that travel at night, but we do not see them. This is when you bump into that something, sometimes these beings.

sentence.sent_text: Bijiinag idash giga-ani-gikendaan gegoo ingoding wenji-maazhi-ayaayan.
“Aaniin da naa owe wenji-maanamanji oyaan” ingoding ikido awiiya.
Mii dash iwe gaa-onji-ikidong, “gego niibaashkaaken.” Aapiji baatayiinowag bebaa-ayaawaad gii-tibikak gaawiin dash giwaabamaasiwaanaanig.
Mii dash imaa bitaakoshkang awiiya gegoo, nashke-ge ingoding awiiya ogowe.

paragraph.text_eng: Just as we travel far, we see the animals that got hit by something. It must be here, it must be where this one promibited teaching comes from; perhaps they were told this, these animals that we see. We sometimes see them that got hit, perhaps a deer.

sentence.sent_text: Ingoji waasa gii-bimi-ezhaad awiya, mii imaa waabamangwaa ogowe awesiinyag gii-bitaagoshkaagowaad gegoo.
Mii-dog omaa, mii-dog owe bezhig gaa-onji-onji’iding ge-wiinawaa maawiin igo gegoo gii-inaadogenag.
Ongow wesiinyag gaa-waabamangwaa.
Ingoding giwaabamaanaan gii-pichibizod awe, waawaashkeshi gemaa-ge.

paragraph.text_eng: ’This is the reason why we would contemplate that. Please! Do not travel at night.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash imaa ge-onji-naanaagadawendangiban iwe gegoo.
Daga!
naa ego niibaashkaaken.

paragraph.text_eng: A prohibitive teaching, when you hear this prohibition, when someone says it, this is one of those very highly honored teachings. I am not sure what the white man would call it.

sentence.sent_text: Onji’idim giishpin noondaman iwe onji’idim gii-ikidod awiya mii sa iwe bezhig gichi-gikinoo’amaadiwin.
Mii iwe amanj ezhinikaadamogwen wemitigoozhi.

paragraph.text_eng: If you are told “this command,” you should listen to this. When someone tells you “that is not to be done” is said to someone, that is one of those high commandments.

sentence.sent_text: Giishpin igooyan onji’idim gidaa-bizindaan iwe.
Awiiya wiindamawik “onji’idim gosha iwe gii-inind awiiya mii iwe gichi-gikinoo’amaadiwin bezhig.

paragraph.text_eng: It is the same as when you are to close your curtains at night. That is it, that is yet another one of those teachings. For those who live in a house as for me a long time ago.

sentence.sent_text: Ayi’ii dash mii na bezhigon ayi’ii gii-ji-gibiiga’iged awiiya gii-ani-dibikak.
Mii go iye, mii go iye miinawaa bezhig gikinoo’amaadiwin.
Owe ingoji waakaa’iganing maawiin eyaadog awiya mewinzha niin ayi’ii.

paragraph.text_eng: I was raised in a wigwam. When it was day time you had the flaps open here so that we can see inside, here in our home. This is what my grandmother told me, “Close those flaps. Close the flaps, it is starting to become night.” All she said was, “Close the flaps; the owl will peek in from there.”

sentence.sent_text: Ayi’ii ingii-pi-dazhi-ombigi’igoo wigiwaaming.
Mii dash owe gii-giizhigak aaniish naa ayaawan onowe baakindesidoon imaa wenji-waabiyaan imaa biindig, imaa endaayaan.
Mii dash ko owe gaa-izhid a nookomisiban “daga gibiiga’an iniwe.
Gibiiga’an mii gosha zhigwa ani-dibikak.” Bizaan igo gaa-ikidod “gibiiga’igen gookooko’oo imaa da-onzaabi.”

paragraph.text_eng: So I started thinking, then there was the time that she told me. The reason why I say this, is the owl will peek through there, the reason we put the curtains down, that is the same one.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash ko owe gaa-izhi-naanaagadawendamaan ingoding igo gaa-izhi-wiindamawid owe.
Owe gosha gaa-onji-ikidowaan gookooko’oo omaa da-onzaabi, ayi’ii iidog owe gaa-onji-gibiiga’igeng mii go iye bezhigon.

paragraph.text_eng: “Some spirits travel around at night,” she said. “Sometimes sickness travels at night. If something is left open like the flaps on the wigwam or the blinds on the window, This is how the sickness enters through the open window and how one catches the illness,” she would say.

sentence.sent_text: “Awiiya babaa-ayaa gii-dibikak” gii-ikido “aakoziwin ge ingoding babaa-ayaamagad gii-dibikak.
Giishpin dash owe gegoo gii-baakising gii-baakindesing sa go owe wigiwaam gemaa-ge waasechigan.
Mii omaa ge-onji-biindigemagak owe mii dash iidog gaa-onji-debinigod awiiya owe aakoziwin,” gii-ikido.

paragraph.text_eng: Because it can see you; it can see you inside when you are still sitting up with the light on.

sentence.sent_text: Mii imaa iidog owaabamigon, owaabamigon imaa geyaabi namadabid gii-dibikak gii-waasakonek imaa biindig.

paragraph.text_eng: So she would say to me, “Shut the curtains; close the door. An owl will look in from here.”

sentence.sent_text: Miichko gaa-izhid gibiiga’an, “Gibiiga’an waasechigan gibaakwa’an ishkwaandem.
“Gookooko’oo omaa da-onzaabi.”

paragraph.text_eng: It is a loving way of saying this so that it will not scare anyone.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iwe iidog dibishkoo go nenegaach ikido ji-zegimaasig awiiya’.

paragraph.text_eng: As I grew a little bigger, I was told what she was really talking about; it was the sickness. You might catch an illness if you dont shut your curtains on your window. 22] That is what my one grandmother told me, but I had two grandmothers. Those are the ones that I listen to, their teachings.

sentence.sent_text: Baamaa dash ge-niin nawaj gii-ani-mindidowaan mii’ gii-wiindamaagoowaan aakoziwin sha iye gaa-idamaan.
Aakoziwin giga-debibinigon giishpin gibiiga’anziwan iwe giwaasechigan.
Mii iwe gaa-ikidod bezhigon nookoyiban, nookoyibaniig gii-niizhowag igiwe.
Apane gaa-gii-naanaagozotawagwaa gegoo ezhi-gikinoo’amaagewaad.

paragraph.text_eng: First of all, I’m going to talk a little here. My name is Zhingwewegaabaw. My late father; I was told, he told me what had happened here with those, those young ones.

sentence.sent_text: Kawe maa indaa-giigid omaa bangii.
Zhingwewegaabaw indizhinikaaz.
Ya’aw akiwenziiyiban, gii-wiindamaagooyaan, gii-wiindamawid o’ow gaa-pi-izhiwebiziwaad agiw, agiw sa aya’aansag.

paragraph.text_eng: See, long ago it is here they lived, long ago before the white man arrived. There was an old man sitting in his wigwam, and a little boy. The old man says to him, “Don’t be playing outside here at night. It isn’t just you playing there. You are playing with a different being.” That little boy didn’t say a thing. When they went to go play there, it was almost night when he told him, “Don’t play there after the sun has gone down.”

sentence.sent_text: Ke maa mewinzha mii omaa sa gii-taawaad mewinzha dabwaa-dagoshing aw Waabishkizid.
Ke a’aw akiwenzii maa gii-namadabid imaa owiigiwaaming, ke ya’aw gwiiwizens gii-inigod iniw akiwenziiyan, “Gego maa dazhitaakegon omaa yo’ow sa da-ni-dibikak, Gaawiin eta go giineta gidazhitaasiin.
Awiya bakaan giwiiji’aa.” Ke gaawiin gegoo gii-ikidosiin aw gwiiwizens.
Gii-maajaawaad wii-o-dazhitaawaad.
Gegaa go gii-ni-dibikad, mii gaa-igod aniw, “Gego dazhiitaaken yo’ow sa ni-bangishimod a’aw, ya’aw sa manidoo.”

paragraph.text_eng: So that boy and some other kids were sitting around near a big tree. And then they asked, “What should we do? Is there anything for us to play here?”

sentence.sent_text: Ke ya’aw gwiiwizens miinawaa aanind agiw aya’aansag iwidi gii-nanaamadabiwaad yo’ow sa chi-mitig.
Ke dash omaa gii-gagswedwewaad, “Wegonen dash ge-doodamang?
Gegoo na omaa gidaa-dazhitaamin?”

paragraph.text_eng: And then one little girl says, “We should hide; you guys should go over there to hide.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish aw bezhig ikwezens ikido, “Gidaa-gaazomin, yo’ow sa oodi keyaa ingoji gidaa-izhaam da-o-gaazooyeg.”

paragraph.text_eng: And then when they went and hid, that little girl went and hid in that big tree that was standing there. And then those boys and girls came back to where they had been standing before asking, “Where is that little girl? Why is she not finding us?”

sentence.sent_text: Ke dash gii-kaazowaad, ke ya’aw ikwezens gii-o-gaazod imaa chi-mitig gaa-niibawid.
Ke ya’aw gwiiwizensag miinawaa ge ikwezensag, gii-pi-izhaawaad omaa mii omaa sa gii-pi-niibawiwaad gagwedwewaad; “Aandish aw ikwezens?
Aaniin dash mekaagosiwiyang?”

paragraph.text_eng: They did not find that little girl.

sentence.sent_text: Gaawiin ogii-mikaasiwaanaan aw, ya’aw sa ikwezens gii-wiindamaagewaad.

paragraph.text_eng: When they told that old man and some others who had lived there, they looked every place. “We didn’t find that little girl.”

sentence.sent_text: Ke dash chi-akiwenzii miinawaa aanind agiw gaa-taawaad imaa mii omaa sa gii-taawaad, kina ingoji gii-izhi-inaabiwag.
“Mii go gaawiin ngii-mikaasiwaanaan a’aw ikwezens.”

paragraph.text_eng: So then those little ones were going home, that old man told them, “Don’t play outside at night.” And then that little boy, he didn’t know either where that little girl had gone.

sentence.sent_text: Ke-sh agiw, agiw sa aya’aansag gii-ni-giiwe’wenzii gii-inigowaad, “Gego dazhitaakegon omaa ni-dibikak.” Ke dash aw gwiiwizens, mii go gaye wiin gii-inendang gaawiin ogikendanziin ya’aw sa ikwezens gaa-ni-izhaad.

paragraph.text_eng: When he was a little boy he would remember that little girl every now and then. When he had become a man, that boy got married. And that man too had a baby. And so as that man began to get old, and his children also began to get big, that man would from time to time think about what had happened to that little girl.

sentence.sent_text: Ke ya'aw gii-ni-gwiiwizensiwiwid aaningodinong oggi-minkwenimaan iniw ikwezensan.
Ke-sh aw gwiiwizens gegaa gii-ininiwid gii-wiidiged.

Ke dash a’aw mii go gaye win a’aw anini gii-ayaawaad aniw biibiiyensan, Mii go gaye wiin aw inini azhigwa gegaa go gii-ni-akiwenziiwid ke dash aniw oniijaanisan mii go gaye wiinawaa gii-ni-mindidowaad, Aaningodinong a’aw ya’aw sa inini gii-inenimaad aniw ikwezensan aw gaa-izhiwebizinid.

paragraph.text_eng: And as his kids too became men, that elder was getting white hair; he too was an old man. Thereafter, one of that man’s children, he too had babies of his own, and they too began to get big.

sentence.sent_text: Ke-sh gaye wiin aniw oniijaanisan gii-ni-ininiwiwaad, ke akiwenzii gii-ni-waabishkindibed gaye wiin, gii-akiwenziiyiwi aw.
Ke dash aw inini bezhig aniw oniijaanisan, Ke mii go gaye wiin gii-ayaawaad aniw obiibiiyensim, ke-sh agiw gaye wiinawaa gii-ni-mindidowaad.

paragraph.text_eng: And see, they too were playing outside here, and then their dad he also said it, “Don’t play there when the sun goes down, after the sun has gone down.”

sentence.sent_text: Miish ge, shke dash gaye wiinawaa wii-tazhitaawag omaa, ke dash iniw obaabaayan mii gaye wiin gaa-ikidod, “Gego owidi dazhitaaken gaye dazhitaasiin owidi ni-bangishimod, ni-bangishimod a’aw manidoo.”

paragraph.text_eng: See they played there, and that little boy also said, “Please, please let’s hide on him.”

sentence.sent_text: Ke dash, gii-tazhitaawag owidi mii go gaye wiin gaa-ikidod aw gwiiwizens, “Daga, daga gaazootawaadaa aw.”

paragraph.text_eng: Then that little girl said, “Yup, you all should hide on him, all of you.”

sentence.sent_text: Ikwezens miish gaa-ikidod aw kwezens gii-ikido, “Eyanh’ gidaa-gaazoonaawaa, ya’aw giinawaa.”

paragraph.text_eng: See then that little girl sat down by a tree. That old lady came around the corner. That old lady had white hair. That little boy said, “Where do you come from?”

sentence.sent_text: “Ke dash aw ikwezens omaa namadabid omaa a’aw mitig,” Dennis Jones.
Keyaa bi-zaagiwed aw gichi-mindimooyenhwi.
Waabishkindibe aw mindimooyenh.
Ya’aw gwiiwizens ikido, “Aandish wenjibaayan?”

paragraph.text_eng: That old lady said, “Oh I’ve come a long ways; I don’t even know which way.” So then that old lady said, “I’m tired; I want to go rest over there.” Then that old lady went over there.

sentence.sent_text: Mindimooyenh ikido, “Oyih, gonezh imbaa-ayaa owidi keyaa gaawiin ngikendanziin.
Ke dash aw chi-mindimooyenh ikido, “Indayekoz oodi keyaa niwii-o-anweb.” Miish iwidi keyaa gaa-ni-izhaad chi-mindimooyenh.

paragraph.text_eng: So then those boys, when they went home, that old man was sitting in his "Wigwam. He was sitting there too, then that little boy says, “Poppa, do you know we sawan old lady come from behind the tree?”

sentence.sent_text: Ke dash agiw gwiiwizensag gii-ni-giiwewaad, namadabid imaa owiigiwaaming ya’aw chi-akiwenzii omaa namadabid gaye wiin.
Miish aw gwiiwizens ikidod, “Paapaa, gigikendaan na ingii-waabamaanaan a’aw chi-mindimooyenh owidi bi-zaagewed mitig?”

paragraph.text_eng: The old man thought, and went and looked at the little boy to ask him, “Where?”

sentence.sent_text: Ayinendang akiwenzii, o-inaabimaad aniw gwiiwizensan gagwejimaad, “Aandi?”

paragraph.text_eng: “Over there, where we play.”

sentence.sent_text: “Iwidi, dazhitaayaang.”

paragraph.text_eng: “Ooh,” thought that old man. He then remembered when they had lost that little girl long ago.

sentence.sent_text: “Ooo,” inendang a’aw chi-akiwenzii.
Mii go ge gii-te-mikwendang gii-wani’aawaad aniw ikwezensan mewinzha.

paragraph.text_eng: When those Anishinaabe who lived there returned, they went over to the edge of the woods to look around, and they didn’t find that old lady.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-izhaawaad iwidi mizizaakwaakwaag iwidi paa-andawabanjigewaad gii-ni-azhegiiwewaad iwidi agiw dash Anishinaabeg gii-taawaad mii go gaa gii-mikawaasiin aw mindimooyenh.

paragraph.text_eng: That old man that was sitting in his wigwam. “I’m going to tell you again, don’t play outside when the sun has gone down. See it isn’t just you; it isn’t just you guys that are playing there, a different being is playing with you.”

sentence.sent_text: Ya’aw chi-akiwenzii imaa namadabid owiigiwaaming.
“Giga-wiindamoon minawaa, gego dazhitaakegon yaw sa manidoo ni-bangishimod.
Ke gaawiin giin eta gaawiin giinetawaa gidazhitaasiim iwidi, bakaan awiya giwiiji’igowaa.”

paragraph.text_eng: That is all I know about that one. That’s it.

sentence.sent_text: Miish eta go minik o’ow giigidowin ezhi-gikendamaan, Mii iw.

paragraph.text_eng: Ok, ok thank you, thanks for the tobacco.

sentence.sent_text: Ahaaaw, ahaw sa miinawaa miigwech awe asemaa.

paragraph.text_eng: I shall talk about sleeping with grandmother. I am not talking about our biological grandmother, this one here on the earth; some may call her our earth mother.

sentence.sent_text: Owe ayi’ii inga-dazhindaan wiipemang awe gookomisinaan.
Gaawanoon awe geget igo gookomis owe mitakamik gookomisinaan gimaamaanaan ge aanind odizhinikaanaawaan.

paragraph.text_eng: This is one of them that I was always told about, here.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iye miinawaa bezhig gaa-pi-waawiindamaagowaan apane, omaa.

paragraph.text_eng: As we lived here in the wigwam, we always slept here on the bare ground. We slept right on the ground, and my grandma would say, “Well let’s go to bed and sleep with our grandmother,” she would say. She was referring to our maker, the maker of Turtle Island. This is where you dream when you are there. It is like sleeping with your grandma when one sleeps on the ground.

sentence.sent_text: Gii-taa-aang omaa ayi’iing wigiwaaming, mii go omaa gaa-nibaa-aang mitakamig.
Mitakamik ingii-izhi-nibaamin, mii dash ko eyii kaa-ikidod awe nooko-iiban, “Haw daga nibaadaa wiipemaadaa gookomisinaan” ikido.
Miidash inowe gaa-inaad owe gaa-gii-ozhitood owe mikinaakom, imaa gaa-daaying Mikinaakominis.
Mii-dog omaa wenji-ayaad awiiya wenji-bawaajiged owe gii.
Dibishkoo wiipemaad awiiya iniw okoomisan owe mitakamig gii-nibaad awiiya.

paragraph.text_eng: Sometimes some will sleep with the balsam fir as a pillow; this is where one of the teachings come from. You will have good dreams if you use the balsam fir as your pillow. Even the inside of the wigwam was covered with balsam fir, and we walked on them inside there in our home. We never had boards, and they used trees to make our wigwam. We used cedar bark and birch bark to cover our lodge along with many other things. We used the things that we got from our Creator, the maker of our earth.

sentence.sent_text: Ishke ge ingoding aam zhingobii eta go awiiya odapikweshimona’ ingoding mii imaa miinawaa bezhig ayaa iwe ayi’ii gikinoo’amaadiwin.
Ge aapichi giga-gichi-ayinaabandam owe apikweshimoyan igiwe zhingobiik nashke ge omaa biindik mii eta go gaa-ina’.
Gaa-inateg owe zhingobiig ingii-apishimomin zhingobiig imbabaa-datakokaanaanaanig omaa biindig omaa endaayaang.
Gaawiin wiikaa nabagisagoog ingii-ayaawaasiwaanaanik awedi gaye mitigoon ogii-wigiwaamikaagenaawaan.
Ingoding ge wanagekwag ingii-apakwemin wiigwaas-abakwaan miinawaa oooo niibiyo gegoo aapiji.
Ingii-aabajitoomin owe gaa-gii-izhi-miininang owe gaa-ozhitood owe gidakiiminaan.

paragraph.text_eng: Since as I think back, how we live today, I too live differently; nowadays I live in a house.

sentence.sent_text: Noongom idash iko naanaagadawendam, noongom gaa-izhigeyeng bakaan mii go ge-niin owe bakaan indizhige noongom waakaa’iganing indayaa noongom.

paragraph.text_eng: Here in my house, when I look at the walls, I do not see any wigwam trees. As I look at the ceiling, I don’t see the top opening of the wigwam only, only, whatever it is, it looks like paper that has been painted over.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke awe gii-ayaang endaa-aa owe aasamisag imaa inaabiyaan gaawiin gegoo abanzhiin niwaabandanziinan.

Miinawaa owe idi ishpiming inaabiyaan gaawiin gegoo anakwa’igan idi niwaabandanziin mii eta go onowe, awegodogwen owe dinowa indigo, indigo owe ayi’ii indigo mazina’iganish owe gaa-zhizhoobii’igaadeg ezhinamaan-ko.

paragraph.text_eng: As for where I sleep, there is a bed there; I have a bed there where I sleep. This is where I sleep, up above the ground, maybe two or three feet above the ground. I sleep here; I no longer sleep with my grandmother, while she still sleeps over there on the bare ground.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa iwidi izhi-nibaayaan nibewin, nibewin iwidi ate nibewin idi nibaayaan.
Mii imaa izhi-nibaayaan waasa ishpiming ingoding booshke, ingoding maagizhaa niizhomizid, nisomizid, apiichi ishpiming.
Nibaa owe gaawiin niwiipemaasii awe nookomis waasa iwidi, waase gewiin iwidi izhi-nibaa mitakamik.

paragraph.text_eng: Once I heard an elder say, it was one of the elders, just recently. This is why we are having a hard time to achieve the things we want. Our grandmother can no longer hear us or see us where we are sleeping. She cannot connect with us to share or give us a dream because we no longer sleep with her.

sentence.sent_text: Mii dash ko awe gaa-izhi-noondawagiban sa go awiiya ekidod bezhig igo gichi-anishinaabe gaa-noondawag noomaya igo.
Mii-goshinaa owe gaa-onji-aya-aa gaa-onji-boyshkamang gegoo gaa-onji-gashkitoosiwang gegoo.
Gaawiin geyaabi gide-bitaakosiinaan awe gookomisinaan gaawiin sa go giwaabamigosiinaan awe aandi ezhi-nibaaying.
Gaawiin ge gibeshwanji’igosiinaan awe ji-miininang owe bawaajigan gii-ikidong aanishinaa gaawiin, gaawiin giwiipemaasiwaanaan.

paragraph.text_eng: This is what I heard the elder say even some people sleep way upstairs, what is called the top floor. This is one of the things that we are losing/dropping today.

sentence.sent_text: Mii iw gaa-izhi-noondawagiban awiiya booshke naa aanind ingoji waa-aasa iwidi ishpiming nibaawag ogidigamigong gii-izhinikaadeg.
Mii iwe miinawaa eniwanitooyang noongom.

paragraph.text_eng: And then there is one that I heard telling and she also asked me to make the leather moccasins these pointed toe moccasins. That is how they were made a long time ago, the old time moccasins used to be pointy toed. This is what she was asking of me to make for her, that one friend of mine.

sentence.sent_text: Miinawaa go bezhig awiiya ingii-noondawaaban dibaajimod awe ingii-pii-anoonig sa go ayi’ii chi-ozhitoowaan ayi’iing bashkweginwekizinan gaa-idamingonowe ayi’ii jiibwiingwekizinan.
Aanishinaa mii iwe gaa-izhinaagokin mewinzha, mewinzha iniwe makizinan jiibwiingweyaawan.
Mii dash iniwe gaa-pi-anoozhid awe bezhig indinawemaagan.

paragraph.text_eng: She shared a dream with me. She dreamt in this way, Where are all the Indians? They no longer leave their footprints on the earth. Nobody else wears moccasins especially those, the way the old time moccasin use to look like. I never see the footprints any more.” That is what her dream told her, the one that asked me to make her those pointed toe moccasins.

sentence.sent_text: Ingii-wiindamaag idash iwe obawaajigan.
Miidog awe gaa-inaabandamogobanen aaniin dinandinaa ongow anishinaabeg?
Gaawiin gosha geyaabi, gaawiin gosha geyaabi bimikawesiiwag omaa mitakamik.
Gaawiin awiiya geyaabi obashkweginwekizinsii aapiji go onowe, mewinzha bashkweginwekizinan gaa-izhinaagokin.
Gaawiin wiikaa indookawi’aasii noongom.” Mii i’miidog owe gaa-inaabandang awe gaa-gii-pi-anoozhid inowe zhiibwiingwekizinan izhinikaadewan i’iw.

paragraph.text_eng: This is one of the things that I wish could be revitalized (the making of the pointed toe moccasin)and then this animal, the animal is very honored to see his leather being used to make jackets from his hide; this is another one of those teachings.

sentence.sent_text: Mii awe miinawaa bezhig ambegish ani-maamookoshkaag indinendam iko miinawaa go awe awesii, aapiji iinzan minwendam awe gii-yaabadad-inig gegoo owe ge-ezhi-ombiinsikowaaganid dash obashkgwegin owe awesii mii iye miinawaa bezhig dibaajimowin.

chapter.eng_title: How the Anishinaabe Overcame Difficulties Long Ago

paragraph.text_eng: I’ve been asked to come here today to do some speaking and tell some stories. But I don’t know what it is I should tell about here. All I know is what those Anishinaabeg did long ago, these ones that raised me.

sentence.sent_text: Ingii-kagwejimigoo omaa da-bi-izhaayaan omaa da-bi-gaagiigidoyaan da-dibaajimoyaan gegoo.
Gaawiin-sh ngikendanziin awegonen ge-dibaajimotawaambaan omaa.
Mii eta go ingiw Anishinaabeg mewinzha eko-gikenimagwaa gaa-pi-izhichigewaad ongow go gaa-nitaawigi’ijig.

paragraph.text_eng: Long ago there wasnt any work, not like there is today for the Anishinaabe to make his living. Those ones that raised me were always busy doing something. You see, they say we were poor. But I didn’t know that we were poor; we always ate. We were never in need of food to eat or clothes to wear.

sentence.sent_text: Nashke gaawiin, gaawiin gii-ayaamagasinoon mewinzha anokiiwin noongom ezhi-anokiid aw Anishinaabe aw bemaadizid.
Ingiw gaa-nitaawigi’ijig apane gii-ojaanimiziwag gegoo gii-izhichigewaad.
Aaniish naa ge ingii-kidimaagizimin giiwenh.
Gaawiin dash ingii-kikendanziimin gii-kidimaagiziyaang apane ingii-wiisinimin.
Gaawiin wiikaa ingii-manezisiimin wegonen waa-mijjiyaang miinawaa wegonen waa-piizikamaang.

paragraph.text_eng: Oh that old man that raised me used to do all kinds of things. I would go with him in the woods; I must of been five-years-old, maybe four, or six. When fall came around he would be out trapping. He did all sorts of stuff. Also he would find work cutting timber once in a while. That is one thing the Anishinaabe was good at; long ago they always cut timber. They were paid real cheap for cutting timber,.06 cents for each 8-foot log that was given, that were stacked up when they cut timber. All the Anishinaabe men cut timber. Even the women all worked too, going around making money, supporting their children well. That’s what they did all winter long, cut timber. They went all over to various places to do it. You see, some of those Anishinaabeg from Lake Lena even went to Montana to go around logging. At that time, indeed it was very far; it is very far to that place called Montana. That is what some of them did that over here, some of them went up north to the place called Ely to cut timber over there. They made their little villages around there like that all winter.

sentence.sent_text: Oonh ko akiwenzii gaa-nitaawigi’id anooj gii-izhichige ko.
Ingii-paa-wiijiwaa imaa megwayaak ganabaj gii-naano-biboonagiziyaan maagizhaa niiwiin maagizhaa ningodwaaso-biboonagiziwaanen.
Zhigwa ani-dagwaagig gii-paa-wanii’ige ko.
Anooj gegoo gii-izhichige.
Miinawaa gaye gii-mikwanokiid aaningodinong gii-kiishka’aakwe.
Mii iw bezhig Anishinaabe gaa-nitaa-izhichiged mewinzha apane gii-kiishka’aakwewag.

Ogii-waanda-wenjida-diba’amawaawaan dash wiin igo giishka’aakwewaad nashke ingoji go ningodwaaso-zhooniyaans, ishwaasozid dekoozid aw mitig izhi-miinaawag gii-okwaakoshimawaad ge gii-kiishka’aakwewaad.
Akina go Anishinaabe gii-kiishka’aakwewag ingiw ininiwag.
Wawaaj igo ge ingiw ikwewag gii-paa-anokiiwag, baa-zhooniiyaakewaad wiin nitaa-bami’aawaad iniw oniijaanisiwaan.
Mii gaa-izhichigewaad gabe-biboon gii-kiishka’aakwewaad.
Anooj gii-paa-izhaawag gii-izhichigewaad.
Nashke ge, biinish igo idi ge ingiw aanind ingiw Anishinaabeg omaa wenjibaawaad imaa Aazhoomoog biinish oodi Montana gii-paa-izhaawag gii-paa-giishka’aakwewaad.
Mii apii geget gii-waasawad waasawad iw Montana izhinikaadeg.
Miinawaa-sh omaa aanind gaa-izhichigewaad.
Miinawaa-sh ge omaa ongow eyaajig oodi keyaa giiwedinong idi Ely izhinikaadeg mii iwidi gii-paa-giishka’aakwewaad gii-paa-odenaawensikewaad iwidi dibishkoo gabe-biboon.
